In high school, one cited study reported 86% uptake for surface-level feedback (e.g., grammar) but only 32% uptake at the meaning level; in a large primary/middle school dataset, 48% of 14,236 learners made no changes at all after AI feedback. These findings indicate that AI tools may help with some writing revisions but do not reliably improve deeper writing outcomes without strong instructional support.
finding.measure: Revision uptake / changes made in response to AI-generated writing feedback; surface-level vs meaning-level revision
finding.study_size: n=14,236 (Jansen et al., 2025 cited); high school sample size not_reported (Yu and Xie, 2025 cited)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that learner engagement with feedback is a central determinant of whether AI feedback is useful, but many younger students do not sufficiently process or use that feedback. It reports that 48% of learners in a large dataset made no revision changes after AI feedback, and that uptake was especially low for meaning-level revisions, implying limited self-regulation and persistence in feedback use.
finding.measure: Engagement with feedback / learner uptake during revision

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes that productive revision depends on critical engagement, metacognition, and the ability to evaluate which feedback is useful. It reports that advanced university writers can use AI feedback frequently when they engage critically, whereas primary and secondary students often lack the deeper processing needed to turn feedback into effective revision, suggesting mixed effects on durable skills.
finding.measure: Critical engagement / metacognitive processing of feedback during revision

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can reduce the burden of providing timely, personalized feedback for teachers because tools can deliver instant comments on student texts. However, it also argues that this efficiency gain is undermined if students do not use the feedback, so the operational benefit is conditional rather than definitive.
finding.measure: Teacher feedback workload / timeliness and scalability of feedback delivery

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in intelligent tutoring systems toward sustainable education: a systematic review
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (Elementary, High School, University, Graduate, General)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic review of how artificial intelligence and information technology are incorporated into intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) to support sustainable education. Rather than testing a single intervention, the authors synthesize 29 studies focused on real educational settings and examine the main challenges, AI methods, pedagogical scenarios, outcomes, and future directions associated with AI-embedded and AI-supported tutoring systems.

The review centers on predictive analytics, learning-behavior analysis, dropout prevention, personalization, instructor support, and explainable AI. The included studies span multiple education levels, but most are in higher education; a smaller subset includes high school cases. Across the reviewed literature, the dominant pattern is that AI/ITS systems are used to predict performance and identify learner behaviors with generally high predictive accuracy, while some studies report improved engagement, participation, or learning after intervention or personalization. However, the review also emphasizes limitations such as data sparsity, feature-extraction challenges, portability issues, and concerns about fairness, transparency, and trust. The authors conclude that future work should strengthen explainability, human-centered design, educational theory alignment, and broader, more generalizable datasets.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI-supported tutoring systems were mainly used for performance prediction and learning analytics rather than direct measurement of a specific subject-matter gain. The review reports that many models achieved high prediction accuracy (e.g., 10 studies), and a smaller number of studies reported improved learning performance after interventions or personalized feedback, but the paper does not pool effect sizes for academic achievement.
finding.measure: Predicted learner performance; learning performance outcomes reported in the included studies

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies examined engagement, dropout prevention, emotions, and satisfaction as outcomes of AI/ITS use. The review reports that learner participation improved with early dropout notification in 5 studies, engagement was enhanced in some cases, and one study reported increased satisfaction; however, the review does not provide pooled quantitative effect sizes.
finding.measure: Engagement, dropout risk/participation, emotions, satisfaction surveys or system logs

finding.finding_summary: The review includes learning-behavior analysis and adaptation/personalization outcomes that are adjacent to durable skills such as self-regulation and metacognitive monitoring. Two studies specifically evaluated self-regulated learning improvement, but the review does not report a pooled effect and the evidence is limited to a small subset of the included literature.
finding.measure: Self-regulated learning surveys and learning behavior analytics
finding.study_size: n=2 studies for self-regulation outcome within n=29 reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion of the review is that AI/ITS systems can reduce teacher workload by automating prediction, monitoring, explanation, and some intervention-related tasks. The paper also notes that several studies used AI to support instructors with decision-making and reminders, suggesting improved operational efficiency, but it does not report a pooled quantitative effect.
finding.measure: Instructor support, monitoring, decision-making, automated reminders, workload-related process outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI-enabled tutoring systems can support sustainable education by improving access, personalization, and data-driven decision-making, while also raising institutional issues around privacy, fairness, transparency, and policy. These are synthesized as system-level implications rather than measured impact estimates, so no pooled quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy/security, fairness, transparency, and sustainability implications

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in language instruction: impact on English learning achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examines whether AI-mediated language instruction improves EFL learners’ English learning achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning compared with traditional instruction. The paper was motivated by growing interest in AI tools for language learning and by a gap in evidence on how such tools affect both achievement and learner dispositions in EFL settings.

The intervention used Duolingo as the AI-mediated platform and compared it against traditional teacher-led instruction. Two intact university classes in mainland China (n=60 total; 30 experimental, 30 control) participated in a 10-week study. Both groups completed pre- and post-tests of English achievement, motivation, and self-regulation; the experimental group also completed interviews (n=14) about their experiences.

Quantitative results showed that the AI-mediated group outperformed the control group on overall English achievement, with improvements reported across grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing. The AI group also showed stronger gains in L2 motivation and self-regulated learning. Qualitative findings suggested that learners valued the platform’s personalized feedback, flexibility, engagement, and anxiety-reducing features, and these experiences helped explain the positive quantitative outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: AI-mediated instruction significantly improved English learning achievement relative to traditional instruction, and the paper reports gains across grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing. The post-test achievement scores were higher in the experimental group (M=73.86, SD=15.26) than in the control group (M=61.11, SD=14.97) after the 10-week intervention, with a significant group effect (F(1,58)=94.35, p<0.001, η2=0.81) and a significant group × time interaction (F(1,58)=8.37, p<0.001, η2=0.23).
finding.measure: English achievement test covering grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing

finding.finding_summary: AI-mediated instruction improved L2 motivation relative to traditional instruction. Post-test motivation was higher in the experimental group (M=3.89, SD=1.8) than in the control group (M=3.35, SD=1.5), and the group × time interaction was significant (F(1,58)=7.43, p=0.04, η2=0.11), indicating differential gains attributable to the AI-based intervention.
finding.measure: 16-item L2 motivation scale (attitude, self-confidence, personal use)

finding.finding_summary: AI-mediated instruction improved self-regulated learning more than traditional instruction. Post-test self-regulation scores were higher in the experimental group (M=3.94, SD=0.73) than in the control group (M=3.37, SD=0.76), with a significant group effect (F(1,58)=11.36, p<0.001, η2=0.64) and a significant group × time interaction (F(1,58)=7.68, p<0.001, η2=0.38).
finding.measure: Self-Regulation Questionnaire (SRQ)

finding.finding_summary: The study also directly discusses self-regulated learning strategies such as goal setting, planning, monitoring, and time management, which are durable skills. Quantitatively, the AI group improved more than the control group on the SRQ (post-test M=3.94 vs. 3.37), and interview data indicated that learners felt empowered to manage their learning more autonomously.
finding.measure: Self-Regulation Questionnaire (SRQ) and interview themes on autonomy/goal-setting/time management

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.population: Junior High School (Gymnasium) students, age 15, with migrant/refugee background learning German as a foreign language
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether ChatGPT can function as a feedback tool to improve second-language writing, with a particular focus on students from refugee/migrant backgrounds who may face additional language barriers. The paper is motivated by the emerging interest in ChatGPT for education and by the need for more evidence on how AI tools might support language learning in socially vulnerable, multilingual classrooms.

The intervention took place in a junior high school in Patras, Greece, with 8 students aged 15 who were learning German as a foreign language. Students first wrote a personal email in German; the researchers then used ChatGPT to revise the texts specifically for grammar and vocabulary. Students reviewed the improved version and later wrote a second, similar email on a related topic, intending to transfer the revised language into their own production.

The main findings were descriptive and showed increases in total words, unique words, and average words per sentence from the first to the revised writing samples. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may be a promising language-learning support tool for foreign language writing, especially for students with refugee/migrant backgrounds, but they stress that the evidence is preliminary because the study used a very small sample, short duration, and no control group or inferential statistical testing.

finding.finding_summary: The study found improvements in foreign language writing after ChatGPT-based feedback on grammar and vocabulary. Across 8 junior high school students, total words increased by an average of 38%, unique words increased (average mean of 19.1 more unique words per student), and average words per sentence increased by approximately 42% from pre- to post-intervention writing samples.
finding.measure: Foreign language writing text characteristics: total words, unique words, average words per sentence

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence technologies and applications for language learning and teaching
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Computer Assisted Language Learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (literature review of L2/FL language learning and teaching studies; includes K-12, undergraduate, and adult studies)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a literature review of artificial intelligence technologies and applications in second and foreign language learning and teaching, with an emphasis on computer-assisted language learning (CALL). Rather than evaluating a single intervention, it surveys research on seven AI-related categories: natural language processing, data-driven learning, automated writing evaluation, computerized dynamic assessment, intelligent tutoring systems, automatic speech recognition, and chatbots.

The paper synthesizes common trends and findings across studies published in CALL-related journals and books from 2010–2022. It highlights that AI tools often support language learning through feedback, personalization, and increased learner autonomy, but the evidence base is uneven across tools and contexts. The authors note that writing is the most commonly studied skill in AI-related CALL research, and they call for more rigorous, theory-driven, and context-sensitive research.

For writing-related AI tools, the review reports mixed but often positive findings: some automated writing evaluation systems improved grammar, lexical richness, or genre-specific features, while others showed no significant gains unless combined with teacher feedback or other supports. The review also suggests that effectiveness may depend on learner proficiency, feedback specificity, teacher preparation, and whether the AI tool is paired with human instruction. Because this is a review article, it does not provide a new experimental effect size, but it summarizes a broad research base relevant to comparative effectiveness questions.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI-supported writing tools such as automated writing evaluation (AWE), corpus-based data-driven learning, and related feedback systems often improved writing-related outcomes, but results were not uniform. Examples cited include improved grammar use and lexical richness for 31 Japanese EFL learners using Grammarly, improved genre-specific linguistic features for 13 Chinese EFL learners using a genre-based AWE system, and no significant improvement in some causal-writing tasks without stronger pedagogical support.
finding.measure: Writing quality, grammatical accuracy, lexical richness, genre-specific writing features, revision performance
finding.study_size: multiple studies; study sizes ranged from n=2 to n=117 in cited primary studies

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI tools were often associated with more positive learner attitudes, increased autonomy, and motivational benefits in language learning. For example, the review notes that AWE and ASR tools supported learner autonomy and that chatbot and ASR-based activities could reduce anxiety and encourage willingness to communicate.
finding.measure: Learner attitudes, autonomy, motivation, willingness to communicate, anxiety
finding.study_size: multiple studies; sample sizes varied across cited studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that some AI-supported activities promoted skills such as critical thinking, self-correction, and metalinguistic awareness, though findings were context-dependent. For instance, chatbot use before group discussion increased student output and supported awareness of critical thinking skills, and some AWE/DDL studies encouraged self-identification of errors and learner training for strategic tool use.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metalinguistic awareness, self-correction, collaborative discussion output
finding.study_size: multiple studies; sample sizes varied across cited studies

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes evidence that ASR and chatbot tools can improve speaking and pronunciation outcomes, but effects vary by tool and learner needs. Examples include improved L2 speaking proficiency with Alexa, better pronunciation and receptive vocabulary with ASR-based websites compared to a control group, and greater performance for a voice-based chatbot than a text-based chatbot or face-to-face condition in speaking tasks.
finding.measure: Speaking performance, pronunciation accuracy, receptive vocabulary
finding.study_size: multiple studies; sample sizes ranged from small case studies to larger classroom studies

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that AI tools could reduce teacher workload or streamline assessment and feedback in some contexts, especially through automated evaluation and diagnostic systems. However, it also emphasizes that teacher mediation and training remain important, and several studies found that the tools were not sufficient on their own for strong instructional gains.
finding.measure: Feedback efficiency, automated assessment, teacher support needs
finding.study_size: multiple studies; sample sizes varied across cited studies

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI will continue to be integrated into language education and that institutions and educators need to prepare for pedagogical, technical, and ethical implications. It also notes that teacher training, implementation support, and responsible use are recurring institutional issues across the literature.
finding.measure: Teacher preparation, implementation readiness, ethical and institutional considerations

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT as an academic support tool on the academic performance among students: The mediating role of learning motivation
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Social, Humanity, and Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether use of ChatGPT as an academic support tool is associated with better academic performance among secondary school students, and whether learning motivation explains that relationship. The authors frame ChatGPT as a conversational AI tool that can provide personalized explanations, immediate feedback, and accessible academic help, potentially improving students' engagement and achievement.

The study used a mixed-method triangulation design with 178 students from a secondary school in Lal-lo, Cagayan, Philippines. Participants were purposively sampled from junior and senior high school, and data were collected with a researcher-developed questionnaire measuring ChatGPT use as academic support and learning motivation, along with academic performance. The quantitative analysis used mediation/path analysis, and the qualitative responses were used to contextualize the results.

Results showed that ChatGPT had a significant positive association with learning motivation, and learning motivation had a significant positive association with academic performance. The indirect effect of ChatGPT on academic performance through learning motivation was significant (β=0.4196, p=0.001; reported as a medium effect, f2=0.238), while the direct effect of ChatGPT on academic performance was not significant (β=0.5994, p=0.706). The authors conclude that learning motivation fully mediates the relationship, suggesting ChatGPT improves performance primarily by increasing students' motivation to learn rather than by a direct performance effect.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT use was positively associated with learning motivation among high school students. The path from ChatGPT to learning motivation was statistically significant (β=0.0827, p<.001), with a large reported effect size (f2=0.6579), indicating that students who used ChatGPT reported higher motivation to learn.
finding.measure: Learning motivation questionnaire scale

finding.finding_summary: Learning motivation was positively associated with academic performance, and the indirect effect of ChatGPT on academic performance through motivation was significant (β=0.4196, p=0.001). The study reports that this mediation effect was medium in size (f2=0.238), while the direct effect of ChatGPT on academic performance was not significant (β=0.5994, p=0.706), indicating full mediation by learning motivation.
finding.measure: Academic performance questionnaire/scale

finding.finding_summary: The ChatGPT scale included items related to critical thinking, analytical skills, problem-solving, and collaborative learning, and the authors interpret ChatGPT as supporting these durable skills. However, these were not analyzed as separate outcomes; they were embedded within the academic support construct rather than reported as standalone measured effects.
finding.measure: ChatGPT as academic support tool scale items related to critical thinking, analytical skills, and collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence (AI)-integrated educational applications and college students’ creativity and academic emotions: students and teachers’ perceptions and attitudes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examines how AI-integrated educational applications affect college students’ creativity and academic emotions, and how both students and teachers perceive the benefits and challenges of these tools. The paper responds to a broader concern that AI in education may simultaneously support learning and introduce new constraints, especially around creativity, engagement, anxiety, and fairness.

The authors conducted qualitative semi-structured interviews with 23 participants at Wenzhou University (15 students and 8 teachers), followed by a quantitative survey of 120 students and 30 teachers. The study focused on AI educational components such as adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring systems, natural language processing applications, collaborative learning platforms, and predictive analytics. Interview data were thematically coded into challenges and merits; survey data were summarized descriptively.

Findings suggest a dual-edged impact. Participants reported that AI can constrain creativity through rigid structures, contribute to emotional disengagement and performance anxiety, create technical frustration, reinforce over-reliance, widen digital inequities, and raise ethical concerns. At the same time, AI was perceived to stimulate creativity, increase engagement, provide personalized feedback, offer emotional support, enable collaborative creativity, expand access to learning resources, and improve academic emotions. Overall, the paper concludes that AI applications can benefit creativity and emotional well-being, but only if implementation issues such as flexibility, human interaction, access, and ethics are addressed.

finding.finding_summary: The study found both negative and positive associations between AI-integrated educational applications and students’ academic emotions. Interview and survey data indicated that AI can increase emotional disengagement, performance anxiety, and frustration, but can also reduce anxiety through constant availability, provide emotional support, and improve positive learning experiences. The quantitative results were descriptive rather than inferential, so no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Academic emotions, including anxiety, engagement, emotional disengagement, emotional support, and emotional resilience
finding.study_size: n=23 qualitative; n=120 students and n=30 teachers quantitative

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examined creativity and problem-solving-related skills and found a mixed pattern. Participants reported that some AI tools constrained creative thinking through rigid formats, while others stimulated creativity by introducing new ideas, supporting problem-solving, and enabling collaborative creativity; the survey showed high agreement for both the constraint and benefit items, but no inferential effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Creativity, problem-solving, and collaborative creativity perceptions
finding.study_size: n=23 qualitative; n=120 students and n=30 teachers quantitative

finding.finding_summary: Although not focused on writing achievement per se, the paper includes an AI writing-assistance-related theme under natural language processing applications and interactive writing assistance. Participants said AI could support brainstorming and feedback for learning activities, but the paper did not measure writing quality, revision, or standardized writing outcomes, so evidence for writing-specific academic effects is not reported.
finding.measure: Interactive writing assistance mentioned as part of NLP applications; no direct writing outcome measured
finding.study_size: n=23 qualitative; n=120 students and n=30 teachers quantitative

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) learning tools in K-12 education: A scoping review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This scoping review examines how artificial intelligence literacy has been taught in K-12 settings and what kinds of learning tools, pedagogies, assessments, and student outcomes have been reported in the literature. The authors searched ACM, EBSCO, Web of Science, and Scopus, used PRISMA procedures, and ultimately included 46 empirical studies published between 1995 and 2023.

The review classifies AI learning tools into intelligent agents, software-based tools, hardware-based tools, and unplugged activities. It also synthesizes four pedagogical orientations—authentic/constructive, reflective, didactic, and unplugged—with project-based learning emerging as the most common approach across kindergarten, primary, and secondary settings. Across the reviewed studies, student outcomes were generally positive in cognitive understanding of AI concepts, as well as affective and behavioral outcomes such as motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, and interest. The review also notes that questionnaires, surveys, artifacts, and performance-based assessments are the most common evaluation methods.

The paper concludes that AI learning tools can support age-appropriate AI literacy development from kindergarten through secondary school, with especially strong use of Teachable Machine, Scratch, LearningML, and robotics platforms. It highlights that younger learners benefit from tangible, visual, and playful tools, while older students can handle more complex software and project-based work. The authors also emphasize major gaps in rigorous causal evidence, consistency in assessment, and theory-driven evaluation, and call for more objective, rubric-based, and outcome-oriented research before large-scale adoption.

finding.finding_summary: Across 46 reviewed studies, the paper reports that AI learning tools and related pedagogies generally improved students’ understanding of AI concepts, including rule-based systems, machine learning principles, AI ethics, and AI limitations. Reported examples include 70% of prekindergarten/kindergarten students understanding knowledge-based systems (Williams et al., 2019a) and primary students significantly outperforming direct-instruction peers on conceptual understanding, AI technical knowledge, and ethical awareness in Dai et al. (2023).
finding.measure: AI conceptual knowledge, technical knowledge, ethics awareness, understanding of machine learning and AI systems

finding.finding_summary: The reviewed studies consistently report gains in motivation, interest, perceived relevance, self-efficacy, confidence, enjoyment, and satisfaction after AI learning activities. For example, in Martins et al. (2023), over 45% of 108 secondary students described the course as enjoyable and 63% wanted to learn more machine learning, while other studies found high satisfaction and confidence in training/validating AI systems.
finding.measure: Motivation, interest, perceived relevance, self-efficacy, confidence, enjoyment, satisfaction

finding.finding_summary: The review reports improvements in durable skills such as computational thinking, collaboration, communication, problem solving, and engagement. For instance, students using AI learning tools developed computational thinking and engaged in scientific inquiry, and some studies reported enhanced collaboration and communication after working with AI systems and shared online feedback tools.
finding.measure: Computational thinking, collaboration, communication, problem solving, engagement

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies link AI learning activities to scientific inquiry and algorithmic reasoning, especially in primary and secondary settings. Students learned supervised learning, gradient descent, KNN classification, search algorithms, and optimization through projects and performance tasks, and the review notes that collaborative and project-based approaches supported scientific inquiry.
finding.measure: Algorithmic reasoning, scientific inquiry, understanding of machine learning procedures and search/optimization concepts

paper_profiles.title: A Chatbot-Based Coaching Intervention for Adolescents to Promote Life Skills: Pilot Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study addresses the design and early user evaluation of a chatbot-based coaching intervention intended to promote life skills and mental well-being in adolescents. The paper is motivated by the challenge of supporting youth coping skills in the context of bullying, cyberbullying, and broader socioemotional demands during adolescence.

The intervention consisted of two gender-personalized chatbots, CRI and CRIS, delivering eight short coaching sessions over four weeks. The sessions combined conversational prompts, reflective questions, exercises, and short video cartoons about bullying/cyberbullying situations to stimulate self-reflection on skills such as emotional self-awareness, social awareness, interpersonal relationships, conflict resolution, assertive communication, coping with sadness/loneliness, leadership, and positive emotions. The study used a participatory co-design workshop with 20 adolescents and then a formative feasibility evaluation with 21 adolescents from a secondary school context in Northeast Italy.

Findings were based on thematic analysis of workshop discussions and descriptive statistics from user-experience questionnaires. Adolescents generally found the chatbot useful, easy to use, innovative, and worth recommending, and they especially liked the video cartoons and the reflective typing process. The authors conclude that the approach is feasible, engaging, and scalable for adolescent life-skills coaching, but they explicitly note that further research is needed to evaluate efficacy on outcomes such as coping strategies and resilience.

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong positive user-reported reception of the chatbot intervention for life-skills coaching, with 16/21 adolescents rating sessions as useful, 19/21 rating them easy to use, and 17/21 rating them innovative. Participants also reported that the videos and typing responses helped them reflect on their feelings and coping in bullying/cyberbullying situations, but no pre-post behavioral or psychological outcome change was tested.
finding.measure: User experience questionnaire ratings; qualitative feedback on self-reflection, usefulness, ease of use, and perceived value

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in language instruction: impact on English learning achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examined whether AI-mediated language instruction improves English learning outcomes compared with traditional instruction, and whether it also affects learners’ L2 motivation and self-regulated learning. The paper was motivated by a gap in evidence on how AI-supported instruction influences both achievement and learner dispositions in EFL settings.

The intervention used Duolingo as the AI-mediated platform and compared it with traditional classroom-based instruction in two intact university classes in mainland China (n=60 total; 30 experimental, 30 control) over 10 weeks. Outcomes were measured with a pre/post English achievement test covering grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing; a motivation scale; and a self-regulation questionnaire. The experimental group also participated in semi-structured interviews (n=14) to capture perceptions of the AI platform.

Quantitatively, the AI group outperformed the control group on overall English achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning, with significant group-by-time effects in all three areas. The qualitative findings suggested that students experienced the platform as engaging, personalized, flexible, confidence-building, and supportive of independent learning. Overall, the study concludes that AI-mediated instruction can positively affect EFL learners’ academic achievement and learning dispositions in university settings, though it does not isolate effects on writing alone from the broader English achievement composite.

finding.finding_summary: AI-mediated instruction produced significantly higher English learning outcomes than traditional instruction on a composite achievement test that included grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing. The experimental group (n=30) improved from M=43.21 (SD=12.69) to M=73.86 (SD=15.26), while the control group (n=30) improved from M=44.39 (SD=13.21) to M=61.11 (SD=14.97); the group effect was significant, F(1,58)=94.35, p<0.001, η²=0.81.
finding.measure: English achievement test (grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, writing)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=15.26; Control post-test SD=14.97

finding.finding_summary: AI-mediated instruction significantly improved L2 motivation relative to traditional instruction. The experimental group (n=30) increased from M=3.12 (SD=1.6) to M=3.89 (SD=1.8), compared with the control group (n=30) from M=3.04 (SD=1.4) to M=3.35 (SD=1.5); the group-by-time interaction was significant, F(1,58)=7.43, p=0.04, η²=0.11.
finding.measure: 16-item L2 motivation scale (attitude, self-confidence, personal use)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=1.8; Control post-test SD=1.5

finding.finding_summary: AI-mediated instruction significantly improved self-regulated learning compared with traditional instruction. The experimental group (n=30) increased from M=2.89 (SD=0.54) to M=3.94 (SD=0.73), while the control group (n=30) increased from M=3.01 (SD=0.69) to M=3.37 (SD=0.76); the group-by-time interaction was significant, F(1,58)=7.68, p<0.001, η²=0.38.
finding.measure: Self-Regulation Questionnaire (SRQ)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post-test SD=0.73; Control post-test SD=0.76

paper_profiles.title: Not quite eye to A.I.: student and teacher perspectives on the use of generative artificial intelligence in the writing process
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate students and teachers view the acceptable use of generative AI (specifically ChatGPT) across the writing process. The authors focus on six writing-related tasks: brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, evaluating, and providing feedback, and they compare perceptions across four levels of AI use: using AI for tasks the person can already do, using AI as a model/idea generator, submitting AI-generated work with disclosure, and submitting AI-generated work without disclosure.

The study used a cross-sectional questionnaire administered to 226 participants (158 students and 68 teachers), with students primarily recruited from a U.S. public research university and teachers recruited internationally. Participants reviewed example ChatGPT prompts and outputs for each task and rated acceptability on Likert scales. The paper is not an intervention study; it is a perceptions study aimed at informing policy and guidance around GenAI use in higher education.

Findings show broad agreement that GenAI is more acceptable for early-stage, supportive uses such as brainstorming and outlining, or for helping with tasks the user already knows how to do. In contrast, using GenAI to complete writing tasks, especially without disclosure, was viewed as least acceptable by both groups. Teachers were generally more restrictive than students for student-oriented writing uses, while teachers were somewhat more accepting than students of using GenAI as a model for feedback and evaluation. The authors conclude that clearer institutional policies and teacher training on GenAI are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure student writing quality or achievement directly; instead it measures perceptions of acceptable GenAI use in writing tasks. Both students (n=158) and teachers (n=68) generally endorsed GenAI for supportive literacy tasks like brainstorming and outlining, but rejected its use to fully generate writing, especially without disclosure. Mean acceptability ratings ranged from 3.55 to 1.22 across tasks/divisions, with students generally more accepting than teachers for student-written output and teachers more accepting for model-based feedback/evaluation uses.
finding.measure: Perceived acceptability of GenAI use across writing process tasks (brainstorming, outlining, writing, revising, feedback, evaluation)

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively addresses perceptions of GenAI use for tasks linked to idea generation and organization, which are related to higher-order writing processes and metacognitive support. Participants were most accepting of GenAI as a model or scaffold for brainstorming/outlining and least accepting when AI completed the task on behalf of the user, suggesting support for limited AI use to augment rather than replace human thinking. No direct skill outcome was measured, so this reflects perceived appropriateness rather than demonstrated gains.
finding.measure: Perceived acceptability of AI-supported brainstorming, outlining, and revision as scaffolds for writing processes

finding.finding_summary: A major finding is that respondents perceived institutions as unprepared for GenAI, with most teachers reporting no institutional AI policy (94.1% NO) and no AI training (95.6% NO); 89.7% said they had not educated students about appropriate AI use. The authors argue that clear university policies and teacher professional development are urgently needed to guide acceptable use and academic integrity.
finding.measure: Survey yes/no items about institutional AI policy, AI training, and whether teachers had taught students about AI use

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI as a possible tool for reducing workload in feedback and evaluation, and participants were generally supportive of using GenAI as a model for teacher feedback or student evaluation. However, the study does not measure actual efficiency gains or workload reduction, so the evidence is limited to perceptions of acceptability rather than performance outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived acceptability of GenAI for teacher feedback and evaluation tasks

paper_profiles.title: EFL Teachers’ Perspectives toward the Use of ChatGPT in Writing Classes: A Case Study at Van Lang University
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how EFL teachers at Van Lang University in Vietnam perceive and use ChatGPT in language instruction, with a particular focus on writing classes. The paper is motivated by a practical problem in crowded university writing classrooms: limited one-on-one interaction, delayed feedback, and heavy teacher workload. The author asks how teachers use ChatGPT, what they think its benefits and risks are for writing instruction, and what support they believe is needed for effective implementation.

The study used a mixed-method design with 20 EFL instructors completing an online questionnaire and 10 of those instructors participating in structured interviews. Participants were experienced university teachers who had used ChatGPT in courses such as writing, research methodology, translation, reading, and grammar; five interviewees specifically used it in writing classes. The results show broadly favorable teacher perceptions: ChatGPT was seen as especially useful for lesson planning, generating materials, suggesting resources, and providing quick responses to student questions. Teachers were more neutral about using it for grading and feedback, and they expressed moderate concern about overdependence, privacy/security, and academic integrity.

Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT is viewed as a promising supportive tool rather than a replacement for teachers. The main recommendations are to provide teacher training, institutional support, and clear guidance for responsible use. Because the study measures teacher perceptions rather than student outcomes, it does not provide comparative evidence that ChatGPT improves high school writing achievement relative to other instructional approaches.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that ChatGPT strongly supported lesson planning and material generation, suggesting clear perceived productivity benefits. In the questionnaire, mean ratings were high for help with lesson planning (M=4.55) and generating learning materials (M=4.45), and teachers also agreed it could save time on grading and feedback (M=3.3), though they were more neutral on that point.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of lesson planning, material creation, and grading/feedback efficiency (Likert-scale questionnaire)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed ChatGPT could improve students' writing performance, especially by helping them generate ideas, obtain immediate responses, and receive suggestions for grammar and vocabulary. On the questionnaire, they strongly agreed that ChatGPT could enhance writing skills (M=3.95), support idea generation through suggested reading resources (M=4.6), and provide helpful feedback for revising grammar and vocabulary (M=3.45).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of ChatGPT's effect on writing skills, grammar/vocabulary, and idea generation in writing classes

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed ChatGPT could increase students' motivation to engage in writing tasks. The relevant questionnaire item showed agreement that integrating ChatGPT in writing classes could boost learning motivation (M=3.65), indicating a generally positive perceived motivational effect.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student learning motivation in writing classes

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expressed concern that students might become overly dependent on ChatGPT, which could weaken critical thinking and problem-solving, even though they also viewed it as an effective tutor. For the concern item, the mean was 3.65, showing agreement that overreliance could be an issue; no direct student performance measure of critical thinking was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of student dependence, critical thinking, and problem-solving in relation to ChatGPT use

paper_profiles.title: “We Need To Talk About ChatGPT”: The Future of AI and Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: SEENG (2023 IEEE/ACM 5th International Workshop on Software Engineering Education for the Next Generation)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper addresses the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and its implications for higher education, especially in software engineering and scientific writing. The authors argue that the tool has created urgent questions about assessment integrity, instructional design, plagiarism detection, and how generative AI should be integrated into courses and institutional policy.

Rather than evaluating a classroom intervention, the paper synthesizes findings from a structured grey literature review of five preprints, informal discussions with lecturers and researchers, and the authors’ own exploratory tests of ChatGPT. The context is higher education, with particular attention to software engineering students and academic writing tasks such as papers, literature reviews, and exam-related written work.

The main conclusions are normative and forward-looking: ChatGPT is likely to be widely used by students, can function as a personal tutor and idea generator, but also raises serious concerns about plagiarism, unreliable references, and assessment validity. The paper proposes recommendations in four areas—teaching, papers, curricula, and regulations—such as clarifying rules for use, updating examination formats, combining plagiarism and AI detection tools, and revising institutional policies. Because it is a position paper grounded in grey literature and informal evidence rather than primary outcome data, it does not provide causal evidence that ChatGPT improves writing outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support scientific writing tasks such as paraphrasing, summarizing literature, and drafting academic text, but it also reports flaws in argumentation, nonexistent references, and concerns about plagiarism. These conclusions are based on exploratory tests and grey-literature findings rather than controlled outcome data, so no effect size or sample-based estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Scientific writing quality, paraphrasing/summarizing ability, and plagiarism risk in written academic text

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims ChatGPT can make students and lecturers more efficient by serving as assistive technology, a personal tutor, and a tool for generating ideas or explanations. This is framed as an opportunity for faster support and more personalized learning, but the paper provides no quantitative productivity metrics.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency/productivity in learning and teaching tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central contribution is a set of institutional recommendations about integrating ChatGPT into higher education via teaching practices, paper assessments, curricula, and regulations. It highlights increased workload, the need for clearer rules, revised examination formats, and updated plagiarism/AI-detection policies, alongside opportunities for innovation and more transparent use.
finding.measure: Institutional policy and assessment recommendations; implications for curricula and examination regulations

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing Academic English Writing through AI-Powered Pedagogy: Practical Exploration of Teaching Process and Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-powered writing tools can improve academic English writing in higher education and how they affect teaching and assessment practices. The author argues that traditional writing instruction is limited by delayed, labor-intensive, and subjective feedback, and positions AI feedback systems as a way to provide more timely, individualized, and efficient support.

The study used a pre-test/post-test experimental design with 60 undergraduate students enrolled in an Academic English course at Dalian Maritime University in China. Students were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n=30) that used AI-powered writing tools (Grammarly, Turnitin, and QuillBot) and a control group (n=30) that received traditional instruction without the tools. Over 10 weeks, both groups completed comparable writing assignments, and the experimental group received AI-generated feedback and assessment after each assignment.

Results showed a substantial improvement in the experimental group's writing scores from pre-test to post-test, while the control group showed no meaningful change. The post-test difference between groups was statistically significant and large (Cohen's d=1.56), suggesting that the AI-supported condition was more effective than traditional instruction in this context. The paper also reports perceived benefits for the teaching process, including timely feedback, higher student engagement, and improved grading efficiency, though these process outcomes were not analyzed with formal quantitative comparisons.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group improved substantially on writing performance after using AI-powered writing tools. Mean writing scores increased from 59.83 (SD=7.45) at pre-test to 70.67 (SD=6.35) at post-test for the AI group (n=30), while the control group (n=30) changed only from 60.10 to 60.40; the between-group post-test difference was significant (t(58)=-9.96, p<.001) with a large effect (Cohen's d=1.56).
finding.measure: Academic English writing scores (pre-test/post-test writing assessment)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the AI tools promoted student engagement and that participants found the feedback useful, based on surveys and interviews in the experimental group. However, these results are described qualitatively and were not reported with formal statistical tests or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Student engagement; survey and interview feedback on usefulness of AI tools

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that AI-powered assessment increased grading efficiency and provided timely, individualized feedback to support instruction. These claims are based on the implementation experience rather than a quantified efficiency metric, so no effect size or statistical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Teaching process efficiency; grading efficiency; timeliness of feedback

paper_profiles.title: Perceptions and Barriers to Adopting Artificial Intelligence in K-12 Education: A Survey of Educators in Fifty States
paper_profiles.venue: Reimagining Education – The Role of E-Learning, Creativity, and Technology in the Post-Pandemic Era
paper_profiles.population: K-12 educators in the United States (PK-12; includes elementary, middle, and high school teachers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines educators’ perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) in K-12 education, with a focus on perceived barriers, readiness, policies, training, access to technology, and willingness to adopt AI tools. The authors frame AI as a potentially transformative set of tools for personalized learning, assessment, and instructional support, but argue that adoption depends heavily on educator attitudes, infrastructure, and professional preparation.

The study uses a mixed-methods survey of 4,528 educators across all 50 U.S. states and Puerto Rico. Respondents reported on district AI policies, comfort with technology, training in teacher-preparation programs, openness to learning new technologies, personal experience with AI tools, access to internet and devices, and familiarity with free AI tools that require little training. The paper does not test a student intervention or measure student achievement; instead, it documents perceptions and implementation conditions around AI adoption.

Findings suggest generally positive educator perceptions of AI and broad openness to learning and using new technologies, but also substantial concerns about resources, training, and unequal access. Differences appeared by age, grade level, and district context: younger educators tended to use AI tools more often, while older educators reported lower comfort with technology but still expressed openness to learning. Rural districts were less likely to report reliable home internet access for students. The authors conclude that successful AI integration in K-12 will require targeted professional development, more equitable infrastructure, clearer district policies, and ongoing support for teachers.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that AI adoption is constrained and enabled by institutional conditions rather than measured student outcomes. Among surveyed educators, 64.07% reported district AI policies, 82.53% reported policies on ethical and responsible technology use, and 75.26% believed implementing AI would require substantial resources, indicating both policy presence and significant implementation barriers.
finding.measure: District AI policies, ethical technology-use policies, perceived resource needs, and access/infrastructure indicators

finding.finding_summary: Respondents generally viewed AI as a tool that could improve instructional and administrative efficiency, although the paper did not directly measure efficiency outcomes. The chapter discusses AI for grading, assignment checking, assessment, scheduling, and freeing teacher time, and survey results show educators were largely open to adopting such tools (56.74% probably/definitely yes).
finding.measure: Educator openness to adopting new technology and perceptions of AI-supported administrative/assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The survey captured educators’ comfort with technology and willingness to learn new tools, which are relevant to adoption readiness rather than student socio-emotional outcomes. Most respondents reported at least some comfort with technology, and 56.74% said they were probably or definitely open to learning new technology, suggesting favorable affective readiness for AI integration.
finding.measure: Self-reported comfort with technology and openness to learning new technology

paper_profiles.title: Development research on an AI English learning support system to facilitate learner-generated-context-based learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This development study addresses how artificial intelligence can be designed to support learner-generated-context (LGC) based learning, with a particular focus on autonomous English learning for Korean secondary-school students. The authors argue that many AIEd tools are still too teacher-directed or monitoring-oriented and do not sufficiently support learners in choosing their own goals, materials, and learning strategies.

To address this, the paper develops and describes a web-based AI English learning support system with four modules: learning content management, learning management, personalized English learning, and content curation. The system uses NLP, OCR, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, and other AI services to help learners turn their own texts, images, and YouTube clips into study materials, schedule learning, practice vocabulary and sentences, and share curated content with peers.

The system was field-tested with three Korean secondary-school students over a seven-day trial. Using surveys, observations, and interviews, the authors found that the system helped students create and practice self-chosen learning content and supported autonomous study, especially vocabulary practice and self-testing. However, the content curation functions had limited uptake, and the experience varied by student background and existing learning habits. The study concludes that AI can support autonomous English learning when aligned with educational theory, but that more diverse content and better mechanisms for sharing and exploration are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The system supported English vocabulary and sentence study through learner-generated content, OCR-based text extraction, and automated practice/test generation. In the field test with n=3 secondary-school students, participants reported that the tool helped them create vocabulary lists from their own materials and study them independently; one student rated practice mode 5/5 and self-testing as useful for memorization, though the study did not report standardized writing or reading outcomes.
finding.measure: Learner-reported use and perceived utility of vocabulary/sentence learning, practice mode, and test mode for English study

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the system increased learners’ autonomy, self-directed study, and willingness to engage with English outside teacher control. Across the three participants, the authors describe higher perceived ability to set goals, manage schedules, and study anytime/anywhere, with satisfaction scores generally high (e.g., overall satisfaction 4/5 to 5/5).
finding.measure: Self-reported autonomy, satisfaction, and perceived ability to manage learning using the system

finding.finding_summary: The system was intended to support planning and self-management, and participants used the calendar-based learning management module to set schedules and track progress. Evidence is mixed because one student used the planning tools extensively (utilization 5/5) while another used them less effectively, and the paper provides descriptive, not comparative, evidence of improved time management and strategy use.
finding.measure: Use of learning scheduling/planning tools and self-reported management of learning activities

finding.finding_summary: The system automated creation of learning content, practice questions, and pronunciation feedback, reducing the need for human instructors to generate materials manually. In qualitative field-test data, students could upload text/images/videos and immediately receive organized vocabulary lists, translations, audio, and self-generated quizzes, indicating efficiency gains in learning-material preparation and feedback delivery.
finding.measure: Automation of content creation, question generation, and feedback in the learning workflow

paper_profiles.title: Automated Evaluation of Writing – 50 Years and Counting
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This theme paper reviews 50 years of automated writing evaluation (AWE), using Ellis Page’s 1966 vision of computer-assisted essay grading as a framework for discussing what the field has achieved and where major challenges remain. Rather than testing a single intervention, the paper synthesizes prior work on automated scoring, automated feedback, content scoring, fairness, interpretability, and the expanding use of AWE in classrooms and standardized testing.

The paper discusses AWE systems used with student writing across educational levels, including high school essays, and highlights that while automated scoring and feedback are now widespread, the effectiveness of feedback for improving writing is mixed and context-dependent. It emphasizes that outcomes may differ by user population (for example, L1 vs. L2 writers, age, skill level, and learners with disabilities), and that current systems must be evaluated differently depending on whether they are used for high-stakes decision making, improving written products, or helping users learn to write better.

Overall, the paper concludes that automated writing technologies have advanced substantially, but their educational value depends on valid, fair, and purpose-aligned evaluation. It argues that feedback-oriented AWE is promising but not uniformly effective, and that the strongest evidence for impact comes from carefully designed studies that examine specific user groups, writing tasks, and intended uses.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report a new experiment; instead, it synthesizes prior research showing that AWE can support writing improvement in some contexts, but the effectiveness of automated writing feedback is inconclusive overall. It cites studies of writing feedback, revision, and automated scoring, including one high-school essay example in Page (1966) with 276 essays and multiple R = 0.65 between machine and average human score, but this is presented as historical context rather than an intervention effect.
finding.measure: Writing quality, automated essay scores, and revision/improvement across drafts

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that use of AWE feedback can affect motivation and self-efficacy, but it frames this as a possible benefit rather than a consistently demonstrated result. No primary quantitative estimate is reported in the paper itself; the discussion is based on cited prior studies and broader reflection on student response to feedback.
finding.measure: Motivation and self-efficacy related to writing assistance

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that one major benefit of AWE is reducing teacher workload by taking over some of the burden of evaluating student writing and providing fast turnaround feedback. This is presented as a longstanding and now widely realized use case, but the paper does not report a new effect estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher evaluation burden, turnaround time for feedback, and scoring automation

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how AI should be integrated into higher education, with special attention to AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It argues that generative AI tools such as ChatGPT can personalize learning, support diverse learners, and improve classroom experiences, but that these benefits come with substantial risks if students and educators lack understanding of the systems’ limitations.

The paper draws on the author’s teaching experience, informal discussions with students and staff at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences, a case study of institutional responses to ChatGPT, and a narrative literature review. The central case concerns how Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences developed AI guidelines for academic writing that require transparency about AI use and prohibit direct copy-pasting. The paper emphasizes that AI should be treated as an informed conversational partner rather than a ghostwriter, and that responsible use depends on full disclosure, critical evaluation of outputs, and explicit training in AI literacy.

A major conclusion is that institutional rules alone are insufficient. The author argues for a broader “culture of AI” built through workshops, regular updates, dedicated budget and staff support, and AI literacy courses embedded across curricula. Prompt engineering is presented as both a practical classroom skill and a way to deepen students’ understanding of AI’s limits, while critical thinking is framed as essential for avoiding hallucinations, misuse, and overreliance on AI-generated content.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that prompt engineering and AI literacy can strengthen students’ critical thinking by encouraging them to evaluate AI outputs, compare responses, and reflect on limitations such as hallucinations. However, it also reports the opposite risk: students may uncritically hand over cognitive work to the machine, which could weaken independent thinking and reduce learning if AI is used as a shortcut.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on AI use in written academic work and warns against direct copy-pasting of AI-generated text, emphasizing that students should use AI only as a sparring partner for drafting and idea generation. It suggests AI can support writing tasks, but also risks undermining authorship, critical engagement, and the integrity of students’ own writing practice if used unreflectively.
finding.measure: Academic writing / written papers

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on institutional policy responses to generative AI, especially the development and implementation of AI guidelines at a Swiss university. It finds that guidelines improve transparency and establish expectations, but also notes major institutional limitations: low compliance is possible, monitoring use is difficult, and guidance alone does not ensure responsible behavior or equitable enforcement.
finding.measure: Institutional AI guidelines and governance practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI can help teachers create curricula, case studies, and interactive classroom materials more efficiently, and can support students with workload and idea generation. At the same time, it notes that prompting high-quality outputs can take substantial time and that educators may need training and dedicated support, limiting efficiency gains in practice.
finding.measure: Curriculum creation and instructional planning workload

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not explicitly studied; broad human learning / education contexts (includes K-12, higher education, and lifelong learning)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the promises and challenges of generative AI (GenAI) for human learning across educational contexts. Rather than testing a single intervention, it synthesizes recent research and argues that GenAI may scale personalized support, diversify learning resources, provide faster and richer feedback, and enable more adaptive assessment approaches.

The paper focuses on how GenAI systems such as large language models, multimodal generators, and autonomous agents could be integrated into learning support, resource creation, feedback, and assessment. It emphasizes that these tools can help learners and educators, but only if humans remain in the loop to validate outputs, preserve pedagogical quality, and align tools with learning goals.

A major part of the paper is devoted to risks and tradeoffs: hallucinations and inaccuracies, transparency problems, privacy concerns, unequal access, biased outputs, cheating and assessment validity threats, and the possibility that students may become over-reliant on AI. The authors conclude that AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and methodological rigor are necessary to ensure GenAI augments rather than replaces human cognition and learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses GenAI feedback and writing support in secondary school essay writing and collaborative second language writing, noting potential gains in task performance and student experience but also risks when AI outputs are inaccurate or when support is removed. It cites evidence that GenAI-generated feedback can improve text revision and motivation in secondary students, but the paper itself is a perspective and does not report a new study of writing outcomes.
finding.measure: essay writing revision, writing performance, and collaborative L2 writing outcomes (as discussed in prior studies)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI may improve engagement and positive experiences through personalized support and feedback, but it also warns about reduced agency, overreliance, and fluency bias. It highlights that performance can appear improved while underlying learning engagement and self-regulation may weaken, especially if AI support is removed.
finding.measure: engagement, agency, motivation, and positive emotions (as reported in prior studies and synthesized here)

finding.finding_summary: This paper centrally focuses on durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, creativity, and self-regulation, arguing that GenAI can support these skills when used as a scaffold but may also weaken them through overreliance. The paper cites evidence of a performance paradox: students may perform better with AI assistance, yet their performance drops when support is removed, suggesting limited transfer to unaided work and possible dependence.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, self-regulation, agency, and metacognitive performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI can increase efficiency by automating feedback generation, resource creation, and parts of assessment, thereby reducing educator workload and speeding support to learners. However, it stresses that these efficiency gains come with computational costs and validation burdens, so the net benefit depends on careful human oversight.
finding.measure: feedback turnaround, resource creation time, and educator workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main institutional-level finding is that GenAI introduces broad system risks and governance challenges, including inequity from the digital divide, privacy and transparency concerns, cheating, and disruption of conventional assessment. It argues that institutions need AI literacy, evidence-based policy, and ethical regulation to prevent harm and ensure equitable access.
finding.measure: equity, privacy, transparency, assessment validity, and policy/governance implications

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT in the digital era: Perspectives on chatbot implementation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how educators and students in higher education in Krabi, Thailand perceive ChatGPT as an educational tool during the digital era. The authors were interested in both the perceived benefits of the chatbot and the challenges or risks associated with its use, including concerns about accuracy, reduced personal interaction, and privacy/security.

Using purposive sampling, the researchers conducted in-depth interviews with 25 participants: 10 educators and 15 students from Thai higher education institutions. The interviews were transcribed and analyzed using content analysis with NVivo, and the paper also draws on related literature to frame ChatGPT’s potential role in education. Participants generally viewed ChatGPT positively as a tool for immediate feedback, answering routine questions, and reducing educator workload.

At the same time, the study highlights important cautions. Participants worried that ChatGPT could provide inaccurate or incomplete information, especially on sensitive or complex topics, and that overuse might reduce meaningful teacher-student interaction. They also raised data privacy concerns, recommending that institutions and providers implement stronger protections and that ChatGPT be used alongside, not in place of, human support. The paper concludes that ChatGPT may be useful in education if used responsibly, with attention to accuracy, ethics, and privacy.

finding.finding_summary: Participants, especially educators, reported that ChatGPT could answer routine questions, provide immediate feedback, and free up time for higher-order tasks such as lesson planning and student support. The study is qualitative and does not report an effect size, but the central finding is that ChatGPT was perceived to reduce educator workload and improve efficiency in managing routine academic queries.
finding.measure: Perceptions from in-depth interviews about workload reduction, routine question answering, and immediate feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly addresses ChatGPT’s role in academic writing support, summarizing prior literature and participant concerns about inaccurate or incomplete responses that could undermine learning outcomes. It also notes that ChatGPT can help with writing-related tasks such as generating ideas and providing feedback, but the study’s own data emphasize the risk of unreliable suggestions rather than measurable writing gains; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Perceptions of ChatGPT use for writing support, feedback, and information accuracy in academic tasks
finding.study_size: n=25 (interviews); no quantitative literacy outcome reported

finding.finding_summary: Participants raised institutional concerns about privacy, data security, and the need for clear communication and access controls when ChatGPT is used in education. The paper also suggests that schools and providers should implement safeguards and guidance, but these conclusions are based on interview perceptions rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceptions of privacy, data security, and implementation safeguards for educational chatbot use

paper_profiles.title: How should we change teaching and assessment in response to increasingly powerful generative Artificial Intelligence? Outcomes of the ChatGPT teacher survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how educators believe teaching and assessment should change in response to rapidly improving generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, and what motivates those changes. The authors argue that generative AI is a major educational disruption because it can produce human-like text for many classroom tasks, raising questions about curriculum, pedagogy, assessment integrity, and the future role of teachers.

The study used a mixed-methods survey of 318 educators from elementary, secondary, and university settings across multiple regions and disciplines. Quantitative items measured perceived impact of ChatGPT-like tools on teaching and assessment, while open-ended responses were thematically coded to identify proposed curricular and assessment changes and motivations for change. Respondents generally expected a major or profound impact, especially those with greater AI awareness, and they proposed changes such as explicitly teaching AI literacy, critical evaluation of AI output, ethical and responsible use, more process-oriented and higher-order tasks, and more supervision or face-to-face assessment to address plagiarism and integrity concerns.

The paper concludes that educators see generative AI as requiring meaningful changes to curriculum and assessment, but their suggestions often remain anchored in existing good teaching practices rather than radically new AI-specific pedagogies. It also suggests that many teachers have limited awareness of the full range of AI capabilities, and that concerns about academic integrity, fairness, and assessment validity are central drivers of proposed change. The study offers a baseline snapshot of teacher beliefs early in the ChatGPT era, rather than evidence that the proposed changes are effective.

finding.finding_summary: Educators expected generative AI to have a major or profound impact on teaching and assessment (teaching mean 2.7/4; assessment mean 2.8/4; n=318), and many recommended institutional changes to curriculum, supervision, and assessment design. However, the paper reports perceptions and proposed changes rather than measured institutional outcomes, so the findings show strong anticipated system-level disruption rather than observed effects.
finding.measure: Perceived impact of generative AI on teaching and assessment; open-ended suggestions for curriculum and assessment change

finding.finding_summary: Teachers frequently proposed shifting instruction toward durable skills such as critical thinking, evaluation of AI outputs, creativity, collaboration, and ethical judgment. These were qualitative findings from 546 coded references about teaching changes and 567 coded references about assessment changes; no direct student outcome effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about teaching and assessment changes; coded themes for critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, ethics, and evaluation

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of respondents said AI should be integrated into writing instruction, including using ChatGPT to support writing, provide exemplars, and offer individualized help, but they also emphasized process writing, drafting, citations, and academic integrity to counter potential misuse. The paper does not test student writing performance; it documents teacher perceptions that generative AI may both support and undermine literacy learning depending on how it is used.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about literacy/writing pedagogy and assessment; references to writing support, drafting processes, citations, and plagiarism

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly reported that AI could improve their workflow, save time, and make assessment and resource creation more efficient. In motivations to change assessment, effort expectancy responses explicitly described AI as making assessment 'easier,' 'more efficient,' and useful for providing feedback, but these are self-reported perceptions rather than measured workload outcomes.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses about effort expectancy and AI support for teaching/assessment workflows

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI in Higher Education: The ChatGPT Effect
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length treatment addresses how generative AI, especially ChatGPT, is reshaping higher education. It aims to help educators, students, administrators, and policymakers understand the technology, build AI literacy, redesign curriculum and assessment, and formulate institutional AI policy in response to both opportunities and risks.

The approach is a conceptual, practice-oriented synthesis rather than a single empirical study. Across chapters, the authors explain how GenAI works, review strengths and weaknesses for curriculum design, propose assessment redesign strategies and an AI assessment integration framework, and outline policy principles such as transparency, fairness, accountability, privacy, and human oversight. The book also includes illustrative examples, case scenarios, and some qualitative findings from stakeholder perceptions in Hong Kong, but the overall work is primarily a comprehensive expert guide focused on higher education contexts.

The main conclusions are that GenAI can be a powerful partner in teaching, learning, assessment, and policy work, but it must not replace human judgment, authenticity, or integrity. The authors repeatedly argue for AI literacy, responsible use, and redesign of assessment and policy so that AI supports—rather than undermines—learning outcomes and educational values.

finding.finding_summary: The book argues that higher education institutions need explicit AI policies, assessment guidelines, and governance frameworks to manage transparency, fairness, accountability, privacy, safety, and human oversight in GenAI use. Its institutional recommendations are largely conceptual and policy-oriented rather than experimentally tested, but it reports that the authors had been contacted by over 200 universities about AI policy and includes a Hong Kong stakeholder study to inform an AI ecological education policy framework.
finding.measure: institutional AI policy development; stakeholder perceptions on GenAI policy

finding.finding_summary: The book presents GenAI as a tool that can improve efficiency in teaching, assessment design, feedback, and administrative tasks by reducing routine workload and enabling scalable support. It describes practical use cases such as drafting materials, generating prompts and exercises, and supporting assessment redesign, but does not report a controlled estimate of productivity gains.
finding.measure: teacher/staff workload and task efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the book examines how ChatGPT and GenAI can be incorporated into curriculum design across higher education disciplines. The authors emphasize strengths such as multimodal support, scalability, customisability, and contextual relevance, while also discussing weaknesses and threats; however, no quantitative learning gains are reported for specific academic subjects.
finding.measure: curriculum design and pedagogical use of ChatGPT/GenAI
