finding.finding_summary: The book frames AI use as connected to durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, and prompt engineering, and it argues that assessments should prioritize higher-order competencies and human–machine partnership. It also shows ChatGPT being evaluated against Bloom’s taxonomy, but the evidence is illustrative and conceptual rather than a measured skill outcome.
finding.measure: higher-order thinking, prompt engineering, Bloom’s taxonomy-aligned capability

finding.finding_summary: The authors suggest GenAI can support learner engagement, confidence, and self-directed activity when used as a learning partner and when feedback is emphasized over grades. The text presents these benefits as pedagogical claims and examples rather than as measured outcomes.
finding.measure: engagement, self-directed learning, learner confidence

paper_profiles.title: AI Chatbots in Chinese higher education: adoption, perception, and influence among graduate students—an integrated analysis utilizing UTAUT and ECM models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how graduate students in China accept and use AI chatbots, with a focus on the factors that shape their behavioral intention and continued use. The authors combine the UTAUT and ECM frameworks to test whether performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, confirmation, satisfaction, personal innovativeness, and behavioral intention explain AI chatbot adoption in higher education.

The study surveyed 373 master’s and doctoral students from Chinese universities using a seven-point Likert instrument and analyzed the data with PLS-SEM. Results showed that confirmation, satisfaction, performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and personal innovativeness significantly predicted attitudes and/or intention in the model, while social influence and facilitating conditions did not. The strongest pattern was that confirmation of expectations increased both performance expectancy and satisfaction, and satisfaction strongly predicted behavioral intention; behavioral intention in turn predicted reported use behavior.

Overall, the paper concludes that graduate students’ continued use of AI chatbots is driven more by whether the tools meet expectations and create satisfying experiences than by social pressure or infrastructure support. The study positions AI chatbots as useful academic support tools in higher education, but it does not experimentally test learning outcomes or writing quality; instead, it focuses on technology acceptance and post-adoption use among Chinese postgraduate students.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that AI chatbot use was associated with higher perceived efficiency and productivity in students’ study and research workflows. Performance expectancy significantly predicted satisfaction (β=0.419, t=8.532, p<0.001), and satisfaction strongly predicted behavioral intention (β=0.059, t=6.408, p<0.001), with behavioral intention also predicting use behavior (β=0.401, t=7.327, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Perceived productivity/efficiency, satisfaction with using AI chatbots for learning and research, behavioral intention, and self-reported use behavior

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies AI chatbot use for learning and research tasks in higher education, including essay writing assistance, question answering, and support for academic/research work. Graduate students reported that AI chatbots helped them complete study tasks and research projects faster, and the overall model showed that these academic-use perceptions significantly shaped intention to continue using the tool.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for learning/research tasks and academic use intentions

finding.finding_summary: The study includes constructs related to personal innovativeness, reflecting a disposition toward trying new technologies, and finds that it significantly predicted behavioral intention to use AI chatbots (β=0.258, t=5.126, p<0.001). This indicates that students who were more open to experimenting with novel technologies were more likely to intend continued AI chatbot use.
finding.measure: Personal innovativeness and behavioral intention

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT in Ukrainian Education: Problems and Prospects
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the perceived prospects, risks, and ethical issues of ChatGPT use in Ukrainian education. The authors aim to synthesize early literature and, more centrally, report results from an online Google Forms survey of 1,035 educational and pedagogical practitioners and teachers across Ukraine.

The study asks how respondents view ChatGPT’s usefulness for teaching, learning, writing, and scientific work, and what downsides they anticipate or have already observed. Respondents generally saw benefits such as saving time, generating ideas, improving writing and documentation, and assisting with lesson preparation; however, they also reported substantial concerns about inaccurate or misleading outputs, dependence on the bot, reduced independence and creativity, academic integrity violations, privacy and confidentiality issues, and cheating during assessments.

Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT should be treated as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for human expertise. The authors argue for critical thinking, fact-checking, ethical safeguards, and contextual rules for use, especially because many respondents expressed uncertainty about accuracy and ethics and because the technology’s risks appear to depend strongly on how it is used.

finding.finding_summary: Respondents saw ChatGPT as helpful for writing-related tasks, including improving texts, generating ideas, paraphrasing, drafting papers, and producing other written materials. At the same time, they reported important downsides for writing practice, including students completing tasks without understanding them, academic integrity violations, and the risk of substituting bot-generated text for independent writing.
finding.measure: Survey responses on perceived benefits and negative consequences of ChatGPT for student writing and writing-related tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports both positive and negative perceived effects on durable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, independence, and problem-solving. Respondents frequently identified dependence on the bot and decreased independence (60.5%, n=626), loss of creativity (30.7%, n=318), and reduced understanding of information as risks, while some also believed ChatGPT could support critical thinking and creativity when used appropriately.
finding.measure: Survey responses on perceived effects of ChatGPT on students’ critical thinking, creativity, independence, and problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: Respondents overwhelmingly viewed ChatGPT as a tool for saving time and improving efficiency in educational work. Reported uses included preparing and improving documentation, creating tasks, drafting answers to student questions, and improving lecture quality; 71.2% (n=737) said it is a fast and convenient way to obtain information that saves time.
finding.measure: Survey responses on time savings, documentation preparation, task creation, and other efficiency-related uses

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional concerns around academic integrity, privacy, fairness, transparency, and assessment policy. Respondents reported risks of using ChatGPT to cheat during tests (51.8%, n=536), to perform work instead of the student (71.9%, n=744), and to generate content that can undermine conventional assessment, while some also recommended that institutions require disclosure and reconsider assessment formats.
finding.measure: Survey responses on ethical issues, academic integrity, cheating, and institutional policy implications

paper_profiles.title: Adolescents’ use and perceived usefulness of generative AI for schoolwork: exploring their relationships with executive functioning and academic achievement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how often adolescents use generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT for schoolwork, how useful they perceive these tools to be, and how those patterns relate to executive functioning (EF) and academic achievement. The authors frame the work around a growing debate about AI in education: whether these tools can support students who struggle with planning, initiation, organization, and task completion, or whether they may encourage overreliance, cheating, and weaker independent learning.

The study includes two Swedish adolescent samples. Study 1 surveyed 385 younger adolescents aged 12–16 (middle school), and Study 2 surveyed 359 older adolescents aged 15–19 (high school). Students reported whether they used generative AI for schoolwork, how frequently they used it, and how useful they found it for tasks such as initiating, structuring, completing, summarizing, improving, explaining, and writing schoolwork. EF was measured with the BRIEF-2 self-report in both studies, and teacher ratings were also added in Study 2. Study 1 also included grades in Swedish, math, and English as an academic achievement measure.

Across both studies, use of generative AI was more common among older students than younger ones, and ChatGPT was the most commonly used tool. The clearest pattern was that adolescents with more EF problems tended to report greater perceived usefulness of generative AI, especially for completing assignments. In Study 1, AI users reported significantly more EF problems than non-users (GEC t(376)=2.55, p=0.011, d=0.37), but academic achievement was not significantly related to AI use or perceived usefulness. The authors emphasize that the findings are correlational and exploratory, and they highlight risks such as academic integrity concerns, uncritical dependence on AI-generated content, possible bias in outputs, and the possibility that using AI as a substitute for effortful thinking could interfere with the development of executive functioning during adolescence.

finding.finding_summary: Students who used generative AI for schoolwork reported more EF-related difficulties than non-users in Study 1. The BRIEF-2 Global Executive Composite was significantly higher for users (n=57) than non-users (n=328), t(376)=2.55, p=0.011, d=0.37, indicating more self-reported executive-function problems among users.
finding.measure: BRIEF-2 self-report Global Executive Composite (executive functioning problems)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central focus is adolescents’ executive functioning, including planning, inhibition, working memory, and organization. Across both studies, more EF problems were associated with greater perceived usefulness of generative AI for schoolwork, especially for completing assignments (e.g., Study 2: r=0.29 with completion usefulness for both self- and teacher-rated EF; Study 1: GEC correlated with perceived overall usefulness r=0.41 and completion usefulness r=0.44). However, the study is correlational and does not show that AI use improves EF; instead, it raises the possibility that students with EF challenges are more likely to rely on AI.
finding.measure: BRIEF-2 self-report and teacher-report EF scales; perceived usefulness of generative AI for initiating, structuring, completing, summarizing, improving, explaining, and writing schoolwork
finding.effect_size: r=0.44 (Study 1 GEC with completion usefulness); r=0.29 (Study 2 self/teacher-rated EF with completion usefulness)

finding.finding_summary: Academic achievement was not significantly associated with generative AI use or perceived usefulness in Study 1. The authors report only weak, non-significant correlations between grades and AI use/usefulness (e.g., frequency of use r=-0.05, usefulness for initiating r=0.02, overall usefulness r=0.03), suggesting no detectable relationship in this sample.
finding.measure: Aggregate grades in Swedish, Math, and English

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that adolescents who used generative AI tended to perceive it as useful for completing schoolwork and, in Study 2, for improving texts and avoiding effort. This indicates that students, especially those with more EF problems, view AI as a productivity aid for task completion rather than as a tool for learning alone (e.g., Study 2 completion usefulness correlated with EF problems at r=0.29; overall usefulness with EF problems r=0.52).
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness ratings for initiation, structuring, completion, summarization, improving texts, explaining concepts, writing texts, and effort avoidance
finding.study_size: Study 1 n=57 users; Study 2 n=189 users
finding.effect_size: r=0.52 (overall usefulness with GEC in Study 2); r=0.29 (completion usefulness with self/teacher-rated EF in Study 2)

paper_profiles.title: Postplagiarism: transdisciplinary ethics and integrity in the age of artificial intelligence and neurotechnology
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual editorial; no study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial argues that education is entering a “postplagiarism” era in which artificial intelligence and neurotechnology become ordinary parts of how people write, learn, communicate, and are assessed. Rather than presenting a primary empirical study, the paper is a conceptual and normative reflection on how academic integrity should adapt to widespread AI-assisted writing, hybrid human-AI authorship, and emerging brain-computer interface technologies.

The article focuses on higher education and, more broadly, the ethical and policy implications of AI for teaching, learning, assessment, and scholarly attribution. It discusses concerns such as the limits of AI detection tools, the continuing responsibility of humans for factual accuracy and academic work, the persistence of attribution norms, and the possibility that future neurotechnology could make cheating detection futile. The main conclusion is that educators and policymakers should prepare proactively for these technologies through transdisciplinary research, equity-aware ethics, and updated integrity practices, rather than relying on traditional plagiarism frameworks alone.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI and neurotechnology will fundamentally reshape academic integrity policy, assessment design, and institutional responses. It claims that detection-based approaches are becoming less viable as AI text generation improves and that future commercially available neurotechnology could make cheating detection an exercise in futility, but these are conceptual claims rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of academic integrity policy, detection practices, and future technology implications

finding.finding_summary: The editorial centers on writing in the age of AI, arguing that human-AI hybrid writing will become normal and that AI can be edited, revised, and remixed into scholarly texts. It also warns that AI-generated outputs may be falsely detected or misclassified, and it explicitly notes concerns about students outsourcing academic writing, but it reports no empirical study of writing performance or writing development.
finding.measure: Academic writing, authorship, attribution, and AI-generated text in educational contexts

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses responsibility, fact-checking, verification, evaluative judgment, and ethical decision-making as key human capabilities that should not be abdicated to AI. It frames these as enduring skills needed in a postplagiarism era, but does not provide empirical measurement of critical thinking, metacognition, or related outcomes.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of fact-checking, verification, evaluative judgment, and responsibility

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes ethics, trust, inclusion, and social justice in relation to AI and education, arguing that technology should be developed and used in ways that support equity and accessibility. These claims are normative and policy-oriented rather than empirical, with no direct measurement of motivation, engagement, or self-regulation.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of equity, inclusion, accessibility, and ethical responsibility

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing STEM learning with ChatGPT and Bing Chat as objects to think with: A case study
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT and Bing Chat can function as Papert-style “objects-to-think-with” in STEM learning. The authors use a constructionist framework to explore how dialogue with generative AI can stimulate reflection, concept formation, critical thinking, and problem solving rather than simply supplying answers.

The study is a qualitative single-case study with two embedded units (ChatGPT and Bing Chat). Because the idea was new and real classroom implementation was difficult, the researchers themselves and a graduate student acting as STEM teachers simulated student interactions in Portuguese/British English and analyzed interaction logs plus reflective journals. The context is secondary-school STEM concepts, but the participants were adult educators/trainees rather than actual students.

The paper concludes that both tools can support reflective learning and concept comprehension when used dialogically and with careful prompting. At the same time, it emphasizes important limitations and risks: the models can give inaccurate or confusing explanations, sometimes reinforce misconceptions, require careful human guidance, and should be combined with collaborative learning and other educational activities to avoid diminished human interaction and unreliable information.

finding.finding_summary: The case study found that ChatGPT and Bing Chat could support students’ understanding of scientific concepts through Socratic-style dialogue, helping participants refine ideas about weight, normal force, freefall, and orbital motion. However, the interactions also revealed repeated confusion, occasional inaccurate or overly complex explanations, and the risk of reinforcing misconceptions, especially when the AI answered in ways that were inconsistent with the participant’s level of understanding.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of interaction logs and reflective journals focused on conceptual understanding in physics/STEM dialogues

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that the AI interactions fostered reflective and critical thinking, prompting participants to question, refine, and revisit their ideas. The dialogue structure encouraged metacognitive engagement and iterative problem solving, with the paper repeatedly describing the tools as supporting deeper thinking rather than merely giving ready-made answers.
finding.measure: Qualitative themes from dialogue transcripts and reflective journals concerning reflective thinking, critical thinking, and problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests the interactions were engaging and motivating, with the AI helping sustain a collaborative, conversational learning experience. At the same time, the authors note limitations such as diminished human interaction and the need to combine AI with collaborative learning activities, indicating that engagement benefits may depend on broader instructional design.
finding.measure: Participant reflections and qualitative interpretation of engagement during AI dialogues

paper_profiles.title: Can artificial intelligence help for scientific writing?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper asks whether ChatGPT and related AI chatbots can help with scientific writing and what limitations, risks, and ethical concerns they introduce. The authors describe potential uses across the writing workflow, including literature search, summarizing papers, generating initial drafts, suggesting titles, translating text, proofreading, and editing. They emphasize that these tools can speed up writing and support organization, but they cannot replace human expertise, judgment, or responsibility.

The paper is not an empirical study; it is an expert commentary grounded in examples and prior reports from medical/scientific writing. Its context is adult scientific researchers and clinicians, especially in critical care medicine, but its arguments are broadly applicable to academic writing. The main conclusions are that AI writing tools may be useful assistants, but their outputs can be generic, inaccurate, biased, or plagiarized, and their use raises concerns about academic integrity, unequal access, authorship, and the need for regulation. The authors argue that human oversight and field expertise remain essential, and that institutions and journals should establish rules and detection mechanisms for ethical use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI chatbots such as ChatGPT can support scientific writing by generating drafts, summarizing literature, translating text, proofreading, and rewriting complex sentences, which may save time and improve readability. However, the authors also emphasize that outputs are not always satisfactory, may be vague or inconsistent, and require expert human review; no empirical effect size or study sample is reported because this is a perspective article.
finding.measure: Scientific writing tasks, drafting, proofreading, summarization, editing quality

finding.finding_summary: The authors repeatedly state that ChatGPT can make writing work faster and easier by helping researchers organize material, generate initial drafts, summarize text, and perform editing and language polishing. They also note that these tools can save time in manuscript preparation and related administrative writing tasks, but they do not provide empirical time-savings data or a measured sample.
finding.measure: Perceived time savings and writing productivity

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on institutional and governance issues around AI writing tools, including the need for international academic regulations, plagiarism detection, authorship norms, and policies to prevent unethical use. It also raises equity concerns about possible paywalls widening access gaps between high- and low-income countries and between junior and senior researchers, but it reports no empirical institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, authorship, plagiarism control, and access equity concerns

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI can assist with organizing and developing ideas, but it cannot replace human creativity, critical thinking, judgment, or responsibility. It also warns that chatbot-generated summaries may be generic and may fail to critically analyze differences among studies, indicating a limitation for independent reasoning rather than a measured learner outcome.
finding.measure: Human critical thinking, creativity, and judgment in scientific writing

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is not about school subjects, it directly discusses scientific writing as a specialized academic task and warns that AI may be less effective for highly technical topics and may require substantial human input. The authors do not provide empirical performance metrics, but they argue that inadequate prompting can produce inadequate results and that automated text is not a substitute for expert scientific analysis.
finding.measure: Scientific writing quality for highly technical academic content

paper_profiles.title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study examines whether ChatGPT can function as a feedback tool to improve second-language writing, with a particular emphasis on students from refugee/migrant backgrounds who may face additional language barriers. The paper is motivated by the rapid emergence of ChatGPT in education and the need to understand both its affordances and limitations for language learning.

The intervention was conducted in a junior high school in Patras, Greece, with 8 fifteen-year-old students in a German-as-a-foreign-language class. Students first wrote a personal email in German, then ChatGPT was prompted to improve the texts’ vocabulary and grammar; students reviewed the revised versions and later wrote a similar email on a related topic. The study compared pre- and post-intervention writing using counts of total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and most frequent words. Results suggested improved text length and lexical variety after ChatGPT-based feedback, with the largest gains reported for total words (mean increase 38%) and average words per sentence (about 42%), although one student showed a decrease on one metric and the authors note the findings are not generalizable due to the very small sample and short duration. The paper also explicitly warns about risks such as cheating, the need for human supervision, the importance of checking accuracy, and the limited scope of the feedback.

Overall, the authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise as a language-learning support tool in multilingual classrooms, especially for students with refugee/migrant backgrounds, but that it should be used responsibly and cautiously. They stress that larger studies in diverse contexts are needed and note methodological limitations including the pilot nature of the study, the small convenience sample, the brief intervention, and the possibility of socially desirable responses and measurement bias.

finding.finding_summary: In this pilot study of 8 junior high school students, ChatGPT-assisted feedback was associated with stronger German writing outputs. Across students, total words increased by a mean of 38%, unique words increased by an average of 19.1 per student (with one exception), and average words per sentence rose by about 42% in the revised/transfer writing task.
finding.measure: German L2 writing quality indicators: total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and most frequent words in personal emails

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted academic writing: recommendations for ethical use
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This commentary addresses the rapidly growing use of large language model (LLM)-based generative AI tools, especially ChatGPT, in academic writing. The authors ask how such tools can be used in ways that are ethically defensible while preserving academic integrity, transparency, and human intellectual contribution. They situate the discussion in the context of healthcare simulation scholarship and broader academic publishing, noting that guidance from journals and publishing bodies is still evolving.

The paper does not evaluate an intervention or report original empirical data; instead, it synthesizes publisher policies, existing literature, and the authors’ reflections on ChatGPT use in manuscript preparation. It identifies major risks of AI-assisted writing, including plagiarism, hallucinated or fabricated content, inaccurate references, bias amplification, and over-reliance that could weaken human critical thinking and scholarly development. The authors propose a tiered framework for ethical use: lower-risk uses include grammar, readability, and translation support; more contingent uses include outlining, summarizing, and brainstorming; and higher-risk uses include drafting de novo text, data interpretation, literature review, and plagiarism checking. Their main conclusion is that generative AI can support academic writing only when human authors retain responsibility, verify outputs, and disclose use transparently.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM-based tools can support aspects of academic writing such as grammar, readability, flow, and translation, but also warns that they can introduce inaccurate translation, plagiarism, hallucinated content, and fabricated references. The discussion is based on prior studies and examples rather than new empirical testing; no single effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Academic writing support, translation quality, originality/plagiarism risk, reference accuracy

finding.finding_summary: A central concern is that overuse of ChatGPT for ideation, drafting, and initial interpretation could reduce human critical thinking and scholarly development. The authors explicitly warn that dependence on the tool may arrest further skill development and cause necessary reasoning skills to be lost over time, but they do not provide original quantitative evidence.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, scholarly development, human competency in research and writing skills

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that generative AI can make some writing tasks more efficient, especially reformatting text, improving readability, and assisting with translation or brainstorming. However, it emphasizes that any efficiency gains are constrained by the need for substantial human review and fact-checking, and thus the paper presents this as a cautious, conditional benefit rather than a measured outcome.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency/productivity in manuscript preparation

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses implications for academic publishing governance, including transparency requirements, authorship rules, and disclosure expectations for AI use in manuscripts. It does not test policy outcomes empirically, but argues that institutions and journals need clear ethical safeguards because AI can threaten integrity through plagiarism, fabricated references, and opaque contribution practices.
finding.measure: Publication ethics, disclosure practices, authorship policy, institutional integrity

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT-like systems, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention experimentally, the authors synthesize early research and provide a conceptual review of how LLMs might support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational technology design across grade levels and settings.

The paper discusses potential uses for students, teachers, and educational systems, including writing support, feedback generation, quiz and content creation, tutoring, language learning, and administrative efficiencies. It also emphasizes major risks and limitations: bias, hallucinations/inaccurate outputs, overreliance by learners and teachers, plagiarism and integrity concerns, privacy/security issues, fairness and access gaps, and the difficulty of distinguishing AI-generated from human-generated work.

Overall, the authors argue that LLMs can be valuable educational tools if used with strong human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, and clear governance. The paper’s main contribution is a balanced framework of benefits, risks, and mitigation strategies rather than empirical evidence of effects on student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, personalized feedback, grading support, and generation of questions, quizzes, and instructional materials. These are described as potential efficiencies rather than measured effects; no study size or effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional risks and governance issues around copyright, plagiarism, bias, fairness, privacy/security, sustainability, and the difficulty of detecting AI-generated work. It also recommends policy, transparency, monitoring, and curriculum changes, but reports no empirical evaluation of these system-level outcomes.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, integrity, privacy, fairness, and institutional readiness

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly warns that learners may rely too heavily on LLMs, which could reduce critical thinking, problem-solving, independent investigation, and evidence-based judgment. It also notes the need to teach fact-checking and corroboration strategies, but provides no direct empirical measurement of skill change.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, and independent inquiry

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents LLMs as tools that can assist reading and writing through grammar corrections, summaries, outlines, style suggestions, and feedback, while also warning about inaccurate suggestions, plagiarism, and overreliance. These claims are conceptual and literature-based rather than empirically tested in this paper.
finding.measure: Reading and writing support, including grammar, style, summaries, and writing assistance

paper_profiles.title: Assessing second-language academic writing: AI vs. Human raters
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Educational Technology & Online Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether ChatGPT-3.5 can score second-language academic writing in a way that is comparable to trained human raters. The authors motivate the work by noting that conventional writing assessment is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and sometimes inconsistent, and they ask whether a large language model could assist or potentially replace part of the rater workload.

Using a paragraph-writing task on unemployment causes, the researchers collected responses from 43 first-year Turkish university students in an English-medium program. Five experienced human raters and ChatGPT-3.5 scored the paragraphs with the same holistic rubric. The study then compared interrater agreement and Spearman correlations among all raters.

Results showed that human raters were more consistent with each other than with ChatGPT, but ChatGPT still showed slight-to-fair agreement with some raters and low-to-moderate positive correlations with two raters. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may be useful as a supplementary scoring tool alongside human raters, but they caution that the system should not be used alone because of limitations such as opaque model processes, vulnerability to being fooled by surface features like length, and the need for finer tuning and better rubrics.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates second-language writing scores assigned to student paragraphs by ChatGPT-3.5 and five human raters. Agreement between ChatGPT and human raters was slight to fair (e.g., κ=.260 with Rater D, p<.001) and correlations were low to moderate and positive for two raters (ChatGPT vs. Rater C rs=.398, n=43, p=.008; ChatGPT vs. Rater D rs=.390, n=43, p=.010), suggesting partial but limited alignment with human scoring.
finding.measure: Holistic paragraph writing scores on a rubric; interrater agreement (Kappa) and correlations (Spearman's rho)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-assisted scoring could reduce the burden of time-consuming, labor-intensive writing assessment and provide faster feedback. However, this is framed as a potential benefit rather than a directly measured outcome in the study, which focuses on score agreement rather than workload or turnaround time.
finding.measure: Perceived/argued teacher workload and scoring efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Evaluating The Efficacy of A Large Language Model in Scaffolding Research Report Writing for EFL Learners
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Basic and Applied Sciences
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT can improve EFL students’ research report writing compared with traditional instruction. The authors frame the work around CALL theory and focus on a constrained academic writing task that requires organization, evidence use, analysis, and language accuracy.

Using a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest design, 60 undergraduate preparatory-year students at Najran University were split into an experimental group that used ChatGPT-4 as a writing assistant and a control group that received traditional textbook-based instruction. The intervention lasted four months and combined explicit prompt training, guided AI use, and teacher oversight; both groups used the same curriculum, rubrics, and instructional time aside from the ChatGPT support.

Quantitative results showed no meaningful pre-intervention differences, but the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group on all five writing domains and on the total achievement score. Effect sizes were large across domains, suggesting substantial gains in content relevance, organization, research and evidence, analysis and critical thinking, and writing quality/presentation. Interview data also indicated that students felt ChatGPT improved grammar, vocabulary, structure, confidence, motivation, and efficiency, while also raising concerns about overreliance, plagiarism, and factual accuracy. The authors conclude that LLMs can meaningfully support research report writing when paired with teacher guidance and academic-integrity safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group using ChatGPT improved significantly more than the control group on research report writing. In the post-test, the experimental group outperformed the control group on all five writing domains and the total score (e.g., total M=16.67 vs. 11.80, t=17.476, p<0.001, η²=0.840), indicating a large positive effect on academic writing performance.
finding.measure: 20-item research report writing achievement test covering content and relevance, organization and structure, research and evidence, analysis and critical thinking, and writing quality and presentation
finding.std_deviation: experimental total SD=1.12; control total SD=1.03

finding.finding_summary: Interview data indicated that ChatGPT increased students' confidence and motivation to write, and students described the tool as easy to use, time-saving, and encouraging. These perceptions suggest beneficial effects on engagement and willingness to participate in writing tasks, although some students also noted overreliance concerns.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on confidence, motivation, usability, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved higher-order writing skills linked to durable skills, especially analysis and critical thinking. The post-test showed a very large advantage for the experimental group in the analysis and critical thinking domain (M=3.02 vs. 1.95, t=18.422, p<0.001, η²=0.854), suggesting stronger reasoning and evaluative performance in report writing.
finding.measure: Achievement test domain score for analysis and critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT saved time and made drafting and revising research reports easier. The study does not report a direct time-on-task comparison, but qualitative evidence consistently framed ChatGPT as a productivity aid for generating outlines, revising text, and improving structure.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on time-saving, ease of use, and drafting/revision support

paper_profiles.title: The impact of using ChatGPT for feedback in EFL writing: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks what empirical evidence exists on the impact of ChatGPT-generated feedback on student writing performance in EFL/ESL contexts. The authors systematically reviewed 30 empirical studies published from 2023 to March 2025, screening studies from Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost and retaining only interventions that measured writing outcomes rather than perceptions alone.

Across the included studies, ChatGPT was used in a variety of feedback-oriented ways: directly by students during drafting and revision, as a support for self- and peer-assessment, and in hybrid models where teachers mediated or adapted AI-generated feedback. Most studies involved university learners, though two focused on upper secondary students. The review found the strongest and most consistent benefits for linguistic accuracy, followed by overall writing quality, organization, content development, and vocabulary.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT can improve writing performance, but its effects are highly dependent on how learners and teachers use the tool. Gains are strongest when ChatGPT is embedded in a learner-centered instructional framework with explicit prompting instruction, critical engagement with AI feedback, and teacher mediation. The review also notes risks of overreliance, reduced learner agency, and uncertain long-term sustainability of gains, especially in the absence of ongoing pedagogical support.

finding.finding_summary: Across 30 empirical studies, ChatGPT feedback was generally associated with improved EFL/ESL writing performance, especially in linguistic accuracy, organization, content, vocabulary, and overall writing quality. The review reports the most frequent gains in linguistic accuracy (13 studies), followed by overall improvement (10 studies), organization (9 studies), content (7 studies), and vocabulary (5 studies), but it does not aggregate effect sizes across studies.
finding.measure: Writing performance / writing quality outcomes (linguistic accuracy, organization, content development, vocabulary, overall writing scores)

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies reported increased motivation, affective engagement, and positive perceptions when students used ChatGPT for writing feedback, but other studies raised concerns about overreliance and reduced confidence or ownership. The review also notes that some interventions improved learner engagement, while short-term gains did not always persist.
finding.measure: Motivation, affective engagement, learner perceptions/ownership

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly emphasizes prompt literacy, critical engagement with AI feedback, metacognition, and autonomous revision as key mediators of writing improvement. Evidence from the included studies suggests that students who critically evaluated and selectively applied ChatGPT feedback improved more than passive users, but overreliance and shallow revision limited deeper skill development.
finding.measure: Prompt literacy, critical engagement, metacognitive revision, autonomous use

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that ChatGPT may reduce feedback burden and support faster, more immediate feedback than teacher-only approaches, and some hybrid models used it to streamline teacher feedback preparation. However, this outcome is secondary to the writing-performance focus, and the paper does not report pooled quantitative evidence on workload or efficiency.
finding.measure: Feedback provision efficiency / teacher workload support

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging A Large Language Model for Precision Enhancement in EFL Email Writing: A Quasi-Experimental Study
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Basic and Applied Sciences
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) can improve EFL students’ ability to write formal business emails, especially in the structural and linguistic components of genre-appropriate email writing. The paper asks two main questions: how effective an AI-powered tool is for improving business writing skills, and how students experience using ChatGPT during the writing process.

The intervention used a quasi-experimental mixed-method design with 60 undergraduate preparatory-year students at Najran University in Saudi Arabia, split into an experimental group and a control group. Both groups completed pre- and post-tests on formal email writing across eight rubric domains (subject line, salutation, writer information, contents, matter of concern, closing line, sign-off, signature), but the experimental group also received ChatGPT-assisted practice over four months while the control group received traditional instruction. The study also included semi-structured interviews with 15 students from the experimental group to capture perceptions of usability, efficiency, and confidence.

Quantitative results showed no meaningful pre-test differences between groups, but the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group on the post-test overall and across all eight email-writing domains. The largest gains were in content development and closing lines, with very large effect sizes reported for the total score (eta squared = 0.738) and for contents (eta squared = 0.690). Qualitative findings suggested that students found ChatGPT easy to use, time-saving, confidence-building, and helpful for producing better subject lines, content, and closings, though some noted risks of overreliance and the need for teacher guidance. Overall, the paper concludes that ChatGPT can meaningfully improve formal email writing when used as a scaffolded, human-in-the-loop instructional aid.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group outperformed the control group on post-test formal email writing scores after four months of ChatGPT-mediated instruction. Overall total score improved significantly (control M=13.23, SD=1.43; experiment M=18.17, SD=1.56; t(58)=12.785, p=0.000), with a very large effect size (eta squared=0.738), and gains were significant across all eight rubric domains.
finding.measure: Formal email writing test scored on eight domains: subject line, salutation, information about the writer, appropriate contents, matter of concern, closing line, sign-off, signature

finding.finding_summary: Interview data indicated that students perceived ChatGPT as confidence-building, motivating, easy to use, and helpful for reducing difficulty in formal email writing. Students explicitly described it as user-friendly, time-saving, and supportive of writing challenges, although some also warned about overreliance.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes and student perceptions of confidence, motivation, usability, and time-saving value

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT helped students organize content, improve coherence, evaluate AI outputs against a rubric, and revise drafts in their own words, suggesting gains in metacognitive writing processes. Students were required to prompt, critique, and justify revisions, and the authors describe these as human-in-the-loop evaluation and reflection activities.
finding.measure: Reflection logs, rubric-based revision process, and interview comments about organization/coherence and critical use of AI outputs

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT was time-saving and productive for formal email writing tasks. The qualitative analysis identified efficiency and productivity as a major theme, with participants stating that the tool helped solve frequent writing problems more quickly than manual drafting.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about time-saving, efficiency, and productivity

paper_profiles.title: Students’ Perceptions of AI-Powered Feedback in English Writing: Benefits and Challenges in Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Changes in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how Chinese EFL university students perceive and use AI-powered feedback tools for English writing, and what benefits, challenges, and instructional role such tools should have. The paper focuses on three forms of AI-supported feedback: automated writing evaluation (AWE), generative AI (GAI), and corpus tools. It is motivated by a gap in research on students’ cognitive and affective engagement with AI feedback, especially their ability to interact critically with these tools rather than simply accept their suggestions.

The study was conducted in a compulsory English writing course for first-year English majors at a provincial university in eastern China (n=210). Using reflective journals, classroom observations, and student writing/screenshots, the author conducted qualitative thematic analysis in NVivo. Students reported that AI tools were especially useful for surface-level language improvement, instant feedback, and autonomous revision, with Grammarly used by 52% of participants and Pigai by 22%.

At the same time, students identified important limitations: AI feedback was often vague, context-insensitive, and weak at handling content development, cohesion, emotions, and creativity. Many students valued teacher feedback more highly for deeper, personalized, and culturally appropriate guidance, and 89% said teacher feedback offered unique depth and flexibility. The paper concludes that AI should complement, not replace, teacher feedback, and proposes a Student-Teacher-AI Collaboration Model (S-T-AI) that assigns AI to technical correction and teachers to higher-order guidance, supported by AI literacy training to reduce dependency and support critical engagement.

finding.finding_summary: Students overwhelmingly reported that AI-powered feedback improved English writing at the surface level, especially grammar, spelling, punctuation, word choice, and clarity. In the qualitative sample of 210 first-year English majors, 84% said these tools helped correct common language issues, and examples showed revisions becoming more concise and precise; however, students also said AI often failed to address higher-order writing concerns such as content, cohesion, and stylistic nuance.
finding.measure: Student reflective journals, classroom observations, and student writing/revision examples about English writing feedback and revision quality

finding.finding_summary: Students described AI feedback as increasing writing confidence because it was instant, accessible, and easy to use, which reduced waiting time for teacher comments. At the same time, they expressed concern that reliance on AI could weaken independent learning and reduce motivation to think through revisions on their own.
finding.measure: Student reflective journals and perceptions of confidence, autonomy, and dependence during writing revision

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally examines critical thinking, metacognitive evaluation, and human-AI interactive negotiation competence (HAINC). Students often cross-checked AI suggestions with corpora, dictionaries, and their own judgments, but they also warned against blindly accepting AI output and noted that AI could misread context or intended meaning. The overall finding is that AI can support critical engagement, but only when students actively evaluate and selectively use feedback rather than overrely on it.
finding.measure: Reflective journals, cross-checking behaviors, and qualitative evidence of critical evaluation of AI feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that AI-powered feedback improved revision efficiency by providing instant, on-demand corrections and reducing dependence on delayed teacher feedback. Tools such as Grammarly and ChatGPT were seen as convenient across devices and platforms, making it easier for students to revise independently and manage writing tasks more quickly.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of feedback speed, convenience, and revision efficiency in reflective journals

paper_profiles.title: Individuality and Commonality in Thesis Writing: Strategies and Classroom Activities
paper_profiles.venue: Academic Writing in Additional Languages (Lx): Teaching, Research, and Emerging Technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how academic writing instruction can help university students balance individuality (authorial voice, stance, personal positioning) and commonality (discipline-appropriate conventions and community norms) in thesis writing. The authors situate the problem within English-medium higher education and argue that students, especially those writing in an additional language, need explicit support to understand discourse communities, genre expectations, and voice.

The chapter presents a curated set of teaching materials from an Introduction to Academic Writing course at the University of Modena and Reggio Emilia, an EMI program for master’s students in Languages for Communication in International Enterprises and Organisations. The course was designed around an integrated process-genre model and organized into pre-writing, writing, and post-writing modules, with activities on discourse communities, thesis structure, source synthesis, stance, hedging, and boosting. The chapter describes the course context, pedagogical rationale, specific classroom tasks, and examples of student reflections, emphasizing iterative refinement of materials from a pilot offering (n=19) to a revised implementation.

Overall, the chapter concludes that a hybrid process-genre pedagogy can support students’ development of academic writing, reflective thinking, and disciplinary awareness while giving them tools to construct an individual academic voice within the constraints of a scholarly community. Because the piece is primarily pedagogical and descriptive, it does not test a comparator against an AI writing assistant; rather, it offers a structured instructional model and classroom activities for thesis preparation.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that the process-genre-based course materials improved students’ academic writing development by helping them analyze abstracts, synthesize sources, write reflections, and practice thesis sections such as the abstract, literature review, and discussion. In the only reported pilot implementation, the materials were associated with high student grades and enthusiastic feedback from students, though the chapter does not provide a controlled effect estimate.
finding.measure: Student writing tasks, reflective writing, formative and summative assessments, and instructor observations/reflections

finding.finding_summary: A central aim of the chapter is to develop critical analysis, reflective writing, metacognition, and the ability to position oneself in a discourse community. The activities ask students to compare abstracts, justify interpretations, and reflect on differences between discourse communities, which the authors frame as building higher-order writing and thinking skills rather than only teaching surface forms.
finding.measure: Comparative analysis tasks, reflective commentary, and student engagement with discourse-community concepts

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that the classroom activities were designed to build writing confidence, engagement, and a sense of inclusion, and they describe positive student reactions to collaborative activities and discussions. While no standardized affective measure is reported, the chapter presents these as important outcomes of the instructional design.
finding.measure: Student reflections, participation in warm-ups and follow-up discussions, and reported enthusiasm/feedback

paper_profiles.title: Reconstructing stance in EFL doctoral thesis writing through generative artificial intelligence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether and how generative AI has changed stance construction in doctoral thesis writing in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts. Rather than comparing AI-generated text to student text directly, the author uses a difference-in-differences design to compare doctoral dissertations from 2019–2021 (pre-diffusion) and 2022–2024 (diffusion period) across applied linguistics subfields with high versus low AI exposure.

The dataset comprises 120 Chinese doctoral theses in applied linguistics, split evenly across high-AI-exposure subfields (e.g., computational linguistics, corpus linguistics) and low-AI-exposure subfields (e.g., sociolinguistics, language pedagogy). The study analyzes introductions using Hyland-style stance categories: hedges, boosters, attitude markers, and self-mentions, supplemented by qualitative textual comparison of representative theses. The author also tests whether thesis topic and methodology moderate the AI effect.

Results suggest that generative AI is associated with a shift toward more direct, conclusive, and less cautious academic writing in high-AI-exposure subfields. In the post-2022 period, hedges decreased significantly, especially expressions of possibility and speculation, while conclusive boosters and authorial identity markers increased. Attitude markers overall declined, but evaluative expressions rose, suggesting a move away from subjective/emotional stance toward more objective argumentation. The effects were strongest in highly AI-adapted topics such as corpus linguistics, indicating that disciplinary context moderates how generative AI reshapes academic writing practices.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies doctoral thesis writing and finds that generative AI is associated with a more direct, assertive, and less hedged writing style in AI-exposed subfields. In the DiD model, hedges decreased significantly (β3=-1.20, p=0.02), conclusive expressions increased (β3=+0.78, p=0.02), and author identity markers increased (β3=+0.62, p=0.01) in the high-AI group after 2022, based on 120 theses.
finding.measure: Stance markers in the introduction sections of doctoral theses (hedges, boosters, attitude markers, self-mentions) per 1000 words

finding.finding_summary: The paper interprets the observed changes as reflecting shifts in rhetorical judgment and critical positioning, especially reduced uncertainty and more conclusive argumentation in AI-exposed fields. Although it does not directly measure critical thinking or metacognition, it substantively examines how generative AI may alter authors’ argumentative caution and stance-taking, which are closely related to durable skills.
finding.measure: Textual indicators of caution, certainty, evaluation, and authorial presence in thesis introductions

paper_profiles.title: Individuality and Commonality in Thesis Writing: Strategies and Classroom Activities
paper_profiles.venue: Academic Writing in Additional Languages (Lx): Teaching, Research, and Emerging Technologies (book chapter, University of Warsaw Press)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses how to teach thesis-writing skills in an English-medium master’s program, with a particular focus on the tension between individuality and commonality in academic voice. The authors argue that students need help both understanding the conventions of their discourse community and developing an authorial stance that is appropriate to academic writing.

The chapter presents a curated set of teaching materials from an Introduction to Academic Writing course at the University of Modena and Reggio Emilia. The course is structured around an integrated process-genre model and includes a sequence of activities on discourse communities, genre awareness, source use, and voice, such as comparing abstracts from different disciplines, reflective writing, and guided writing tasks. The materials were first piloted with 19 students in autumn 2022 and then refined for implementation in 2023; the chapter reports largely positive student feedback from surveys, formative/summative assessments, and instructor reflections cited from the pilot study.

Overall, the chapter concludes that combining process and genre pedagogies can help novice thesis writers move from merely reproducing conventions toward more reflective and purposeful academic writing. The activities are intended to support critical analysis, metacognitive awareness, and the ability to balance disciplinary norms with an individual academic voice. The paper is primarily pedagogical and descriptive rather than a controlled effectiveness study, but it suggests the approach is promising for EAP/EMI contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter presents a structured EAP thesis-writing curriculum intended to improve students’ academic writing, especially reflective commentary, abstract writing, literature review synthesis, and thesis-related genre awareness. In the pilot implementation with 19 master’s students, the authors report largely positive outcomes, including high student grades, enthusiastic feedback, and effective instructor evaluations, though no controlled effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Student writing tasks, reflective writing, formative and summative assessments, student surveys, instructor reflections
finding.study_size: n=19 (pilot course); additional qualitative reflections not separately quantified

finding.finding_summary: A central goal of the chapter is to develop critical analysis, self-reflection, metacognition, and synthesis skills through comparative analysis of abstracts and guided reflection. The authors describe these skills as growing across the course, and students’ reflections reportedly showed increased awareness of discourse-community differences and genre features.
finding.measure: Comparative analysis task, reflective writing, student reflections

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports that the teaching activities were designed to increase writing confidence and engagement through collaborative, learner-centred tasks, peer review, and guided reflection. In the pilot course, the authors describe enthusiastic student feedback and productive classroom discussion, suggesting improved engagement, though no quantitative engagement effect is reported.
finding.measure: Student surveys, classroom participation, written reflections

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that the refined course design improved usability and manageability of the curriculum by prioritising interactive learning and reducing overload within a three-credit course. The main evidence is qualitative: instructor reflections from the pilot indicated the original curriculum was too extensive, leading to revisions to better balance educational efficacy and workload.
finding.measure: Instructor reflections; course design revision process

paper_profiles.title: Individuality and Commonality in Thesis Writing: Strategies and Classroom Activities
paper_profiles.venue: Academic Writing in Additional Languages (Lx): Teaching, Research, and Emerging Technologies
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate / Graduate students (Master’s students in an EMI EAP thesis-preparatory course)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses how to teach academic writing for thesis preparation in an English-medium master’s program, with a particular focus on helping students balance individuality (authorial voice, stance, and originality) and commonality (disciplinary conventions, genre expectations, and discourse-community norms). The authors situate the problem within EAP/EMI contexts and argue that thesis writing should be taught not as grammar correction alone, but as a socially situated, genre-informed practice.

The chapter presents a curated set of pedagogical materials from an Introduction to Academic Writing course at the University of Modena and Reggio Emilia. The course was designed for Master’s students in the multilingual program Languages for Communication in International Enterprises and Organisations, using an integrated process-genre model and a hybrid EGAP/ESAP orientation. The chapter explains the curriculum structure, then details classroom activities focused on discourse communities, abstract comparison, source use, stance, hedging/boosting, and reflective writing, drawing on sociocultural, constructivist, and inquiry-based learning principles.

Evidence discussed in the chapter comes from implementation of course materials, including a pilot with 19 students in autumn 2022 and a refined version used in 2023. The authors report that the pilot produced generally positive results, including high grades, enthusiastic student feedback, and favorable instructor evaluations, but also revealed the challenge of covering too much content in a three-credit course. Their overall conclusion is that a blended process-genre approach can support students’ academic writing development and voice construction, while peer review, guided reflection, and explicit attention to genre and discourse-community expectations are central to effective instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports that the thesis-writing course materials supported students’ academic writing development, especially through activities on abstracts, literature reviews, stance, and reflective writing. In the pilot implementation with n=19 students, the authors describe high student grades and generally positive feedback, suggesting improved writing performance and engagement, though no standardized effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student writing tasks, reflective writing, formative and summative assessments, student surveys

finding.finding_summary: The course is reported to have generated enthusiastic student feedback and supported writing confidence through structured activities and collaborative work. The authors emphasize increased engagement, reflective participation, and a learner-centred environment, but provide no quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Student surveys, student reflections, class participation

finding.finding_summary: The chapter centrally targets critical thinking, reflection, and metacognition through comparative analysis, synthesis, self-reflection, and genre awareness. In the pilot, students’ reflections showed that the comparison of abstracts helped them notice discourse-community differences and grapple with genre analysis, indicating gains in analytical and metacognitive skills; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Comparative analysis tasks, reflective writing, instructor observations, student reflections

finding.finding_summary: The materials were effective pedagogically but also exposed a practical constraint: the curriculum was too extensive for a three-credit course. The authors state that pilot feedback led to revision of the materials to improve balance between educational efficacy and workload, indicating an efficiency challenge alongside instructional success.
finding.measure: Instructor reflections, panel discussion on curriculum revision, pilot implementation feedback

paper_profiles.title: Individuality and Commonality in Thesis Writing: Strategies and Classroom Activities
paper_profiles.venue: Academic Writing in Additional Languages (LX): Teaching, Research, and Emerging Technologies (book chapter, University of Warsaw Press)
paper_profiles.population: Graduate/Master’s students in an EMI/EAP university program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter addresses how to teach thesis-writing skills to graduate students in English-medium and additional-language academic contexts, with a particular emphasis on balancing individuality (authorial voice) and commonality (disciplinary conventions). The authors argue that thesis writing requires students to learn the rhetorical and linguistic expectations of discourse communities while also developing a meaningful personal academic stance.

The chapter presents a curated set of classroom materials from an Introduction to Academic Writing course at the University of Modena and Reggio Emilia in Italy. The course is positioned within an EMI Master’s program and is organized through an integrated process-genre framework, combining pre-writing, writing, and post-writing modules. It includes explicit instruction on academic discourse communities, genre awareness, source use, stance, hedging, boosting, and peer review, supported by authentic tasks such as comparing abstracts, reflective writing, and guided commentary.

The paper is primarily descriptive and pedagogical rather than experimental. It reports the design and refinement of the materials, including a pilot implementation with 19 students in autumn 2022 and subsequent revision for use in 2023. The chapter concludes that a hybrid process-genre approach can support students’ awareness of academic voice and genre conventions, while student reflections suggest the activities helped them engage critically with discourse communities and begin articulating their own stance in academic writing.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that the instructional sequence supported students’ academic writing development, especially in thesis-related genres such as abstracts, literature reviews, and discussion sections. In the reported pilot implementation (n=19), outcomes were described as largely positive, with high student grades and positive feedback on writing-related tasks, but no standardized writing effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Academic writing performance, including reflective writing, thesis-related tasks, student grades, and instructor evaluation of written work
finding.study_size: n=19 (pilot course); subsequent refined implementation size not reported

finding.finding_summary: The activities were explicitly designed to foster critical analysis, reflection, metacognition, and the ability to synthesize sources and articulate stance. Student reflections indicated that the comparative and guided tasks helped them understand genre differences and begin developing an individual academic position, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Critical analysis, reflective writing, source synthesis, stance/voice awareness, and metacognitive engagement
finding.study_size: n=19 (pilot course); student reflection excerpts from the course, exact reflection sample size not reported

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Effects of Generative AI Assistance on Writing Self-efficacy
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2026 ACM CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This pilot study asks how different configurations of generative AI assistance affect students’ writing self-efficacy during argumentative writing. Rather than treating AI support as a single treatment, the authors compare four conditions: no AI, sentence-level AI, ideation-level AI, and full-process AI, using a 2 × 2 between-subjects experimental design. The work is motivated by concern that AI may improve writing performance while also altering learner agency, ownership, and confidence.

The study was conducted with 13 Korean undergraduate students who completed two argumentative writing tasks in an online session using ChatGPT. After each task, participants completed a post-task writing self-efficacy survey on a 0–100 scale. The main quantitative patterns showed that ideation-level AI had the most positive trajectory in self-efficacy change, sentence-level AI produced consistent decline, full-process AI yielded high but mostly stable self-efficacy, and no-AI was lowest on average with high variability.

Because this was a small pilot, the authors frame results as exploratory rather than definitive. Still, the findings suggest that where AI intervenes in the writing process matters more than simply whether AI is used. AI that supports idea generation while leaving sentence construction to the writer may better preserve agency and support sustainable confidence, whereas sentence-level revision and full-text generation may weaken ownership or trigger unfavorable comparisons with AI output.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies writing self-efficacy and finds that AI configuration shaped confidence differently across conditions. In 13 Korean undergraduates, ideation AI showed the strongest positive change in self-efficacy (ΔM = +11.1, SD(Δ) = 16.2), sentence AI declined for all 5 participants (ΔM = −5.7, SD(Δ) = 5.6), full AI was nearly stable (ΔM = +0.5, SD(Δ) = 6.7), and no AI showed a slight increase (ΔM = +1.3, SD(Δ) = 2.4).
finding.measure: Writing self-efficacy (0–100 continuous scale; post-task questionnaire)

finding.finding_summary: The study examines argumentative writing support and the perceived ability to perform writing tasks, but it does not report scored writing quality outcomes such as rubric-based essay quality. Instead, it measures writing self-efficacy during two argumentative writing tasks and reports that AI support type affected writers’ confidence in performing literacy-related processes such as idea generation, grammar correction, and argument construction. The evidence is therefore indirect for writing achievement, but central to academic writing processes.
finding.measure: Argumentative writing task context; self-efficacy items related to grammar, vocabulary, coherence, evidence use, and writing process

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly discusses learner agency, ownership, and process management as part of writing self-efficacy. Ideation AI was associated with positive change in process-related confidence, while full AI was linked to stable self-efficacy but qualitative signs of reduced ownership, and sentence AI was associated with decline, suggesting different AI configurations can support or undermine metacognitive control over the writing process.
finding.measure: Writing self-efficacy subscales, especially Management of the Writing Process; qualitative post-task reflections

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This qualitative case study examines how secondary EFL students prompt ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots while completing a writing task. The paper asks what kinds of prompt content students use and what patterns emerge in their prompt engineering pathways during a machine-in-the-loop writing activity.

The intervention/approach is not an evaluated instructional program but an observational analysis of students’ first-time use of SOTA chatbots for writing. Four high-achieving Form 1 students in a Hong Kong secondary school completed the same timed blog-writing task on iPads while screen recordings captured their prompts. The authors coded 36 usable prompt turns and identified six prompt types, including auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, greetings, search-engine-like prompts, and chatbot-suggested prompts.

The main conclusion is that students used a trial-and-error process and displayed different prompt engineering pathways, with some pathways appearing more sophisticated than others. Students often refined prompts by making small word changes, reused ideas across prompts, and sometimes switched chatbots to test outputs. The authors conclude that EFL students likely need explicit prompt engineering instruction to move beyond unsystematic experimentation and to use chatbots more effectively for writing support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test whether ChatGPT improved writing quality or writing scores; instead, it qualitatively analyzes how four secondary EFL students used chatbots while composing a blog entry. The central finding is descriptive: students completed the task through varied prompt engineering pathways (36 coded turns after excluding 2 accidental prompts), but the study provides no comparative writing outcome or effect size.
finding.measure: Prompt types, prompt sequences, and completed blog-writing task output

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that students were engaging in iterative trial-and-error prompting, refining instructions, changing questions, and reusing ideas across turns, which the authors interpret as evidence of developing prompt engineering skill. The observed behavior suggests growth in metacognitive strategy use and technology-mediated problem solving, although no direct skill assessment was conducted.
finding.measure: Observed prompt engineering pathways and prompt content coding

finding.finding_summary: Students showed persistence in completing the writing task and continued experimenting with prompts across multiple turns, but the study does not measure motivation, engagement, or self-regulation directly. The authors infer that students were learning through trial-and-error, yet they also characterize them as unsophisticated users who lacked instruction on how to prompt effectively.
finding.measure: Observed persistence and iterative prompting during a timed writing task

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of AI-Driven Tools on Student Writing Development: A Case Study From The CGScholar AI Helper Project
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether CGScholar AI Helper, a curated generative-AI writing feedback tool, can support the writing development of 11th-grade English Language Arts students. The authors frame the study as part of a broader research-and-development effort to build and refine a classroom-mediated AI feedback system, rather than an unmediated chatbot, and they emphasize alignment with teacher rubrics, prompt engineering, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using teacher-selected texts.

The intervention was tested in a public high school in the Midwestern United States with one ELA teacher and six struggling writers in an 11th-grade class. Students wrote a short paragraph response to two teacher-selected readings, received AI feedback based on the teacher’s rubric, revised, and then received a second round of AI feedback before final teacher evaluation. Data came from students’ drafts, revised drafts, focus group feedback, teacher post-survey, and researcher observations, analyzed thematically.

The main conclusion is that the AI Helper generally supported writing improvement when feedback was closely tied to the teacher’s materials and rubric. Five of the six students improved on at least one rubric criterion, and one student improved on three criteria. The strongest gains were in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, analyzing Indigenous culture, and introducing/connective use of evidence. Students and the teacher reported that the feedback was direct, specific, and actionable, though it was also viewed as too long and too elaborate, leading the team to add chat functionality and consider feedback-length controls in later iterations.

finding.finding_summary: The case study found that CGScholar AI Helper supported writing development for 11th-grade ELA students. Five of six students improved on at least one rubric criterion and one student improved on three criteria after receiving AI feedback and revising their drafts, with gains most evident in compare/contrast, composing defensible claims, analyzing, and introducing/connectivity of evidence.
finding.measure: Teacher rubric ratings of student writing drafts and revised drafts across six criteria (Compare and Contrast, Identify, Compose, Introduce and Connect, Support Evidence, Analyze)

finding.finding_summary: Students and the teacher reported that the AI feedback was helpful, direct, specific, actionable, and encouraging, and that it motivated students to revise their work. Focus group comments indicated that the tool gave students something to 'go off of' and helped them know what to fix, suggesting improved engagement with revision.
finding.measure: Focus group feedback, teacher post-survey, and researcher observations of student revision behavior

paper_profiles.title: Machine-Assisted Grading of Nationwide School-Leaving Essay Exams with LLMs and Statistical NLP
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
