This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) and statistical NLP methods can automate scoring of Estonian national school-leaving essays reliably enough for high-stakes use. The central problem is the burden and inconsistency of human essay grading in a small-language, nationwide exam system, especially as Estonia moves toward fully digital assessment. The authors focus on whether machine-assisted grading can match or approximate the consensus of human assessors while remaining rubric-driven and suitable for human-in-the-loop workflows.

The study uses two cohorts of digitally produced trial-exam essays from Estonia: 781 ninth-grade essays and 764 twelfth-grade essays, each scored by two human assessors. The authors prompt several commercial LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o4-mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0 Flash) to score rubric categories separately in zero-shot mode, then compare their outputs to human average scores. They also build supervised regression models from 108 linguistic features to predict five language-correctness rubric categories, and they test vulnerability to prompt injection as well as the model’s ability to write essays itself.

Results show that LLMs generally achieve near-human performance on many rubric dimensions, with total-score MAE roughly 2.66-4.97 on a 0-27 scale and many predictions falling within the human scoring range. The statistical NLP pipelines perform slightly better on some mechanically measurable categories such as punctuation and vocabulary, while LLMs are more flexible across broader rubric dimensions. The paper concludes that machine-assisted grading is feasible for national-scale exam scoring, but should be deployed with human oversight because of bias, prompt-injection vulnerability, and the need for careful rubric design.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that LLM-based grading can approximate human scoring of high-school essay writing on a national exam. Across 9th- and 12th-grade datasets (n=781 and n=764 essays, respectively), model total-score MAE ranged from 2.66 to 4.97 on a 0-27 scale, and many predictions fell within the human score range; several rubric categories were near human-variance levels.
finding.measure: Essay scoring on national writing-exam rubrics (content, vocabulary, syntax, punctuation, orthography/morphology, structure/formatting)
finding.study_size: n=1545 essays total (n=781 grade 9; n=764 grade 12)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM-assisted grading can substantially reduce scorer workload and enable faster processing of large exam cohorts. It reports that automated scoring is viable at national scale and highlights the ability to generate fine-grained subscore profiles for more detailed feedback than manual grading typically permits.
finding.measure: Feasibility of national-scale automated grading; token/cost estimates and workflow efficiency considerations

finding.finding_summary: The findings support the feasibility of integrating LLM-assisted assessment into a national high-stakes exam system under a human-in-the-loop model. The authors conclude that such systems can be deployed in a regulated setting while preserving human oversight, compliance, and auditable workflows, especially in Estonia’s transition to digital exams.
finding.measure: Policy/implementation feasibility for national exam grading systems and human-in-the-loop deployment

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Explainable AI for LLM Text Attribution: Differentiating Human-Written and Multiple LLMs-Generated Text
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of distinguishing human-written text from text generated by large language models (LLMs), motivated in part by concerns about plagiarism and declining writing skill development in educational contexts. The authors argue that as students increasingly use tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Bard, LLaMA, and Perplexity, instructors need reliable ways to attribute text to its source.

The study proposes a machine learning pipeline for text attribution using 600 essay observations: 300 human essays from the Kaggle LLM detection dataset and 300 essays generated by five LLMs. After preprocessing and TF-IDF feature extraction, the authors compare Random Forest, XGBoost, and RNN models on binary classification (human vs. LLM) and multi-class classification (human plus five source labels). They also apply LIME for explainability to identify class-specific linguistic features.

Results show strong performance in binary classification, with accuracies of 97% for Random Forest, 98% for XGBoost, and 94% for RNN; multi-classification is harder but still performs well for Random Forest (97% accuracy), with lower performance for XGBoost (94%) and RNN (88%). The authors additionally compare their binary detector against GPTZero and report that their model achieves 97.5% accuracy versus GPTZero’s 78.3%, while also recognizing the full test set. The paper concludes that targeted ML plus XAI can improve content attribution and plagiarism detection, though it is fundamentally a text-detection study rather than a study of educational outcomes or writing instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed ML detector improved text-attribution efficiency by classifying all test observations and outperforming GPTZero on the held-out binary test set. The authors report 97.5% accuracy for their model versus 78.3% for GPTZero, and note that GPTZero failed to recognize about 4.2% of observations while their model classified the complete test dataset.
finding.measure: Binary text attribution accuracy comparing the proposed model with GPTZero
finding.study_size: n=120 test observations for GPTZero comparison (20% of 600); n=600 total dataset

paper_profiles.title: WRITE+SYNC: Software Cache Write Covert Channels Exploiting Memory-disk Synchronization
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a software covert-channel vulnerability in operating systems, not an educational intervention. The authors investigate how delayed write caching and memory-disk synchronization calls such as sync, fsync, fdatasync, msync, and fcntl can be exploited to transmit information covertly between processes.

The proposed WRITE+SYNC attack family uses one process to modulate whether data in the write buffer is synchronized to disk and another process to measure synchronization latency as a signal. The paper develops single-file/page protocols and three optimizations: multi-bit encoding, asynchronous communication, and one-time transmission. It evaluates transmission rate, bit error rate, and timing behavior on Linux and macOS, including sandbox scenarios, and demonstrates practical non-education attacks such as website fingerprinting and performance degradation.

Because the work is a computer security systems paper focused on covert channels, it does not study students, teachers, writing instruction, or AI in education. Its main conclusion is that synchronization primitives can be misused as high-speed covert channels in software caches, especially where read-only access is possible, and that mitigation likely requires patching, detection, or isolation strategies.

paper_profiles.title: AI and jobs. A review of theory, estimates, and evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the economic theory and empirical evidence on how generative AI affects labor markets, with a focus on job exposure, productivity, substitution, and work organization. It does not study a single educational intervention or school-based sample; instead, it synthesizes findings from theory papers, ex-ante exposure studies, randomized experiments, field experiments, digital trace data, surveys, and administrative data.

The review organizes the literature around three levels: macroeconomic production-function approaches, task-based models, and team/collective-intelligence perspectives. It also compares different AI exposure measures built from O*NET, expert judgments, patent text, and related data sources, highlighting their strengths and limitations.

Across the ex-post evidence reviewed, the paper concludes that AI often raises productivity, but the magnitude depends strongly on context and task complexity. It reports sizable gains in controlled RCTs and field experiments, mixed distributional effects across skill groups, declining demand for some substitutable writing/translation tasks, and growing evidence of reduced demand for novice workers in some settings. The paper’s main contribution is a synthesis of labor-market evidence rather than a direct evaluation of educational AI tools, so it offers only indirect relevance to high-school writing assistants.

finding.finding_summary: Across reviewed experimental studies, AI use is associated with sizable productivity gains, typically about 20–60% in controlled RCTs and 15–30% in field experiments, though effects vary by task and setting. The paper emphasizes that gains are context-dependent and often stronger for novice workers on simple tasks, while implementation frictions can reduce the realized effect in natural settings.
finding.measure: Productivity / task completion speed / output in experimental and field settings

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes evidence that AI can improve performance on complex tasks and support reasoning, but it also notes that benefits are mixed for higher-skill users and may depend on task structure, expertise, and context. In simple tasks, some observed gains may reflect automation or 'passive pasting' rather than genuine learning or metacognitive improvement.
finding.measure: Performance on complex tasks, reasoning, and expert/specialist task completion

paper_profiles.title: Write asymmetry of spin-orbit torque memory induced by in-plane magnetic fields
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates a device-level problem in spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory (SOT-MRAM): write asymmetry, or the tendency for switching current to differ between the two resistance directions. The authors ask whether the asymmetry, already known in spin-transfer torque MRAM, also appears in SOT-MRAM and what physical factors drive it.

Using Ta/CoFeB/MgO Hall-bar devices fabricated on silicon substrates, the study measures anomalous Hall resistance and current-induced switching under varying in-plane magnetic fields and field tilt angles. The authors compare up-to-down and down-to-up switching currents, estimate spin-orbit torque efficiency through effective perpendicular field measurements, and contrast the results with coherent-switching and domain-expansion models. They find that switching currents are intrinsically asymmetric in their devices and highly sensitive to the angle and magnitude of the applied field.

The main conclusion is that the asymmetry is not a minor artifact but a fundamental feature of the measured SOT switching behavior, largely dominated by domain expansion rather than coherent switching. However, the asymmetry can be reduced or eliminated by carefully tuning the applied field so that the torque efficiencies for the two switching directions become symmetric. The findings are presented as a guideline for designing more symmetric SOT-MRAM devices, including field-free architectures.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates switching-current asymmetry and switching behavior in SOT-MRAM devices, which is directly relevant to write performance and device efficiency. It shows that the write asymmetry can be very large (|ΔIc|/|Ic|min > 1000% for |H| > 400 Oe), but that it can also be tuned toward zero at certain fields (e.g., H ≈ ±200 Oe), indicating the potential for more efficient and symmetric operation.
finding.measure: Critical switching current (Ic), switching-current asymmetry (ΔIc/|Ic|min), and spin-orbit torque efficiency (χ) from anomalous Hall measurements

paper_profiles.title: Optimizing Write Fidelity of MRAMs via Iterative Water-filling Algorithm
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of optimizing write fidelity for magnetic random-access memory (MRAM) under energy and latency constraints. The authors model write failures as a function of normalized write current and duration, then formulate a biconvex optimization problem to minimize mean squared error (MSE) for multi-bit words, with bit-position weights reflecting the greater importance of more significant bits.

The proposed approach uses alternating convex search (ACS) and then derives closed-form update rules for the two subproblems, yielding an iterative water-filling / cave-filling algorithm that is more computationally efficient than generic ACS. The paper is centered on MRAM device/storage optimization rather than education or AI-assisted writing.

Empirically, the paper reports that the proposed algorithm matches the solution quality of the original ACS and performs comparably to a global nonlinear solver (MADS/NOMAD) while being more efficient. For an 8-bit word, the method reduces MSE by a factor of 21 under the stated model, and in an MNIST neural-network-storage simulation it achieves about 40% write-energy reduction for the same classification accuracy.

paper_profiles.title: Writing on Dirty Paper with Resizing and its Application to Quasi-Static Fading Broadcast Channels
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a communications-theory variant of Costa’s dirty paper coding problem, in which the sum of a desired signal and known interference is multiplied by a random resizing/fading coefficient that is known to the decoder but not the encoder. The authors analyze how much rate is achievable when the encoder uses dirty paper coding (DPC) designed for average SNR rather than instantaneous channel state, and compare it with the case where the decoder also knows the interference.

The paper is entirely theoretical and uses information-theoretic derivations rather than an empirical study with human participants. In the ergodic fading case, it shows that DPC is asymptotically lossless at high and low SNR, with small finite-SNR loss for common fading distributions such as Rayleigh, Rician, and Nakagami. In the quasi-static case, it proves that DPC achieves the same outage probability as if the interference were known at the decoder, and then applies this robustness result to quasi-static fading broadcast channels without transmitter CSI, where the DPC-based rate region can strictly dominate time-division.

paper_profiles.title: CatAlyst: Domain-Extensible Intervention for Preventing Task Procrastination Using Large Generative Models
paper_profiles.venue: CHI '23: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of task procrastination and loss of focus during cognitively demanding digital work such as writing and slide editing. The authors argue that many AI productivity tools aim to directly substitute for human work, but their usefulness is limited by model accuracy and by the assumption that users are already engaged. Instead, they propose CatAlyst, an intervention system that uses large generative models to generate a continuation of interrupted work and present it as a notification, with the goal of lowering the hurdle for resumption rather than replacing the user’s task.

The system was implemented as a web-based writing tool and a Chrome-based slide-editing prototype. CatAlyst detects interruption from interaction logs, generates likely continuations using GPT-3, and prompts users with a notification showing the beginning of the generated continuation. The paper reports a controlled within-participant study of 12 adults doing Japanese essay writing, a five-day in-the-wild writing study with 10 adults, and a second controlled study for slide editing with 12 adults. Across studies, the authors compare CatAlyst to conventional encouraging-message interventions and to no intervention.

In the writing study, CatAlyst reduced interest-retrieval time (18.8 s vs. 135.0 s), increased progress after resumption (63.5 chars vs. 17.7 chars), and lowered frustration, while maintaining comparable text quality; total writing time was not significantly different. In the slide-editing study, CatAlyst likewise reduced recovery time and improved productivity relative to a conventional intervention, while lowering cognitive load. The longer-term writing study suggested that these benefits persisted over five days and that participants generally perceived the system as useful and were willing to continue using it. Overall, the paper concludes that imperfect but context-aware generative models can support task engagement and digital well-being even when they are not accurate enough to directly replace user work.

finding.finding_summary: CatAlyst improved writing-task engagement and efficiency in a controlled study of n=12 adults writing Japanese essays. Compared with a conventional encouraging-message intervention, it significantly shortened interest retrieval time (18.8 ± 25.1 s vs. 135.0 ± 303.7 s, p=0.002) and increased progress after resumption (63.5 ± 186.2 chars vs. 17.7 ± 36.3 chars, p=0.041), while text quality did not significantly differ across conditions.
finding.measure: Japanese essay writing performance, interest retrieval time, progress after resumption, and rated text quality (consistency, readability, overall quality)
finding.std_deviation: Interest retrieval time SDs: 25.1 s (proposed), 303.7 s (control); progress-after-resumption SDs: 186.2 chars (proposed), 36.3 chars (control)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention reduced frustration and helped participants re-engage with writing tasks, indicating benefits for task persistence and self-regulation during cognitively demanding work. In the controlled writing study (n=12), frustration on NASA-TLX was significantly lower in the proposed condition than in both control and none conditions (post-hoc p=0.019 vs. each), and interview data suggested the generated continuation helped participants overcome distraction and regain interest.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX frustration subscale; interview/self-report on interest and re-engagement
finding.study_size: n=12 in controlled study; n=10 in 5-day study

finding.finding_summary: The paper also studied slide-editing tasks, showing that CatAlyst’s context-aware generated continuations could support a non-writing academic task. In the slide-editing study (n=12), the system reduced the time participants spent recovering their interest in the task and reduced total task time relative to a conventional intervention, while also lowering cognitive load.
finding.measure: Slide-editing task recovery time, total task time, cognitive load

finding.finding_summary: The intervention supported resumption behavior and reduced the hurdle to getting started, which aligns with persistence and self-regulation. Participants reported that the generated continuation helped them decide what to write next and made it easier to return to the task after distraction; the paper also found higher progress immediately after resumption in the proposed condition.
finding.measure: Behavioral resumption after distraction; progress after resumption; participant comments on task re-entry

finding.finding_summary: CatAlyst aimed to improve productivity by helping workers resume interrupted work more quickly. In the writing study (n=12), total writing time did not differ significantly across conditions (control 2557.3 ± 2196.5 s, proposed 1747.3 ± 1660.0 s, none 2231.2 ± 1359.8 s; p=0.174), but the proposed condition trended shorter and did not reduce text quality. In the slide-editing study, the paper reports reduced time spent on the task and increased productivity relative to the conventional intervention.
finding.measure: Total writing time; slide-editing task time/productivity
finding.study_size: n=12 writing study; n=12 slide-editing study
finding.std_deviation: Writing time SDs: 1660.0 s (proposed), 2196.5 s (control), 1359.8 s (none)

finding.finding_summary: In the five-day in-the-wild writing study with n=10 participants, the system was viewed positively and many participants wanted to keep using it. The authors report that eight of ten participants expressed motivation for continued use, suggesting favorable usability and perceived usefulness over longer exposure.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview responses about overall impressions and willingness to continue using the system

paper_profiles.title: Substantial reduction of write-error rate for voltage-controlled magnetoresistive random access memory by in-plane demagnetizing field and voltage-induced negative out-of-plane anisotropy field
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Magnetism and Magnetic Materials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a materials-engineering problem rather than an education problem: how to reduce write error rate (WER) in voltage-controlled magnetoresistive random access memory (VC-MRAM). The authors investigate whether combining an in-plane demagnetizing field (IDF) with a voltage-induced negative out-of-plane anisotropy field (NOAF) can improve reliable switching in magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs).

The study uses numerical simulations based on a macrospin/Langevin model of magnetization dynamics in elliptical and circular MTJs. The authors compare conventional dynamic switching, heavily damped switching, and the proposed scheme, varying pulse duration, effective anisotropy, and external magnetic field. For the elliptical MTJ, the optimal condition reported is Hext = 800 Oe and Keff(+V) = -60 kJ/m3, which yields a minimum WER of 3.2 × 10^-5, compared with 2.5 × 10^-2 for the elliptical case with Keff(+V) = 0 kJ/m3 and 2.6 × 10^-4 for the circular MTJ baseline.

The main conclusion is that an appropriate combination of IDF and voltage-induced NOAF shortens switching time and lowers the energy difference between the post-pulse magnetization state and the equilibrium state, thereby reducing WER by about one order of magnitude versus conventional dynamic switching. The paper is entirely about memory-device physics and reliability; it does not study students, teachers, writing tools, or any educational intervention.

paper_profiles.title: Introductory Chapter: Controversies in the Diagnostics and Management of Acute Appendicitis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter reviews controversies in the diagnosis and management of acute appendicitis, focusing on how clinicians recognize the condition, when to use laboratory tests and imaging, and how to decide between immediate surgery and nonoperative management. It is a narrative medical overview rather than an empirical study, drawing on prior research and historical clinical observations.

The chapter argues that acute appendicitis remains difficult to diagnose reliably using symptoms alone, because presentations are variable and many signs are nonspecific. It reviews the value and limits of clinical scoring systems, laboratory markers, and imaging modalities such as ultrasound, CT, and MRI. The author also discusses evidence suggesting that some uncomplicated cases may resolve spontaneously or respond to antibiotics, and that short in-hospital surgical delays can sometimes be safe, though the literature is mixed.

The chapter is written for surgeons and clinicians managing abdominal pain, with emphasis on adult and pediatric appendicitis. Its main conclusion is that careful history and physical examination remain important, but no single test is sufficient; diagnostic and management decisions should balance accuracy, timing, risks of imaging, and the possibility of nonoperative treatment. The chapter calls for larger multicenter randomized trials to clarify optimal care.

paper_profiles.title: 100 Ideas for Active Learning
paper_profiles.venue: University of Sussex Library / Active Learning Network
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book is a practical handbook of active learning ideas intended to help educators design, adapt, and share participatory teaching practices. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it compiles short chapters written by multiple contributors across higher education and related contexts, with an emphasis on inclusive, collaborative, and digitally enhanced learning.

The opening sections explain the rationale for active learning, describe the structure of the volume, and provide a manifesto and methods note based on a co-writing activity at an active learning conference. The text argues that active learning supports deeper learning, engagement, and transferable skills, but also explicitly notes that many of the ideas in the book are not based on rigorous testing or longitudinal evaluation. Because this is a handbook and not a research study, it does not present a population sample, intervention evaluation, or empirical outcomes in the usual sense.

The volume is most relevant as professional guidance for educators in higher education and other adult learning settings. It includes discussion of digital tools, assessment, collaboration, and inclusion, but the text provided does not contain study-level evidence about AI writing assistants, high-school students, delayed outcomes, or longitudinal persistence.

paper_profiles.title: The role of large language models in personalized learning: a systematic review of educational impact
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how large language models (LLMs) and related AI systems affect education compared with traditional approaches. It focuses on whether LLM-based learning environments improve student engagement, retention, emotional and social development, assessment fairness, real-time progress monitoring, and the simulation of teaching-like interactions.

The review synthesizes 55 studies published from 2020 to 2024, using database searches and PRISMA-style screening. Across the included literature, the authors argue that LLMs can provide personalized feedback, adaptive pacing, multilingual support, and more immediate responses than conventional classrooms, which may improve engagement, retention, and some aspects of emotional and social support.

The paper is not an original experiment; it is a systematic review of peer-reviewed and related scholarly studies spanning higher education and other settings. Its main conclusion is cautiously favorable: LLMs appear promising for personalized learning and broader educational support, but the literature still has important gaps around bias, privacy, long-term effects, and rigorous validation of claimed benefits.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that LLM-based systems may improve student engagement, motivation, and emotional well-being through personalized feedback, empathetic interactions, and real-time support. It cites prior studies indicating a 40% increase in self-reported emotional well-being with AI-powered conversational systems (Chen et al., 2023), but the review itself does not provide a pooled effect size or original sample size.
finding.measure: self-reported emotional well-being, engagement, motivation, emotional support

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that LLMs can support durable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, and problem-solving by enabling interactive dialogue, virtual group discussions, and role-play scenarios. It cites earlier studies suggesting peer communication improvements of up to 28%, but does not present primary estimates or a meta-analytic effect size.
finding.measure: critical thinking, peer communication, collaboration, problem-solving

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, LLMs are described as improving overall academic learning through personalized content, adaptive pacing, and immediate feedback, with the authors citing a 32% increase in retention rates in AI-integrated learning environments from prior studies. The review emphasizes that these systems can improve knowledge acquisition and comprehension, but the reported figures are secondary citations rather than original study estimates.
finding.measure: knowledge retention, comprehension, academic learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs improve operational efficiency by automating feedback, supporting progress monitoring, and aiding assessment and grading tasks. It describes these tools as reducing delays and enabling faster, more scalable responses than traditional teacher-led processes, but it does not report a direct empirical effect size for workload or productivity.
finding.measure: feedback turnaround, progress monitoring, grading/assessment support

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that LLMs could improve equity, access, and assessment practices, but it also highlights persistent institutional concerns about bias, privacy, ethics, and governance. It recommends bias audits, transparency, human oversight, and regulatory guidance, indicating promise at the system level but unresolved implementation risks.
finding.measure: fairness, privacy, governance, institutional adoption considerations

paper_profiles.title: Proactive and reactive engagement of artificial intelligence methods for education: a review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad review of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning methods used across the end-to-end education process. The authors organize prior work into two major phases: proactive engagement of AI, which covers admissions logistics, curriculum/content design, timetabling, and content generation; and reactive engagement of AI, which covers tutoring aids, performance assessment, and outcome prediction.

The review is based on 195 original research articles published between 2003 and 2022, identified through Google Scholar and filtered through inclusion/exclusion criteria. The paper does not present a new intervention or empirical study of learners; instead, it synthesizes trends in algorithms, data sources, application areas, and ethical concerns in AI for education research.

Because the review spans educational contexts from preschool through professional/vocational education, it is not limited to a single population, though it explicitly includes middle and high school students among its target audiences. The authors conclude that AI in education has expanded substantially, with especially mature work in intelligent tutoring systems, performance assessment, and prediction, but they also emphasize continuing concerns about fairness, transparency, privacy, infrastructure, and uneven adoption. They also note that generative AI and the COVID-19 pandemic have further accelerated interest in the field.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review synthesizes 195 AIEd studies and finds that AI applications are widespread across curriculum design, question generation, timetabling, tutoring, and assessment. The paper reports growth in the field over the last two decades, but because it is a review it does not provide a single effect size on learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Scope and trends of AI applications in education research

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies affect-aware tutoring aids, engagement-oriented interactive tutoring systems, and learning-style-aware systems as active research directions, suggesting that AI is being used to support motivation, engagement, and self-regulated learning. However, the paper only summarizes prior work and does not meta-analyze learner-level effects.
finding.measure: Presence and scope of research on engagement, affect, and self-regulation support

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights AI applications aimed at personalization, knowledge tracing, hint generation, and self-regulated learning, all of which are tied to durable skills such as metacognition, reflection, and collaborative problem solving. The paper’s evidence is descriptive rather than causal, so no pooled outcome estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Coverage of AI systems targeting metacognition, self-regulation, and collaboration

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the review is operational efficiency in education, including admissions logistics, scheduling/timetabling, content curation, automatic question generation, grading, and performance monitoring. Across the reviewed literature, the authors report that AI systems can reduce review time, automate repetitive tasks, and improve resource allocation, but the paper does not aggregate quantitative effects across studies.
finding.measure: Administrative and instructional task automation/efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses institutional uses of AI in admissions, yield prediction, curriculum design, and broader educational governance, and it emphasizes ethical issues such as fairness, transparency, and privacy. It concludes that AI adoption may improve institutional decision-making and access, but can also reproduce bias and raise governance concerns.
finding.measure: Institutional applications, ethics, and governance implications of AI in education

paper_profiles.title: Human-AI Collaboration for Smart Education: Reframing Applied Learning to Support Metacognition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter argues that generative AI tools and intelligent virtual assistants (IVAs) such as ChatGPT can reshape education by shifting emphasis away from routine sentence generation and toward higher-order metacognitive skills, editing, prompt design, and applied learning. Rather than presenting new empirical data, the authors synthesize prior literature and propose a pedagogical reframing in which AI serves as a tutor, drafting aid, and collaborative partner while students remain responsible for evaluation, revision, and final judgment.

The chapter is situated primarily in postsecondary education, especially composition and writing instruction, though it speaks broadly to K-16 contexts. It proposes classroom activities and sample assignments in which students generate AI drafts, critique and refine them, reflect on the process, and work through heuristic worksheets that are meant to build critical thinking and self-regulation. The authors also discuss implications for teachers and institutions, including potential workload reduction, the need to adapt assessment and credentialing, and the growing importance of prompt engineering and digital fluency.

The main conclusion is that human-AI collaboration should be used to support metacognition and applied learning rather than replace human instruction. The chapter emphasizes that AI can personalize support, increase efficiency, and scaffold writing development, but that students still need human-guided opportunities to develop critical evaluation, contextual judgment, and durable skills for future work. No original outcome data or experimental evidence are reported; the chapter is conceptual and prescriptive.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that AI writing assistants can support writing development by generating drafts and providing feedback, while students focus on editing, revision, and higher-level composition. However, it also explicitly notes a concern that an editorial role may not foster sentence-level writing skills, and no empirical study or effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Writing instruction, sentence-level writing, editing quality, composition performance

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the chapter is that AI-assisted editing, prompt refinement, and dialog with chatbots can strengthen metacognition, critical thinking, reflection, and self-regulation. These claims are illustrated through proposed classroom activities and sample assignments, but the chapter does not report measured outcomes, sample sizes, or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Metacognitive reflection, critical thinking, self-regulation, prompt engineering ability

finding.finding_summary: The chapter claims that generative AI can reduce educator workload by drafting lesson plans, rubrics, assessments, syllabi, and other instructional materials, thereby freeing teachers to focus more on individual student support. This is presented as a conceptual benefit rather than an empirically tested effect, so no study-level statistics are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, lesson-planning efficiency, instructional preparation time

paper_profiles.title: Addressing student use of generative AI in schools and universities through academic integrity reporting
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how schools and universities should respond to student use of generative AI, especially when AI is used in ways that may violate academic integrity. Rather than testing an intervention empirically, it argues for a conceptual and policy framework that distinguishes legitimate assistance from dishonest misuse and emphasizes proof, intent, and due process.

The article proposes a six-domain Academic Integrity Reporting (AIR) framework: limitations, policy parameters and enforcement, literacy education, intent, issue-based coaching/remediation, and reporting/monitoring. To motivate this framework, the author reviews prior literature and examines academic integrity policies from 24 post-secondary institutions, finding that public universities more often name GenAI explicitly, while allied health/nursing schools more often use broader AI language. Across policies, missing or incorrect citation of AI-generated content is treated as plagiarism, and many institutions allow faculty to set local AI-use parameters.

The paper’s main conclusion is that institutions should move away from blanket bans and purely punitive responses toward transparent, instructional, and evidence-based integrity systems. It argues that AI literacy, neutral documentation, remediation, and centralized reporting can better support fairness, consistency, and student learning while still addressing misconduct.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily a conceptual and policy analysis, not an empirical test of student outcomes. Its central finding is that post-secondary institutions need clearer, more transparent, and more scalable academic integrity policies for GenAI use, and that current policies vary substantially across institutions (24 institutions reviewed).
finding.measure: Review of academic integrity policies and conceptual policy analysis

paper_profiles.title: History of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots: past, present, and future development
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (technology history review; no human study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative historical review of the development of chatbot and generative AI systems, tracing major milestones from early statistical models and rule-based programs to modern transformer-based systems such as ChatGPT and Bard. The authors synthesize academic literature and industry sources to describe how chatbot technology evolved through pattern matching, AIML, machine learning, and large language models.

The paper does not test an intervention or evaluate outcomes in a human sample; instead, it surveys technological development, key architectures, and representative systems including ELIZA, PARRY, ALICE, Siri, XiaoIce, ChatGPT, and Bard. It emphasizes the shift from simple scripted response systems to adaptive, data-driven conversational agents with broader capabilities in dialogue, personalization, and task assistance. The paper concludes that chatbots will likely continue expanding into domains such as healthcare, business, and research, while noting concerns about privacy, ethics, and security.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Applications of Generative AI in High School STEM Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether generative AI can improve learning outcomes in high school STEM classes, with physics as the focal subject. The author frames the work around a practical question in education: whether tools like ChatGPT/Bing AI can support student learning, engagement, and understanding, and whether providing students with explicit AI literacy training changes those effects.

The study uses a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design in Tomball Memorial High School with AP Physics 1 and on-level physics students. Students were assigned to one of four conditions: control, search engine only, generative AI only, or generative AI plus a literacy program. The intervention lasted two class periods and included a teacher lecture, a study period using the assigned tool, a post-test, and a survey. Quantitatively, the author reports that untrained generative AI use performed worse than control and search-engine use in AP Physics, while the AI literacy program improved performance relative to AI alone. In on-level physics, group differences were not statistically significant. Survey results suggested no clear perceived benefits, and the author concludes that short-term AI use may not reliably improve outcomes, but AI literacy training may be important for safer and more effective use of generative AI in classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The study measured changes in physics test scores after a lecture plus a 20-minute study period using either search engines, generative AI, or generative AI with a literacy program. In AP Physics, the ANOVA showed a significant group effect (p=0.011), with the search-engine group outperforming the untrained GAI group (p=0.0062) and the GAI-LP group outperforming the GAI group (p=0.0256); in on-level physics, the group effect was not significant (p=0.619).
finding.measure: Pre-test/post-test physics score difference on AP Physics 1 topics (momentum and impulse) and on-level physics topics (electricity and circuits)
finding.study_size: n=171 total quantitative participants; AP Physics n=91, on-level physics n=80
finding.std_deviation: AP Physics SDs: control 1.355, SE 1.387, GAI-LP 1.225, GAI 1.791; on-level SDs: control 1.700, SE 2.250, GAI 2.199, GAI-LP 1.569

finding.finding_summary: The paper also examined survey responses about engagement, enjoyment, understanding, and confidence during the learning process. The author reports that the GAI group showed slightly higher engagement than the other groups, but confidence intervals overlapped substantially and the MANOVA was not significant (Pillai’s Trace p=0.115), indicating no reliable difference across experimental conditions. The literacy program’s perceived impact was also low in the survey, despite better assessment performance.
finding.measure: Post-survey ratings of understanding, confidence, engagement, and enjoyment of the learning process

finding.finding_summary: The discussion interprets the AI literacy program as supporting better responsible and ethical use of generative AI, which the author links to improved confidence and more effective use of the tool. However, this outcome is only indirectly measured through survey items and post-test performance rather than a direct durable-skills instrument, so the evidence is limited. The strongest directly reported result is that students in the GAI-LP condition outperformed the GAI-only condition in AP Physics.
finding.measure: Indirect indicators from survey responses on confidence/understanding and treatment comparison in physics score gains

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE), a high-stakes high school exit exam. The authors frame the study as an evaluation of ChatGPT’s potential to support learners in exam preparation and to complete exam-style questions across multiple subjects.

The approach is a benchmark-style assessment of GPT-3.5/ChatGPT on the VNHSGE evaluation set. The dataset includes 30 essay prompts for literature and 1,700 multiple-choice questions across mathematics, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education. The model was prompted zero-shot and graded by exact-match/correctness against human-expert ground truth. The paper also compares ChatGPT’s scores with Vietnamese student score distributions and reports natural/science and social combination scores using the Ministry of Education and Training graduation formula.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT would pass the exam overall, with combined scores ranging from 6.35 to 6.94 across 2019-2023 and average subject scores from 4.8 to 7.92 depending on subject. It performed relatively well in English, literature, biology, and history, but less well in chemistry and some geography/civic education items, especially where visual/chart understanding or higher-order reasoning was needed. The study suggests ChatGPT may be a useful study aid, but it is not a longitudinal study of student transfer or persistence after use of AI tools.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed strongly on the literature component of the VNHSGE. Reported literature scores ranged from 5.63 to 7.5 across 2019-2023, with an average of 6.8 on a 10-point scale, and the paper states that ChatGPT was usually above the majority of Vietnamese students, except in 2022. The literature test included 30 essay prompts, so this is evidence that the model can generate acceptable written responses in this exam context, though no effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Literature exam performance on 30 essay-style prompts / literature section score (10-point scale)
finding.study_size: n=30 essays (literature dataset); year-level score comparisons 2019-2023

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT achieved passing-level math performance on the VNHSGE, with mathematics scores from 5.2 to 6.6 across 2019-2023 and an average of 5.88. The authors compare these scores to Vietnamese student score distributions and note that ChatGPT’s math performance was lower than the majority of students, but still sufficient to contribute to an overall passing score. The study does not report an effect size or inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Mathematics multiple-choice exam score (10-point scale) and correct-answer counts
finding.study_size: n=1,700 multiple-choice questions across subjects; year-level math results 2019-2023

finding.finding_summary: Across non-math, non-language subjects, ChatGPT showed mixed performance. It scored relatively well in history and biology, but lower in chemistry and some geography/civic education items; for example, the paper reports chemistry averages of 4.0-6.25 (average 4.8) and history averages up to 7.75 in 2023. The authors attribute weaker geography performance partly to GPT-3.5’s inability to analyze images/charts, which are central to the geography exam, but no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Subject exam scores in physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and civic education (10-point scale)
finding.study_size: n=1,700 multiple-choice questions across subjects; year-level scores 2019-2023

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can handle some questions requiring reasoning, explanation, and answer justification, especially in subjects like literature, biology, and history, but it performs less well on more complex analytical tasks in mathematics, civic education, and geography. This is an indirect measure of durable skills because the study evaluates exam responses that require critical thinking and problem solving, yet it does not measure student skill growth or persistence over time. No effect size or causal estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Performance on exam questions requiring explanation, reasoning, and problem solving
finding.study_size: n=1,700 multiple-choice questions plus 30 literature essays

finding.finding_summary: Scientific-subject performance was mixed: ChatGPT performed relatively well in physics and biology, but weakly in chemistry. The paper reports physics scores from 5.75 to 6.5 and biology scores from 5.25 to 6.0, while chemistry ranged from 4.0 to 6.25 with the lowest average subject score (4.8). The authors conclude that performance varies by subject difficulty and question type; no effect size or confidence interval is provided.
finding.measure: Physics, chemistry, and biology exam scores on the VNHSGE

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central institutional claim is that ChatGPT could pass the VNHSGE and therefore may have implications for exam preparation, assessment design, and AI use in education. The authors suggest the model could support learners and educators and note potential implications for academic integrity and educational practice, but they do not test policy changes or institutional outcomes directly. No effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Overall passing performance on a national high school graduation exam; discussion of educational implications
finding.study_size: n=1 model evaluated on VNHSGE dataset spanning 2019-2023

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can support second-language learners in developing critical thinking and argumentative writing through a structured prompting framework called the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW). The authors build CGCAW by combining the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model and Tan’s framework for argumentative writing, then compare a guided ChatGPT condition against an unguided ChatGPT condition.

The study was conducted with 10 students from a state university, randomly assigned to experimental and control groups. All participants wrote a short argumentative essay in 40 minutes on the topic of social media’s benefits or harms to society. The experimental group used CGCAW prompts designed to scaffold position, explanation, evidence, and conclusion development; the control group could use ChatGPT freely without the structured guidance.

Essays were scored by three raters or tools: Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor. Results were mixed. ChatGPT’s scoring suggested the guided group performed better on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but Grammarly and the instructor ratings favored the control group, especially for grammar, overall language mechanics, thesis clarity, and summary quality. The authors conclude that the framework may help specific argumentation and critical-thinking-related aspects of writing, but it needs refinement, and they recommend longer-term, repeated-use studies to assess persistence and durability of effects.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined argumentative essay writing quality among 10 undergraduate second-language learners (n=10) using a guided ChatGPT framework versus unguided ChatGPT use. Results were mixed across raters: ChatGPT scoring favored the guided group on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence (Group 1 mean total 74 vs. Group 2 mean total 72.2; SD=7.6 vs. 5.5), but Grammarly and the course instructor rated the control group higher overall (Grammarly mean 92.2 vs. 90.6; instructor mean 56 vs. 35).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality scored by ChatGPT, Grammarly, and course instructor on clarity, logical coherence, evidence use, persuasiveness, thesis, reasoning, and summary quality
finding.std_deviation: SD=7.6 (Group 1 ChatGPT total), SD=5.5 (Group 2 ChatGPT total)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on critical thinking as the main intended outcome, using the Paul-Elder model to target reasoning elements such as point of view, concepts, assumptions, information, inferences, and implications. The evidence is mixed but suggests the guided ChatGPT framework improved some critical-thinking-linked writing features—especially clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use—while not improving other dimensions rated by Grammarly or the instructor. No standardized critical-thinking test was reported, so the finding is inferred from essay-based indicators rather than a direct critical-thinking measure.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-related performance inferred from argumentative essay features (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, thesis development, reasoning)
finding.std_deviation: SD=7.6 (Group 1 ChatGPT total), SD=5.5 (Group 2 ChatGPT total)

finding.finding_summary: The discussion reports that some participants could not complete the task within the 40-minute window, and the authors note unfamiliarity with the CGCAW framework and limited time as barriers to completion. Although no validated engagement or self-regulation scale was used, the paper suggests reduced task completion/persistence under the guided condition for at least two participants, indicating a possible short-term burden on task persistence and self-regulation.
finding.measure: Task completion during timed essay writing; anecdotal reports of time insufficiency and inability to finish

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how secondary school English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students use prompts when completing a writing task with ChatGPT and other state-of-the-art chatbots. The authors are motivated by the idea that effective use of AI writing assistants requires prompt engineering skill, and they ask what kinds of prompt content students use and what patterns emerge across their prompt sequences.

The study uses a qualitative case-study design with four high-achieving form-one students in a Hong Kong secondary school. Students completed a timed blog-writing task on iPads using the POE app (which included ChatGPT, Sage, and Dragonfly) for the first time, while screen recordings captured each prompt turn. The researchers coded 36 prompts into nine prompt-content categories, including auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, search-engine style prompts, greetings, and chatbot-suggested follow-ups.

Findings show that students largely relied on trial-and-error rather than a broad or systematic prompt repertoire. No student used all prompt types, and several prompt forms appeared only once; the most common were auto-complete and auto-complete plus natural language instruction plus question. The authors conclude that students were exploring chatbot capabilities and progressively refining ideas for their writing, but they were not yet sophisticated prompt engineers. They argue that EFL classrooms should provide explicit prompt engineering instruction so students can move beyond ad hoc experimentation and better support their writing with chatbots.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure writing quality directly, but it substantively examines how four secondary EFL students used ChatGPT/SOTA chatbots to support a blog-writing task. Across 36 coded prompt turns, students used a limited range of prompt types and relied on trial-and-error; the authors conclude this indicates developing, but unsophisticated, prompt engineering for writing support.
finding.measure: Prompt engineering behaviors during an EFL writing task; coded prompt types and sequences

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on prompt engineering as a durable skill involving strategy use, adaptation, and refinement while writing with AI. Students showed exploratory, trial-and-error behavior, minor prompt modifications, and some progression toward more sophisticated prompt combinations, which the authors interpret as learning to engineer prompts over the course of the task.
finding.measure: Prompt sequencing, prompt-type variety, and refinement strategies

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses students’ exploratory behavior, persistence through trial-and-error, and use of chatbot memory during the task, but it does not directly measure motivation or engagement. The evidence suggests students persisted in completing the writing task and kept revising prompts, yet the study provides no quantified social-emotional outcomes.
finding.measure: Observed persistence and trial-and-error engagement during task completion

paper_profiles.title: LLMs as Writing Assistants: Exploring Perspectives on Sense of Ownership and Reasoning
paper_profiles.venue: In2Writing ’24 (ACM Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how people perceive ownership and authorship when using large language models (LLMs) as writing assistants. The authors focus on a psychological dilemma: users may accept and submit AI-assisted text as their own authorship while not fully feeling that they own the content. They also investigate whether these perceptions differ across creative versus non-creative writing tasks.

The study uses a brief survey with 35 participants, mostly university students aged 18–24, to compare responses about general writing tasks (e.g., assignments, formal letters) and creative writing tasks (e.g., poems, stories, birthday wishes). Participants reported stronger feelings of contribution and ownership for non-creative writing, while creative writing led them to credit the LLM more and feel less ownership. The paper also reports that reminding participants of their role in prompting the model increased perceived ownership, and reminding them of their editing role increased authorship/ownership claims further.

Overall, the paper concludes that ownership and authorship are related but distinct in LLM-assisted writing. Human involvement in prompting and editing appears to increase perceived ownership, suggesting that transparency about user contribution may shape how people evaluate AI-assisted text. The work is exploratory and human-centered rather than an intervention study, and it emphasizes implications for the design of writing assistants, disclosure practices, and accountability in AI-generated content.

finding.finding_summary: The survey found that participants felt a stronger sense of contribution and ownership in non-creative writing tasks such as STEM assignments and formal letters, while feeling less ownership in creative writing such as poems, stories, and birthday wishes. In the authors' sample of 35 participants, creative tasks led people to credit LLMs more, whereas reminders about prompting and editing increased ownership/authorship claims.
finding.measure: Self-reported contribution and sense of ownership in LLM-assisted writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that reminding participants about their role in prompting the LLM increased their sense of ownership, and reminding them about editing the LLM output further increased authorship claims to 62.9%. This indicates that active human involvement in ideation and revision can strengthen perceptions tied to metacognitive ownership and accountability.
finding.measure: Self-reported ownership/authorship after prompt-reminder and editing-reminder conditions

finding.finding_summary: Participants' sense of ownership varied with task type and increased when their contribution was made salient, indicating that perceived responsibility and pride in the work were sensitive to the collaborative writing process. The paper frames these responses as a psychological dilemma involving attachment, authorship, and ownership in AI-assisted writing.
finding.measure: Self-reported sense of ownership, contribution, and authorship

paper_profiles.title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 202
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether the European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) adequately addresses competitive risks created by the rapid rise of generative AI systems. The authors argue that the DMA, which was designed for traditional digital platform gatekeepers such as operating systems, app stores, and search engines, should be expanded to explicitly include generative AI services as core platform services.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or student outcomes. Instead, it analyzes how generative AI systems could become gatekeepers through computing-power advantages, early-mover advantages, data access, and vertically integrated ecosystems. It discusses examples such as OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Meta, and suggests that current and emerging practices in generative AI could weaken contestability, diversity, and user autonomy.

The main conclusion is normative and regulatory: the DMA should be amended so that certain generative AI developers are treated as gatekeepers and subject to corresponding obligations. The paper argues this would help prevent entrenched market positions and support fairness, openness, and innovation in the generative AI ecosystem.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI is creating new gatekeeping and concentration risks that current DMA rules do not fully address. It proposes policy changes—treating some generative AI services as core platform services and some developers as gatekeepers—to improve contestability, fairness, and diversity in the market.
finding.measure: Policy and regulatory analysis of the EU Digital Markets Act and generative AI market structure

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT v Bard v Bing v Claude 2 v Aria v human-expert. How good are AI chatbots at scientific writing?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how well six AI chatbots can perform scientific writing tasks in the humanities, using archaeology, historiography, linguistics, and genetic history as the topical context. The authors were especially interested in whether chatbots can generate correct answers to complex scholarly questions and whether they can produce original scientific contributions, rather than merely reproducing existing information.

The study compared ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Bard, Bing Chatbot, Aria, Claude 2, and two ChatGPT-4 plugins (Bing and ScholarAI) using two one-shot prompts about the migration of South Slavs and the settlement of Alpine Slavs in the Early Middle Ages. Responses were tagged by two expert authors for quantitative accuracy and qualitative precision, with human-generated text used as a benchmark. The authors also analyzed reasoning errors, hallucinations, and citation biases in the generated outputs.

The main finding is that all systems fell short of human expert writing and none produced genuine original scientific content at scale. ChatGPT-4 performed best overall on quantitative accuracy and showed the most original contribution among the models, but it still failed to approach the level expected of a strong undergraduate response and could not reliably handle the narrow Q2 topic without errors. Bing’s outputs were heavily shaped by Wikipedia, ScholarAI generated faulty references, and Aria and Claude 2 performed poorly. The paper concludes that current AI chatbots can assist with broad information gathering and drafting, but they are not yet reliable tools for original scholarly reasoning in the humanities.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates AI chatbot performance on humanities scientific writing tasks, measuring quantitative accuracy and qualitative precision on two 500-word prompts (Q1 and Q2). ChatGPT-4 performed best, with about 24% correct content on the detailed breakdown and a score of -5, but all systems still fell well below the level expected of a senior undergraduate student and none produced sustained original scholarly writing.
finding.measure: Quantitative accuracy and qualitative precision of chatbot-generated humanities scientific writing responses

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that the chatbots did not demonstrate strong critical thinking, source comparison, or on-the-fly reasoning. The authors note reasoning errors such as linking South Slavic migration to climate cooling or fertile lands, and emphasize that none of the systems critically compared multiple sources in the way a human expert did.
finding.measure: Human expert tagging of reasoning quality, critical comparison of sources, and correctness of causal explanations

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly assesses AI-generated writing quality in a scientific writing task, including correctness, adequacy, and originality of prose. ChatGPT-4 produced the strongest writing among the models, but overall the systems failed to generate credible scholarly text and were often generic, derivative, or incorrect; the authors explicitly state that the chatbots were not able to produce original scientific contributions in humanities writing.
finding.measure: AI-generated 500-word scientific writing responses scored for correctness and original scientific contribution

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines whether AI chatbots can answer complex scientific questions in the humanities accurately and coherently. ChatGPT-4 was strongest, but the models frequently produced hallucinated references, causal reasoning errors, and unsupported claims; the authors conclude that current systems are far from reliable scientific reasoners in this domain.
finding.measure: Tagged correctness of answers to complex scientific questions and evaluation of causal/reasoning errors

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests AI chatbots can help with low-stakes drafting and information gathering, especially for broad topics, but their usefulness is limited by errors and poor sourcing. Bing and ChatGPT-4 were described as roughly comparable to an undergraduate’s initial research steps, while some tools were likened to general internet search rather than dependable scholarly writing assistants.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of chatbot outputs as research/drafting aids

paper_profiles.title: High School Science Profile Predicts Adults’ Views on the Future of AI and STS
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This longitudinal study asks whether adolescents’ high school science profile predicts how they engage with artificial intelligence (AI) as adults and how they view broader science–technology–society (STS) issues. The author argues that, despite widespread claims that K-12 science education should prepare students for an AI-shaped future, there is little empirical evidence linking school-period science experiences to later AI-related behaviors and beliefs.

The study uses Korea Employment Education Panel II (KEEP II) data, following a cohort of general high school students in South Korea from 2016/2017 to 2023 (n=2,348). Science interest and science achievement were measured in high school; adult outcomes at age 24 included AI use, positive and negative perceptions of AI, and three STS views: human–AI replacement, future quality of life, and monopolization of science and technology benefits. Structural equation modeling found that science achievement, but not science interest directly, predicted later AI use (β=.18, p<.001). AI use was positively associated with both optimistic and critical views of AI, and these perceptions in turn related to more nuanced STS beliefs. Indirect effects suggested that science interest can matter later through science achievement and AI use, making this one of the rare longitudinal studies connecting secondary science education to adult AI engagement.

finding.finding_summary: High school science achievement positively predicted later AI use in adulthood, while science interest did not show a significant direct path to AI use. In the fitted SEM, science achievement had a significant standardized path to AI use (β=.18, p<.001) in a longitudinal sample of n=2,348 tracked from high school to age 24.
finding.measure: High school science achievement (stanine grade) predicting adult AI use across translator, recommender, facial/image recognition, and speech recognition services

finding.finding_summary: The paper also shows that science interest had indirect positive associations with adult AI perceptions and STS views, mediated by science achievement and AI use. However, these are not direct motivational or persistence outcomes; they are modeled as long-run pathways from adolescent science interest to adult technology engagement in the same longitudinal sample (n=2,348).
finding.measure: High school science interest predicting adult AI use, AI perceptions, and STS views via indirect effects
finding.effect_size: indirect effects reported; exact standardized values include .023* to .019^

finding.finding_summary: Adult AI use and perceptions were linked to broader STS views about human–AI relations, quality of life, and monopolization. AI use positively predicted views on human–AI relations (β=.08, p<.01) and life quality (β=.118, p<.001), while negative AI perceptions strongly predicted belief that science and technology benefits will be monopolized (β=.474, p<.001).
finding.measure: Adult STS beliefs: human and AI, life quality, and monopoly items measured at age 24

paper_profiles.title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceive a generative AI (GenAI) tool designed to support creative mathematical writing. The study asks what educational benefits and challenges emerge when students use an AI-powered system to create, modify, and evaluate math stories that combine mathematical ideas, writing, and images.

The intervention centered on a three-step instructional sequence: Ask, Represent, and Transform. In Ask, students analyzed story-based math problems; in Represent, they visually modeled their thinking; and in Transform, they prompted GPT-4 and DALL·E 3 to generate culturally relevant math stories from their own ideas. The tool was implemented in six classrooms with 79 fifth-grade students across two U.S. schools, and the researchers collected focus-group interviews from 10 students, one-on-one interviews with six teachers, open-ended survey responses, and classroom observation notes.

Using thematic analysis, the authors identified four benefit themes and two challenge themes. Reported benefits included fostering creativity in math, strengthening mathematical understanding, improving AI literacy, and supporting affective outcomes such as interest, curiosity, and ownership. Reported challenges included students’ difficulty critically evaluating AI output and generating coherent prompts, as well as AI-related limitations such as being too perfect, lacking feedback and adaptivity, reducing opportunities for autonomy and social connection, and offering limited communication modes. The paper concludes that GenAI can support elementary math learning and writing, but only when paired with deliberate instructional and interface design that preserves student agency and opportunities for reflection.

finding.finding_summary: Students and teachers reported that the GenAI-supported creative math writing activity helped students understand math problems more deeply, represent mathematical ideas visually, and uncover misconceptions. The paper does not report inferential effect sizes, but the qualitative evidence from 79 fifth-grade students and 6 teachers indicates positive perceived support for mathematical understanding during story-based fraction work.
finding.measure: Perceptions/interviews about mathematical understanding, problem breakdown, and knowledge representation during story-based math writing

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students perceived GenAI as supporting creative writing processes, including generating, revising, and elaborating stories with greater originality and flexibility. Although the written product was mathematical in content, the core activity involved writing and storytelling, and the qualitative data suggest the tool helped students produce and improve text-based narratives.
finding.measure: Perceptions/interviews about creative mathematical writing, story drafting, and revision

finding.finding_summary: Participants described increased interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and sense of ownership when working with the GenAI system. Students reported that math became more fun and engaging, while teachers observed higher attention and motivation; however, these are qualitative perceptions rather than measured gains.
finding.measure: Perceptions/interviews about interest, curiosity, enjoyment, and ownership in learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students developed prompt engineering strategies, evaluated AI strengths and weaknesses, and engaged in divergent/convergent thinking while co-creating stories with AI. Teachers and students also noted opportunities for higher-order reasoning in problem construction, though the evidence is qualitative and centered on perceptions rather than performance outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceptions/interviews about prompt engineering, evaluation of AI outputs, and creative/divergent thinking

finding.finding_summary: Some participants described the AI system as helping generate drafts quickly and reduce the time and effort needed to start stories, suggesting increased productivity in writing tasks. At the same time, teachers noted limitations because the system did not provide timely feedback, so the overall operational benefit was mixed and mainly qualitative.
finding.measure: Perceptions of speed, drafting support, and workflow efficiency in story creation

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation of ChatGPT and Microsoft Bing AI Chat Performances on Physics Exams of Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates how well ChatGPT and Microsoft BingChat answer Vietnamese high school physics multiple-choice questions drawn from the National High School Graduation Examination (2019–2023). The study is motivated by the growing interest in large language models (LLMs) for education and the lack of Vietnamese physics benchmarks for assessing their capabilities at the high-school level.

The authors use the VNHSGE physics dataset and compare LLM performance across question difficulty levels (knowledge, comprehension, application, and high application). They also compare model scores with Vietnamese student score distributions from the national exams. ChatGPT and BingChat both solve many knowledge/comprehension items and some application items, but struggle on high-application questions; BingChat is generally more accurate, while ChatGPT is described as more stable/consistent.

Across five exam years, the paper reports average accuracies of 61% for ChatGPT and 66% for BingChat, versus a maximum-case of 78.5% and a minimum-case of 48.5% for the constructed max/min comparisons. When converted to exam scores, the models perform below Vietnamese students on average, though the authors argue LLMs could still support learning through immediate feedback and individualized practice. The paper concludes that these models are not yet substitutes for human reasoning in physics instruction and need stronger domain-specific reasoning to handle advanced application-level problems.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT and BingChat performed below Vietnamese high school students on physics exam questions and struggled especially with high-application items that require multi-step reasoning. Across the five-year evaluation set (200 multiple-choice questions from 2019–2023), ChatGPT averaged 61% accuracy and BingChat 66%, with the paper concluding that neither model could reliably answer the most demanding physics problems.
finding.measure: Accuracy on high school physics multiple-choice exam questions; comparison with Vietnamese student score distributions

finding.finding_summary: On the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination physics dataset, both models answered knowledge and comprehension questions better than the most difficult high-application questions, indicating a clear drop in performance as task complexity increased. The paper reports that ChatGPT and BingChat were unable to provide reasonable solutions on at least one representative application-level item without advanced reasoning.
finding.measure: Question-level correctness by difficulty category (knowledge, comprehension, application, high application)

paper_profiles.title: Guardrails for avoiding harmful medical product recommendations and off-label promotion in generative AI models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the risk that generative AI systems may recommend medical products for uses that are not approved by regulators, thereby producing off-label promotion rather than neutral discussion. The authors argue that because large generative models are trained on broad internet-scale data with limited human oversight, they can learn and reproduce unvetted product-indication associations that may be unsafe or legally problematic.

To study this, the paper proposes a post-hoc detection pipeline for off-label promotion in multimodal large language model outputs. The method standardizes user queries, runs biomedical named entity recognition, matches products and indications to FDA labeling data, and then flags any non-approved product-indication association as potential off-label promotion. The authors evaluate the approach on Claude 3 Sonnet in a shopping-style medical product question-answering setting, using 35 pharmaceuticals and 14,300 synthetic queries generated from known off-label uses.

The results show that 15.4% of model responses contained off-label indications, with off-label indications identified for 33 of 35 products. On a random sample of 2,000 responses, the proposed detector achieved 85.75% precision, 80.47% recall, and 83.02% F1. The main conclusion is that general-purpose multimodal models can surface potentially harmful off-label recommendations, and that lightweight guardrails can help detect and filter such outputs before they are shown to users.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a guardrail method for detecting off-label promotion in generative AI outputs and argues it could be used to enforce regulatory compliance in medical-product interactions. In the evaluated Claude 3 Sonnet setting, the detector identified off-label indications in 15.4% of 14,300 synthetic responses, with performance of precision=85.75%, recall=80.47%, and F1=83.02% on a 2,000-sample human-annotated set.
finding.measure: Rate of off-label indications in model responses; detector precision/recall/F1 against human annotations
finding.study_size: n=14,300 synthetic queries; n=2,000 annotated sample

paper_profiles.title: MusicScaffold: Bridging Machine Efficiency and Human Growth in Adolescent Creative Education through Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a central tension in adolescent creative education with generative AI: prompt-output systems make creation fast and accessible, but may fail to help students develop deeper expressive strategies, autonomy, or transferable creative understanding. The authors ask whether AI can be designed not just to generate outputs, but to scaffold learning and growth in music composition.

To address this, they first conducted a four-week exploratory study with 60 middle school students using commercial AI music generation tools (e.g., Suno and Udio) in regular music classes.
