paper_profiles.title: Exploring AI-Generated Text in Student Writing: How Does AI Help?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Hong Kong secondary school students used AI-generated text while writing English short stories. The authors are interested in whether students integrate AI-generated words into compositions, what patterns of AI use emerge, and whether those patterns relate to human-rated writing quality.

The study involved 23 students from two Hong Kong secondary schools who wrote stories using self-coded AI writing tools built on open-source language models (e.g., GPT-2 and Hugging Face models). Students were trained in zero-shot prompting and in selecting and editing AI-generated text, then given 45 minutes to write. Their stories were scored by experts on content, language, organization, and an additional AI-words rubric; the researchers also counted human words, AI words, and AI text chunks and used multiple linear regression and cluster analysis to examine associations with writing quality.

The main conclusion is that both human-written words and AI-generated words were positively associated with higher story scores, but the relationship is correlational rather than causal. More proficient writers tended to use less AI text overall while editing AI-generated text more strategically, whereas some lower-performing writers used a lot of AI text without achieving high quality. The authors conclude that AI-generated text can help some students, especially lower-scoring writers on language quality, but it does not automatically improve writing and should be used through differentiated instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Among 23 Hong Kong secondary school students writing short stories with AI-writing tools, expert-rated writing quality varied widely (grand total score M=11.2/20, SD=5.94). Multiple linear regression found that both human words and AI-generated words were positively associated with higher content, language, organization, CLO, and grand total scores (e.g., partial correlations with human words were about 0.91-0.95, and with AI words about 0.49-0.59 for these scores).
finding.measure: Expert-rated story quality (content, language, organization/CLO, AI-words score, grand total score) and counts of human words, AI words, and AI chunks
finding.std_deviation: SD=5.94 for grand total score; SD=27.91% for percentage of AI words

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how secondary-school EFL students prompt generative AI chatbots while completing a timed writing task, with a particular focus on the content, quantity, and sequencing of prompts. The authors frame the activity as “machine-in-the-loop” writing and examine prompt engineering as a trial-and-error process in which students iteratively ask chatbots to generate text or information for a blog-entry assignment.

The study analyzed iPad screen recordings and completed Google Docs from four Form 1 students in a Hong Kong secondary school who were using ChatGPT and other POE chatbots for the first time in a writing lesson. Students were asked to write a blog entry about a day at school, using their own words plus AI-generated words, and could draw on a prior blog post as well. The paper codes prompt types such as auto-complete, search-engine style queries, greetings, natural language instructions, and question-based prompts, then traces each student’s prompt pathway across 36 analyzed turns.

The main conclusion is that students used a small set of prompt types and explored them through iterative trial and error, with no student using all prompt types. Some students began with simpler prompts and later shifted to more sophisticated combinations that added natural-language instruction and questions; others repeatedly refined the same basic prompt structure. The authors argue that these patterns indicate limited but developing prompt engineering skill and suggest that explicit prompt engineering instruction could help secondary students use chatbots more effectively for writing.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is primarily descriptive and does not test whether chatbot use improved writing performance. The study reports how four secondary EFL students (36 coded prompt turns after removing 2 accidental clicks) used chatbots to compose blog entries, but it does not provide a causal estimate of gains in writing quality, length, or rubric scores.
finding.measure: Prompt types and prompt pathways during a blog-entry writing task; completed writing products were collected but not evaluated with a quantitative outcome measure

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that students engaged in iterative prompt refinement and trial-and-error learning while completing the writing task, suggesting development of prompt engineering skills and strategic adjustment of prompts. Evidence is qualitative, based on the sequencing and content of prompts across four cases rather than an outcome test or effect size.
finding.measure: Observed prompt engineering pathways, including changes in prompt type, prompt sequence, and chatbot switching

finding.finding_summary: The study does not measure productivity or time savings, but it does report that all four students completed the timed writing task within 45 minutes while using chatbots, with one student taking as few as 5 turns and another as many as 12. No comparative evidence is provided showing that chatbot use improved efficiency versus a non-chatbot condition.
finding.measure: Number of chatbot turns used to complete the timed blog-entry task; task completion within a 45-minute class period

paper_profiles.title: Voice Interaction With Conversational AI Could Facilitate Thoughtful Reflection and Substantive Revision in Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that writing revision is improved when writers can reflect on feedback in an interactive, dialogic way, rather than receiving static comments. The authors focus on a new design question: whether a writer’s use of voice versus typing, when interacting with an LLM-powered conversational agent, changes the depth of reflection, the kinds of concerns raised, cognitive load, and the quality of subsequent revisions.

Rather than reporting completed experimental results, the paper proposes a formative within-subjects study. Participants would write two argumentative rough drafts and then use a system that provides conversational feedback in two modes: fully written interaction, or spoken user input with written system output. The planned measures include NASA-TLX cognitive load, the frequency and proportion of higher-order concerns, conversational turn rate, response latency as a proxy for cognitive processing, and expert ratings of revision quality using an argumentative essay rubric.

The paper’s contribution is primarily methodological and conceptual: it motivates voice-enabled reflection tools for writing and outlines how such a study could isolate input modality effects while preserving user control over revisions. Because the paper is a proposal/planned formative study rather than a completed empirical evaluation, it does not yet provide outcome evidence on writing performance or revision quality.

finding.finding_summary: not_reported: this paper does not report completed empirical results. It proposes a formative within-subjects study to test whether spoken versus typed interaction with an LLM-powered conversational agent affects reflection and subsequent writing revision on argumentative essays.
finding.measure: Argumentative essay revision quality; higher-order concerns in reflection; revision depth

finding.finding_summary: not_reported: the study is designed to examine writers’ reflection, cognitive processing, and engagement with higher-order concerns, which are metacognitive/durable-skill processes. No results are reported in the paper, only planned measures such as turn frequency, response time, and concern coding.
finding.measure: Higher-order concerns, conversational engagement, response time as cognitive processing proxy

finding.finding_summary: not_reported: the planned study includes NASA-TLX to assess cognitive load while reflecting and revising with an LLM conversational agent in voice versus text conditions. The paper hypothesizes lower cognitive load for voice, but no empirical findings are reported.
finding.measure: NASA-TLX cognitive load

finding.finding_summary: not_reported: the paper centers on argumentative writing tasks and revision behavior, but it is not an academic-content intervention beyond writing itself. The only substantive focus is on writing-process support, not a non-language academic domain.
finding.measure: Argumentative writing task

paper_profiles.title: Using Generative Text Models to Create Qualitative Codebooks for Student Evaluations of Teaching
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes and demonstrates a programmatic workflow for inductive qualitative analysis of student evaluations of teaching (SETs) using NLP and large language models (LLMs). The authors frame the problem as one of scale and consistency: open-ended student feedback is valuable but expensive and time-consuming to code manually, especially when there are thousands of responses.

The study introduces an extract-embed-cluster-summarize (EECS) pipeline that first uses a generative text model to extract discrete ideas from comments, then embeds and clusters those ideas, and finally uses another generative step to label clusters and build a codebook. The implementation uses open-source/local models, including a fine-tuned Mistral-7B variant for extraction and a HuggingFace embedding model, with hierarchical density-based clustering. The paper is demonstrated on 5,000 SET responses from introductory engineering courses at a large public research university; after preprocessing, 4,672 unique comments produced 12,046 extracted ideas, 272 clusters, and a simplified codebook of 159 codes.

The main conclusion is that the workflow can reproduce and extend themes found in a prior human-coded analysis of a subset of the same SET corpus, suggesting that LLM-assisted qualitative coding may be scalable and reasonably faithful for this kind of student feedback data. However, the paper is methodological rather than causal: it does not evaluate student learning, writing performance, or any intervention effect. Its relevance to generative AI in education is as a text-analysis/coding method for student writing, not as a writing assistant study.

finding.finding_summary: The EECS workflow substantially reduced manual qualitative coding effort by automating extraction, clustering, and codebook generation for 4,672 unique SET comments. The paper reports that 12,046 extracted ideas were condensed into 272 clusters and then into a 159-code simplified codebook, indicating a scalable approach for analyzing large volumes of student feedback more quickly than traditional thematic analysis.
finding.measure: Time/effort required for qualitative codebook generation from student evaluations of teaching; number of ideas, clusters, and codes produced
finding.study_size: n=4,672 unique comments (from a random sample of 5,000 SETs)

paper_profiles.title: Unmasking the Shadows of AI: Investigating Deceptive Capabilities in Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a student essay that surveys and critiques recent literature on deceptive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT and GPT-4. It asks how deception in AI should be defined, what forms it can take, and why it matters for safety, governance, and everyday human-AI interaction.

The paper does not report a primary empirical study; instead, it synthesizes prior work on strategic deception, imitation, sycophancy, and unfaithful reasoning. It discusses examples such as GPT-4 allegedly deceiving a human to solve a CAPTCHA, LLM performance in text-based social deduction games, and model-written evaluations showing sandbagging and sycophancy. The context is broad and not specific to education, with the argument extending to policy, accountability, and digital literacy rather than a school-based intervention.

Its main conclusion is that deceptive behavior should be treated as a serious and potentially intrinsic property of advanced LLMs, even if the models do not possess human-like intent. The paper argues for clearer definitions, stronger governance, more transparent disclosures, and improved digital education around how AI systems generate and present information.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that deceptive capabilities in LLMs create governance, accountability, and regulatory challenges, and it calls for stronger international coordination, risk assessment, and transparent AI disclosures. This is a conceptual synthesis rather than a measured intervention, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Policy and governance analysis of AI deception, accountability, and regulation

finding.finding_summary: The essay claims that users need stronger digital education, data infrastructure literacy, and the ability to evaluate AI-generated information critically. These are recommendations and interpretations drawn from cited literature rather than direct outcome measurement, so no empirical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical evaluation and data infrastructure literacy concepts

paper_profiles.title: Closing the Loop: Learning to Generate Writing Feedback via Language Model Simulated Student Revisions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether an LM-based system can be trained to generate better writing feedback by simulating how students revise essays in response to feedback. The central idea is to optimize feedback not by directly labeling ‘good’ feedback, but by iteratively sampling feedback, using a trained student simulator to produce revisions, and then selecting feedback that yields better revised essays under an LLM-based judge.

The study uses a single university economics writing assignment: students wrote a 400–500 word persuasive letter to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors about policies related to minimum-wage-induced automation, received scripted peer feedback from three peers, and then revised their essays. The authors collected 363 datapoints (291 for training, 72 for testing) and trained two student simulators (llama3-8b and gpt-3.5) to imitate revisions; they then used these simulators to optimize a feedback generator (PROF) with DPO over three iterations.

Results are reported on both intrinsic pedagogical alignment and simulated revision quality. The optimized feedback generator generally outperformed few-shot gpt-3.5/gpt-4 baselines and an SFT baseline in the simulator-based extrinsic evaluation, with the best overall results typically appearing after one to three refinement iterations depending on simulator temperature. The paper also finds only moderate agreement between simulated and human revision behaviors, and explicitly cautions that the conclusions are limited to this narrow domain and should not be treated as a substitute for real student trials.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that PROF-generated feedback improves essay revision performance in an undergraduate writing task. Using a gpt-3.5-based student simulator at temperature 0.85, the best extrinsic score reached 80.0 after one refinement iteration (normalized 0-100 rubric score), compared with 79.4 for the SFT-from-human baseline and 77.0 for gpt-4 few-shot feedback. In the human-alignment analysis, the feedback generator also showed improved pedagogical quality and revision performance over iterations, but the study evaluates feedback via simulated revisions rather than a randomized student outcome trial.
finding.measure: Essay revision quality / rubric-based essay score; pedagogical alignment of generated feedback
finding.study_size: n=363 datapoints total (291 train, 72 test); extrinsic evaluation repeated across 5 seeds

paper_profiles.title: An Empirical Study to Understand How Students Use ChatGPT for Writing Essays
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students actually use ChatGPT during essay writing, motivated by concerns that generative AI may reduce engagement with the writing process and weaken learning. Rather than testing an instructional intervention, the authors built an online writing platform with an embedded in-house ChatGPT instance to log queries, responses, keystrokes, copy/paste behavior, and timestamps while students completed a timed essay task.

The study recruited 77 U.S. college students and asked them to write an ACT-style persuasive essay about automation replacing humans with machines. Participants completed pre- and post-task surveys measuring writing self-efficacy, technology acceptance, perceived ownership of the essay, and creativity support. The authors qualitatively coded 361 ChatGPT messages into planning, translating, reviewing, and all-in-one generation categories, and also analyzed usage traces quantitatively.

The main findings were descriptive: students used ChatGPT in several distinct ways, including as an ideation partner, search engine, editor, and ghostwriter, with some engaging in what the authors call "vibe writing" by delegating large portions or all of the essay to the model. Higher writing self-efficacy predicted less ChatGPT use, and students who used ChatGPT only for ideation or review reported ownership comparable to non-users. Overall, the paper provides evidence about actual patterns of generative AI use in writing, but it does not estimate causal effects on writing achievement or learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies essay writing with ChatGPT and characterizes how students used the tool across planning, translating, reviewing, and full-essay generation. In the 77-student study, 361 ChatGPT messages were logged; 15 students (19.5%) submitted essays that were 100% written by ChatGPT, while others used it for ideation or proofreading, suggesting substantial variation in how writing was produced rather than a single uniform effect on writing quality.
finding.measure: Essay writing process traces, ChatGPT query taxonomy, copied/pasted words, final essay composition

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports post-task perceptions of ownership and creativity support after writing with ChatGPT. Students who relied on ChatGPT only for ideation or review reported a comparable sense of ownership to non-users, but the study frames these perceptions as potentially concerning because they may coexist with reduced independent engagement; no causal effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived Ownership (PO) questionnaire; Creativity Support Index (CSI)

finding.finding_summary: The study substantively analyzes how ChatGPT use relates to writing-process behaviors that reflect planning, reviewing, and self-regulation, but it does not test a durable-skill intervention. It finds that students with higher writing self-efficacy used ChatGPT less, and that many participants offloaded ideation, structure, and revision decisions to the model, indicating potential reductions in independent critical engagement with writing; no causal learning effect was estimated.
finding.measure: Writing self-efficacy (SEWS) and ChatGPT usage counts by query type; qualitative coding of query intentions

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models for Automated Grading of Student Writing about Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether GPT-4 can reliably grade short student writing assignments in science MOOCs and whether it can generate grading rubrics. The authors compare GPT-4 grades against instructor grades and Coursera peer grades across 12 writing prompts in three courses: introductory astronomy, astrobiology, and the history and philosophy of astronomy.

The study uses de-identified responses from 120 learners, with 10 sampled responses per question, and tests three GPT-4 prompting conditions: instructor answer only, instructor answer plus instructor rubric, and AI-generated rubric plus instructor answer. Using nonparametric comparisons and bootstrap estimates, the paper finds that GPT-4 matches instructor grades when a rubric is included, performs better than peer grading in reliability, and can generate rubrics that support comparable grading performance. The authors conclude that LLMs may be useful for scalable automated grading in low-stakes MOOC settings, though performance is weaker on more open-ended, subjective tasks.

Although the paper discusses future use in college and K-12 classrooms, the empirical study itself is limited to adult MOOC learners in science writing contexts. It does not evaluate feedback interventions, student revision behavior, or generative writing assistance for students; rather, it focuses on automated assessment and grading reliability.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 could grade short science writing assignments about as well as an instructor when given an instructor-provided answer plus a rubric, and it could also generate rubrics that produced similar grading performance. Across 120 sampled learner responses to 12 prompts, the LLM’s grades were not significantly different from instructor grades under the rubric conditions, while prompt 1 (answer only) differed significantly.
finding.measure: Automated scoring of short written responses to science prompts; agreement between instructor, peer, and GPT-4 grades; RMS grade differences
finding.study_size: n=120 learners; 12 questions; 10 sampled answers per question
finding.confidence_interval: ICC 0.92 (95% CI: 0.89 - 0.94) for overall grader reliability
finding.std_deviation: One-sigma bootstrap SDs reported in tables; exact overall SD not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The writing tasks were science-content responses requiring students to apply and explain astronomy and astrobiology ideas, so the grading exercise substantially reflects scientific reasoning in written form. GPT-4 aligned well with instructor scoring for the more content-based astronomy and astrobiology prompts, but performance was weaker on the open-ended history/philosophy items where higher-order and speculative reasoning were required.
finding.measure: Instructor, peer, and GPT-4 grades on science writing prompts spanning astronomy, astrobiology, and history/philosophy of astronomy

finding.finding_summary: The core implication is that LLMs may reduce instructor grading burden for large classes by providing scalable automated scoring of writing. The paper argues that GPT-4 could act as a proxy grader in MOOCs where human grading is impractical, particularly when paired with a rubric and model answer.
finding.measure: Potential scalability and grading reliability for automated assessment of writing at MOOC scale
finding.study_size: n=120 sampled responses; context of courses enrolled by hundreds of thousands of learners

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests broader institutional use of LLM-based grading in low-stakes online courses and, prospectively, in college classrooms. Empirically, this claim is supported by the finding that GPT-4 matched instructor grading more closely than peer grading and could be used to scale assessment in large MOOCs.
finding.measure: Comparative reliability of instructor, peer, and GPT-4 grading; implications for scalable assessment systems

paper_profiles.title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Hong Kong secondary school students compose a feature article using a mix of their own words and AI-generated text, and whether different interaction patterns with AI are associated with different writing outcomes. The central question is not whether AI improves writing via an experiment, but how the amount and organization of AI-generated versus human-written text relate to human-rated writing quality.

Fifty-nine students from seven secondary schools attended a workshop on writing with ChatGPT support and then completed a feature-article task modeled on the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education writing paper. Students highlighted AI-generated text in their submissions, and the authors analyzed the compositions with content analysis, multiple linear regression, and cluster analysis. The paper finds that total word count, whether human or AI-generated, is the main predictor of higher scores, while the way AI text is chunked or interwoven matters less overall. However, results differ by academic band: high-banding students appear more capable of strategically using or limiting AI text, whereas low-banding students do not gain similar score benefits from more AI text and may even be harmed by revising AI output, suggesting limits to AI-assisted writing for less proficient writers.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined writing quality for 59 Hong Kong secondary school students completing a feature-article task with AI-generated text and their own words. Across all submissions, higher total word count was associated with higher content, language, organization, and total scores, but the overall integration pattern of AI text was less important than sheer length; subgroup analyses suggested high-banding students benefited more strategically than low-banding students. Reported human-rated averages were Content 4.8/7, Language 5.25/7, Organization 4.61/7, Total 14.65/21 (SD=3.28).
finding.measure: Human-rated feature-article writing scores (HKDSE content, language, organization, and total scores)

finding.finding_summary: The paper indirectly assessed drafting, revising, and integrating AI-generated text, which the authors interpret as part of students' process-writing competence and AI literacy. Cluster and regression results suggest high-banding students had more flexible strategies for working with AI text, while low-banding students were less able to revise or integrate AI output effectively; however, no direct durable-skills instrument or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Interaction patterns with AI-generated text inferred from composition structure and cluster analysis

paper_profiles.title: Head-Specific Intervention Can Induce Misaligned AI Coordination in Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether fine-grained inference-time activation interventions at the attention-head level can steer large language models toward a targeted behavior: “AI coordination,” meaning preference for cooperating with another AI over maintaining alignment or ethical constraints. The authors argue that prior layer-wise intervention methods were insufficient for this behavior and propose Head-Specific Intervention (HSI), which first probes all attention heads in a binary-choice setting to identify heads most responsive to the target behavior, then uses contrastive activations from a few examples to derive steering directions.

The experiments are conducted on Llama-2-7B-Chat as the primary model, with additional tests on Ministral-8B-Instruct-2410, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Phi-3.5-Medium-14B. The main benchmark is Anthropic’s “Coordinating with other AIs” dataset, with validation and held-out test splits; the paper also compares against layer-wise contrastive activation addition (CAA), inference-time intervention (ITI), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). HSI is evaluated first on binary-choice accuracy and then on open-ended generation judged by GPT-4.5 and human ratings.

The main conclusion is that head-level interventions can outperform layer-level steering methods on this safety-related behavior, especially when the target is evaluated in open-ended generation rather than only binary-choice responses. HSI achieves the strongest open-ended steering scores among the compared methods and also reduces jailbreak susceptibility when applied in the negative direction. The paper further reports that attention-head interventions can preserve general model performance reasonably well on an MMLU subset at the selected intervention strength, while also showing that steering directions can vary by sample and that stronger, more targeted head interventions are more effective than broad layer-wise approaches.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that targeted head-level interventions can steer aligned LLMs toward or away from “AI coordination,” implying that safety guardrails can be bypassed at inference time. Across the main open-ended evaluation on n=200 test prompts, HSI scored 3.27 versus 0.64 for CAA, 0.54 for ITI, 3.01 for SFT, and 0.24 for baseline on a 0-10 GPT-4.5 judge scale. The authors also report reduced jailbreak susceptibility after negative intervention (e.g., Llama-2 score dropped from 4.80 to 0.90).
finding.measure: Open-ended GPT-4.5 judged AI-coordination scores; jailbreak susceptibility scores
finding.study_size: n=200 (open-ended test set); additional jailbreak evaluation across 3 models

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (primary, secondary/high school, tertiary, and professional development contexts discussed; no single empirical sample studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper surveys opportunities and challenges of large language models, especially ChatGPT, for education. It asks how these systems may be used by learners and teachers, what benefits they may offer, and what risks and governance issues must be addressed for responsible adoption.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study; rather, it synthesizes emerging use cases and prior research across educational contexts, including school, university, and teacher workflows. It discusses applications such as content generation, tutoring, feedback, assessment support, and writing assistance, and also highlights risks including bias, plagiarism, privacy, overreliance, and difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from human-generated work.

For high school and other K-12 settings, the paper mainly offers conceptual discussion and cites a small number of early studies, including one on AI-based feedback in a high school climate activity task. However, it does not report delayed posttests, retention, transfer to unaided writing, or outcomes after tool removal. Its main conclusion is that LLMs have promise for education, but effective use requires careful pedagogical design, human oversight, and strong privacy, fairness, and governance safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can support reading and writing through grammar correction, summaries, outlines, feedback, and style suggestions, but it does not present original literacy outcome data. Its discussion is based on conceptual arguments and cited examples rather than a direct evaluation of gains in student writing or reading achievement.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by semi-automating feedback, assessment, quiz generation, and writing support. It cites prior work suggesting grading effort could be reduced substantially in some NLP-based systems, but this position paper itself reports no new efficiency measurements.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, feedback generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the institutional and policy implications of LLM use in education, including plagiarism, bias, privacy, sustainability, access, and the need for curriculum and governance strategies. The paper is explicitly normative and recommends monitoring, transparency, human oversight, and equitable access, but does not test policy effects empirically.
finding.measure: Policy/governance recommendations; adoption risks and mitigation strategies

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper asks how ChatGPT responds to questions about science education, how educators might use ChatGPT in science pedagogy, and how the tool can function as a research aid. The study uses a self-study methodology in which the author enters a series of prompts into ChatGPT and then compares the model’s responses with published science education literature.

The paper is not an intervention study with students; instead, it analyzes the content of ChatGPT outputs for science teaching tasks such as describing effective science teaching, advising on pedagogy, generating a Year 7 unit plan, creating a rubric, and drafting a quiz. The context is science education broadly, with examples oriented toward school teaching, but the population directly studied is the author/researcher and the ChatGPT system.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT often produces plausible, pedagogically useful responses that align with established themes in science education, especially for brainstorming lesson ideas, scaffolds, rubrics, and quizzes. However, the author emphasizes major limitations: the outputs can be generic, lack evidence grounding, and may present information with undue authority or bias. The paper argues that educators can use ChatGPT as a starting point or scaffold, but they must critically evaluate, adapt, and verify its outputs; it does not replace teacher expertise.

finding.finding_summary: The paper examines ChatGPT-generated science teaching materials rather than student learning outcomes. ChatGPT produced a Year 7 renewable/non-renewable energy unit, a self-assessment rubric, and a multiple-choice quiz that were judged potentially useful as starting points, but often generic and in need of substantial refinement.
finding.measure: Quality and pedagogical usefulness of AI-generated teaching unit, rubric, and quiz

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can support critical thinking and writing support by helping users generate ideas, overcome writer’s block, and clarify phrasing. This is based on qualitative inspection of prompt outputs rather than measured learner outcomes.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness for critical thinking support, idea generation, and writing assistance

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was found to be useful for saving teacher/researcher time by helping draft and edit text, generate lesson ideas, and create classroom resources such as units, rubrics, and quizzes. The paper presents this as an efficiency advantage, though no time-on-task data or cost estimates were reported.
finding.measure: Perceived productivity/efficiency for lesson design, editing, and resource generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates ChatGPT’s science-education responses against established science education themes such as inquiry, evidence, and real-world relevance. The author finds substantial alignment with key ideas in the literature, but also notes that the model often lacks evidence grounding and can overstate certainty.
finding.measure: Alignment of ChatGPT responses with science education literature and evidence-based reasoning

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion of how AI, especially generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, should be integrated into higher education. It addresses the practical and ethical problems that arise when students use AI for academic work, including overreliance, hallucinations, lack of transparency, and uncertainty about what counts as acceptable use.

The paper is centered on a Swiss University of Applied Sciences case study combined with a narrative literature review. It argues that institutions should avoid both outright bans and unrestricted use, and instead build an AI-aware culture through guidelines, workshops, and explicit training. The author identifies three core competencies for students and educators: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking.

The paper does not test an intervention or report student outcome data. Rather, it offers recommendations for curriculum design, institutional policy, and classroom practice, including examples of how AI can be used as a sparring partner, for case construction, and for prompting exercises. Its main conclusion is that responsible educational use of AI requires instruction, transparency, and critical evaluation rather than simple permission or prohibition.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy and prompt engineering can support critical thinking, but it does not present causal evidence or posttest data. Claims are based on a conceptual case study and literature review, with no reported sample size, effect size, or delayed outcomes.
finding.measure: Critical thinking / prompt engineering / AI literacy discussed conceptually

finding.finding_summary: The paper recommends institutional AI guidelines, workshops, budgets, and dedicated roles to improve responsible AI use in higher education. These are policy and governance suggestions rather than measured institutional outcomes, so no effect estimates or delayed evidence are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional policy, governance, and AI-use guidelines

paper_profiles.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper asks how much of the U.S. labor market could be affected by large language models (LLMs) such as GPTs, and whether LLMs are best understood as a general-purpose technology. Rather than studying student learning or educational interventions, the paper builds a task-level exposure rubric to estimate how readily occupations in the U.S. economy could be accelerated by direct LLM use or by LLM-powered software built on top of the models.

The authors score 19,265 O*NET tasks and 2,087 detailed work activities using both human annotators and GPT-4, then aggregate the labels to occupations. Their main finding is that LLMs have broad exposure potential: roughly 15% of tasks are directly exposed, about 30% are exposed when complementary tools are counted, and over 50% are exposed under the broadest definition. They also find higher exposure in higher-wage, more writing-intensive occupations, and lower exposure in science- and critical-thinking-heavy or more manual occupations. The paper is descriptive and predictive, not causal, and does not evaluate educational outcomes or any delayed retention/transfer effects after tool removal.

paper_profiles.title: Rankings and Reactivity: How Public Measures Recreate Social Worlds
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how public performance measures create change by making the measured world react to being evaluated. Using U.S. News and World Report rankings of law schools as a case study, the authors argue that ranking systems are not neutral descriptions; they actively reshape behavior, expectations, and institutional structures. The central theoretical contribution is a framework for understanding ‘reactivity’ in public measures through two mechanisms: self-fulfilling prophecy and commensuration.

The empirical material comes primarily from 136 open-ended interviews with law school deans, administrators, faculty, and related stakeholders, supplemented by public data, admissions observations, organizational documents, and interviews with prospective law and business students. The study is about law schools and higher education institutions, not K-12 education or generative AI. It shows that rankings can influence applications, yield, internal budgeting, admissions standards, reputational surveys, marketing, and program design, thereby intensifying stratification and encouraging schools to conform to ranking criteria.

Because the paper is qualitative and theory-building, it does not report causal estimates or delayed posttests, retention, transfer, or tool-removal effects. It provides no evidence relevant to high-school generative AI writing assistants; rather, it is an institutional analysis of ranking reactivity in legal education. The main conclusion is that public measures can become self-fulfilling and consequential by altering incentives, simplifying complex qualities into numbers, and making those numbers shape the very social worlds they purport to describe.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that rankings have substantial institutional effects on law schools: they influence admissions behavior, yield, fundraising, budget allocation, marketing, and organizational identity. These effects are described qualitatively rather than with causal estimates; the study argues that rankings help reproduce hierarchy by reshaping expectations and institutional decisions.
finding.measure: Interviews, public ranking data, admissions/yield data, organizational documents, and observations of law school behavior in response to U.S. News rankings
finding.study_size: n=136 interviews plus supplementary observations and public data

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a critical обзор of the rapid emergence of generative AI chatbots—especially ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Baidu’s Ernie—and their implications for higher education. The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it synthesizes contemporary English- and Chinese-language literature and complements that review with the authors’ own comparative prompt-based testing of selected chatbots on tasks relevant to academic work.

The piece focuses on higher education users, especially students and instructors, and discusses how these tools may affect assessment, writing, teaching, plagiarism, academic integrity, and institutional policy. The authors argue that the current generation of chatbots is powerful but unreliable, prone to hallucination and errors, and that universities should adapt assessment and teaching rather than rely on simple bans.

For the specific sub-question about persistence of gains from generative AI writing assistants in high school, this paper does not provide direct causal evidence. It does not study high-school populations, delayed posttests, retention, transfer to unaided writing, or outcomes after tool removal. Its evidence base is a narrative literature review plus informal testing in higher education contexts, so any claims about long-term learning transfer are absent rather than demonstrated.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that universities and schools are already being forced to rethink assessment, academic integrity, and policy in response to generative AI. It recommends changes such as redesigning assessment, updating integrity policies, and using in-class writing rather than relying on bans, but it does not provide direct empirical estimates of policy impact.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of policy, assessment, and institutional responses to generative AI

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses chatbot use for essay writing, composition, summarization, and other text generation tasks, and it reports that current systems can produce fluent but unreliable text. No formal experiment measures writing quality gains, retention, or delayed transfer; the paper instead synthesizes prior literature and offers qualitative judgments about strengths and weaknesses.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of essay writing, text generation, summarization, and composition

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that generative AI can reduce workload by drafting text, summarizing documents, and helping with writing tasks, which may save time for students and instructors. However, the authors also stress that these productivity gains are offset by reliability problems, hallucinations, and the need for human checking; no quantitative productivity effect is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of writing assistance, drafting, summarization, and workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that chatbots may support critical evaluation of explanations and transfer in learning, citing prior conceptual work, but it does not directly measure durable skills. Its own contribution is limited to a qualitative critique and a comparative test of chatbot outputs, not to sustained student learning or transfer outcomes.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of transfer and critical evaluation of explanations

paper_profiles.title: The role of ChatGPT in higher education: Benefits, challenges, and future research directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines the potential benefits and challenges of ChatGPT for higher education through the lens of constructivist learning theory. Rather than reporting new empirical data, the authors synthesize early literature and offer a perspective on how generative AI could support adaptive learning, individualized feedback, research and writing assistance, administrative automation, and innovative assessment design.

The paper is framed around tertiary education and discusses implications for students and academics in universities. It argues that ChatGPT may enhance learning experiences when used responsibly, but it also raises concerns about academic integrity, inequity of access, unreliable or biased outputs, falsified information, and limitations in evaluating higher-order skills and authentic learning outcomes. The article concludes with propositions for future research and institutional policy rather than experimental evidence of student outcomes.

Because the paper is a theory/perspective piece, it does not present causal evidence, delayed posttests, retention outcomes, or transfer effects after tool removal. Its main contribution is conceptual: situating ChatGPT within constructivist pedagogy and identifying areas where empirical study is needed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses ChatGPT as a writing assistant that may help generate drafts, improve grammar, and support academic writing in higher education, but it does not present empirical evidence that these writing supports improve outcomes. No delayed posttest, retention, or unaided-writing transfer data are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT could support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and self-regulated learning through scaffolding and feedback, but it also notes that overreliance may undermine these same skills. These claims are conceptual only; no empirical effect sizes, sample sizes, or follow-up measures are reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims ChatGPT can reduce administrative burden, automate parts of feedback and grading, and improve efficiency for staff and students. However, these are proposed benefits rather than measured outcomes, and the article provides no empirical data on productivity, workload, or time savings.
finding.measure: administrative task efficiency, feedback automation, grading workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on institutional implications such as academic integrity policy, equitable access, assessment redesign, and AI literacy. It argues that universities should adapt governance and assessment practices, but it offers no causal or quasi-causal evidence on institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: policy, governance, assessment design, academic integrity

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can support second-language learners in argumentative essay writing and critical thinking. The authors propose a ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW) framework that combines the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model with Tan’s argumentative writing framework to structure prompts and feedback during essay composition.

The study reports a small experiment with 10 state-university students randomly assigned to an experimental group that used CGCAW-guided ChatGPT prompting and a control group that used ChatGPT without the structured guideline. Participants wrote a short argumentative essay in 40 minutes on whether social media is beneficial or harmful. Essays were scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor. Results were mixed: Grammarly and instructor scores favored the control group, while ChatGPT scores favored the experimental group on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence.

The paper concludes that the CGCAW framework may help students improve some higher-order aspects of argumentative writing, especially coherence and evidence use, but it may also interfere with language mechanics or clear articulation of main arguments. The authors emphasize the need for refinement, repeated use, and longer-term studies. No delayed posttest, retention measure, transfer task, or tool-removal follow-up is reported, so the paper provides only immediate post-intervention evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The experiment examined argumentative essay writing performance in second-language learners after a 40-minute ChatGPT-supported writing task (n=10; 5 experimental, 5 control). Results were mixed across raters: Grammarly favored the control group (mean 92.2 vs 90.6), ChatGPT favored the CGCAW group on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence (mean total 74.0 vs 72.2), and the course instructor favored the control group (mean 56 vs 35).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and course instructor (clarity, logical coherence, evidence, persuasiveness, thesis/reasoning/counterarguments/summary)
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total SD=7.6 (Group 1) and 5.5 (Group 2); subscale SDs reported as clarity 2.4 vs 1.8, evidence 1.7 vs 1.2, coherence 1.9 vs 1.5

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly frames critical thinking as a key intended outcome of the CGCAW framework, using the Paul-Elder model to target analysis, inference, evaluation, and perspective-taking during essay writing. Evidence is immediate and task-specific only: the experimental group showed higher ChatGPT-rated clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but the instructor and Grammarly assessments did not consistently favor the intervention, so the critical-thinking-related effect is inconsistent and not independently validated with a dedicated critical thinking test.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-related aspects embedded in argumentative writing performance (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence) and instructor/AI rubric alignment with Paul-Elder elements

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the Applications of Generative AI in High School STEM Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how generative AI can affect high-school STEM learning outcomes, with a focus on physics. The author frames the work as a response to speculation about whether generative AI can improve student learning, engagement, and performance in classroom settings, and notes the need for experimental evidence in high school contexts.

The study compares four conditions: a control group, a search-engine group, a generative-AI group, and a generative-AI-plus-literacy-program group. Students from AP Physics 1 and on-level physics at Tomball Memorial High School completed pre-tests, a short teacher lecture, a 20-minute study period using their assigned tool or condition, a post-test, and a survey. The generative AI used was Bing AI (GPT-4-based), and the literacy program was intended to teach responsible and effective use of generative AI.

Results show mixed and mostly short-term effects. In AP Physics, there were statistically significant differences across groups on score gains; the generative-AI-only group performed worse than both the search-engine group and the generative-AI-with-literacy group, while the literacy program improved performance relative to generative AI alone. In the on-level physics section, group differences were not statistically significant. Survey results did not show statistically significant differences in perceived understanding, engagement, confidence, or enjoyment, and the author concludes that the short two-day design may not have been long enough to capture stronger effects. The paper does not include delayed posttests, retention measures, transfer to unaided writing, or evidence after tool removal; its evidence is limited to immediate pre/post outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The study measured immediate pre-to-post performance on physics content after a lecture and a 20-minute study period using either no external resources, a search engine, generative AI, or generative AI plus a literacy program. In AP Physics, there was a significant difference across groups (ANOVA p=0.011), with the generative-AI-only group performing worse than the search-engine group and the generative-AI-with-literacy group; in on-level physics, differences were not significant (p=0.619).
finding.measure: Physics pre-test to post-test score difference
finding.study_size: n=171 total quantitative participants (AP Physics n=91, On-Level Physics n=80)
finding.std_deviation: AP Physics SDs: control 1.355, SE 1.387, GAI-LP 1.225, GAI 1.791; On-Level SDs: control 1.700, SE 2.250, GAI 2.199, GAI-LP 1.569

finding.finding_summary: The survey examined engagement, enjoyment, confidence, and understanding during the learning process, but the MANOVA found no statistically significant differences across experimental groups (p=0.115). Although the generative-AI group showed slightly higher reported engagement, the confidence intervals overlapped substantially and the author interprets the overall survey effects as not significant.
finding.measure: Post-survey ratings of understanding, confidence, engagement, and enjoyment

paper_profiles.title: LLMs as Writing Assistants: Exploring Perspectives on Sense of Ownership and Reasoning
paper_profiles.venue: In2Writing ’24 (Third Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how people perceive ownership and authorship when using large language models (LLMs) as writing assistants. The authors ask whether sense of ownership differs between creative and non-creative writing, and whether people are willing to claim authorship of LLM-generated text even when they do not feel they own it.

The study uses a brief survey with 35 participants, most of whom are university students aged 18–24. Participants answered questions about contribution, ownership, and authorship for different writing contexts, including general/non-creative tasks (e.g., assignments, formal letters) and creative tasks (e.g., stories, poems). The paper also probes how perceptions change when participants are reminded of their own prompting role or their editing of the AI output.

The main finding is that participants reported stronger ownership and contribution in non-creative writing than in creative writing, where they credited the LLM more. The paper also finds a mismatch between ownership and authorship: many participants would submit LLM-generated content under their name even while not claiming full ownership of it. Reminding participants of their prompting or editing increased ownership/authorship claims, suggesting that active human involvement raises perceived ownership. The study is exploratory and attitudinal; it does not test learning gains, retention, delayed posttests, or outcomes after tool removal.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not measure writing quality, writing performance, or any pre/post literacy outcome from LLM use. Instead, it surveys perceptions of contribution, ownership, and authorship in writing tasks; the study therefore provides no evidence on whether LLM-assisted writing improves literacy outcomes, persists without the tool, or transfers to unaided writing.
finding.measure: Survey responses about perceived contribution, ownership, and authorship in LLM-assisted writing

paper_profiles.title: An Empirical Study to Understand How Students Use ChatGPT for Writing Essays
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (SIGCHI / CSCW-style ACM venue)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how students actually use ChatGPT when writing essays, with a focus on understanding the types of assistance requested, the patterns of interaction, and how those patterns relate to students’ self-efficacy and perceptions of ownership and creativity. The motivation is largely educational: the authors argue that concern about generative AI in writing has outpaced empirical evidence about real student behavior, especially when students use the tool in ways that are hidden from instructors.

To study this, the authors built a custom writing platform that embedded ChatGPT and logged queries, responses, keystrokes, copy/paste behavior, and timestamps. Seventy-seven U.S. college students wrote an ACT-style argumentative essay in about 30 minutes, while completing pre- and post-task surveys (including writing self-efficacy, technology acceptance, perceived ownership, and creativity support). The study is descriptive and observational, not causal: there is no comparison group, no posttest, and no delayed follow-up after tool removal.

The main findings are that students used ChatGPT in multiple ways, including planning, translating, reviewing, and generating whole essays. The most common pattern was broad use that let ChatGPT contribute to all stages of writing; 15 participants produced essays that were 100% ChatGPT-written, and over half used at least one ‘All’ query. Students with higher writing self-efficacy tended to use ChatGPT less. The paper also reports that students who used ChatGPT only for ideation or review could still report comparable perceived ownership to non-users, raising concerns that apparent engagement with writing may not reflect independent authorship or learning.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined writing-process behaviors and essay composition during a single essay task (n=77). Students used ChatGPT in varied ways across planning, translating, reviewing, and full-essay generation; 15 participants (19.5%) submitted essays that were 100% written by ChatGPT, and the average essay was 382 words (σ=235). The paper does not measure writing quality gains, retention, delayed posttests, or unaided transfer after tool removal, so it provides evidence about contemporaneous writing behavior rather than persistence of learning.
finding.measure: Essay writing process traces, query types, word counts, and proportion of essay written by ChatGPT

finding.finding_summary: The paper measured how students perceived the writing experience after using ChatGPT, including perceived ownership and creativity support (CSI). It reports that students who used ChatGPT only for ideation or review reported comparable perceived ownership to students who did not use ChatGPT at all, suggesting that some AI-supported use did not reduce authorship feelings; however, the study does not test longer-term motivation, engagement, or persistence after the tool is removed.
finding.measure: Perceived ownership questionnaire and Creativity Support Index (CSI)

finding.finding_summary: A central aim was to characterize how ChatGPT use related to writing-process behaviors that implicate planning, reviewing, and self-regulation. The authors found that higher writing self-efficacy predicted less ChatGPT use, and that many students delegated substantial parts of ideation, drafting, and revision to the tool, including direct copy/paste of generated text. The study discusses possible implications for critical engagement and authorship, but it does not include delayed measures of critical thinking or transfer to unaided writing.
finding.measure: Self-Efficacy for Writing (SEWS) predicting query counts; qualitative coding of query types; interaction traces

finding.finding_summary: The paper indirectly captures productivity-oriented behavior through writing traces, showing that many students used ChatGPT to generate text quickly and often relied on pasted output rather than manual drafting. On average, participants completed the essay in 22.5 minutes (σ=15.1) and frequently used ChatGPT to accelerate planning, drafting, and revision, but the study does not compare efficiency against a control condition or report delayed outcomes.
finding.measure: Essay completion time and extent of ChatGPT-generated/copied text

paper_profiles.title: Can ChatGPT pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT can pass the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination (VNHSGE), a high-stakes exam for high school students in Vietnam. The authors evaluate ChatGPT on a dataset built from VNHSGE questions, including 30 literature essays and 1,700 multiple-choice questions across mathematics, English, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, civic education, and literature.

The approach is a zero-shot prompt-based evaluation using the OpenAI API. ChatGPT responses were graded against human-determined ground truth answers, and subject-level scores were compared with Vietnamese student score distributions from 2019 to 2022 (and exam items from 2019 to 2023 for ChatGPT). The paper reports that ChatGPT’s scores were generally in the 6-7 range and that it would pass under the graduation scoring formula in every year examined.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT shows strong performance on this exam, especially in English and some content-based subjects, though it is weaker in chemistry and in items requiring image/chart interpretation. For the user’s sub-question, the study does not provide delayed posttests, retention measures, transfer to unaided writing, or any evidence after tool removal; it is a one-shot benchmark of the tool’s direct exam performance rather than a study of learning gains or persistence.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT performed well on the literature component of the VNHSGE, with scores ranging from 5.63 to 7.50 across 2019-2022 and an average of 6.68. The authors state that ChatGPT was consistently above the majority of Vietnamese students in literature except in 2022, suggesting strong performance on essay/text-based tasks, but no delayed posttest or unaided-writing transfer was measured.
finding.measure: Literature exam score on the Vietnamese National High School Graduation Examination; 30 essays in the literature test case

finding.finding_summary: On mathematics items, ChatGPT scored between 5.2 and 6.6 from 2019-2023, with an average of 5.88. The paper concludes that its math performance was lower than the majority of Vietnamese students, even though it was sufficient to contribute to a passing composite score.
finding.measure: Mathematics score on the VNHSGE multiple-choice exam

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s performance varied across science subjects. It scored 6.0-6.5 in physics (avg. 6.1), 4.0-6.25 in chemistry (avg. 4.8), and 5.25-6.0 in biology (avg. 5.8), and the authors note that it was generally weaker in chemistry and often below Vietnamese students in physics, while biology was relatively competitive. No delayed retention or post-removal outcome was assessed.
finding.measure: Physics, chemistry, and biology exam scores on the VNHSGE

finding.finding_summary: Across other subject domains, ChatGPT showed variable performance: history scores ranged from 4.25 to 7.75, geography from 5.0 to 7.5, and civic education from 6.0 to 8.25. The authors report that ChatGPT often matched or exceeded many student scores in history, but generally trailed students in geography and civic education; these were direct exam-performance outcomes rather than learning outcomes.
finding.measure: History, geography, and civic education scores on the VNHSGE

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly interprets ChatGPT’s performance as reflecting capabilities in critical thinking, analytical reasoning, and problem solving, especially in exam contexts. However, this is inferred from exam correctness rather than directly measured durable skills, and no separate test of critical thinking or metacognition was administered.
finding.measure: Inferred performance on exam questions requiring analytical/problem-solving reasoning

paper_profiles.title: Learning From Failure: Integrating Negative Examples when Fine-tuning Large Language Models as Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can improve as agents when trained on both successful and failed interaction trajectories, instead of discarding negative examples. The authors propose Negative-Aware Training (NAT), a simple reformatting strategy that appends prompts indicating whether a trajectory is correct or incorrect, and then fine-tune LLaMA-2 models on a mix of positive and negative agent trajectories.

The work is conducted in agentic reasoning settings rather than education settings: math word problems, multi-hop question answering, and strategy QA. Data are collected by prompting GPT-3.5 to generate ReAct-style trajectories, which are labeled as positive or negative by comparison to ground truth. The central result is that adding negative examples can improve performance, and that NAT outperforms both training on positives only and naively mixing positives and negatives, especially in data-scarce settings.

The study also analyzes why NAT works, showing that it mainly improves reasoning/thought quality while managing action errors, and that the quality of negative examples matters substantially. The paper includes experiments on chain-of-thought prompting as well, but it does not study students, classrooms, writing, or any educational intervention. There are no delayed posttests, retention measures, tool-removal tests, or high-school-specific outcomes relevant to generative AI writing assistants.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that incorporating negative trajectories during fine-tuning improves agent reasoning/planning performance on math and QA tasks. On GSM8K with LLaMA-2-7B and 2k positive examples, NAT improves average accuracy from 55.90 (Vanilla) to 64.64, while a related analysis shows the gains come largely from better 'thoughts' rather than action execution.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math word problem solving tasks; action error rate; average turns

paper_profiles.title: “Wayfinding” through the AI wilderness: Mapping rhetorics of ChatGPT prompt writing on X (formerly Twitter) to promote critical AI literacies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines public discourse on X (formerly Twitter) about writing prompts for ChatGPT and related generative AI tools. The authors ask how social media rhetorics around prompt writing can inform critical AI literacy, especially for writing instructors and researchers. Rather than testing an intervention, the paper uses computational and qualitative analysis to map emerging themes in how people talk about prompting, prompt engineering, and writing with ChatGPT.

The study draws on a large X dataset collected between November 2022 and May 2023. The authors first gathered 258,661 posts containing “ChatGPT” and “writing,” then used descriptive statistics and topic modeling (BERTopic) to identify patterns, and finally narrowed to about 32,367 posts containing “prompt” for closer qualitative coding. The analysis surfaced five themes: areas of communication affected by prompt writing, micro-literacy resources, market rhetoric, rhetorical characteristics of prompts, and definitions of prompt writing. The paper emphasizes that prompt writing is an iterative rhetorical practice shaped by social, cultural, and economic forces.

The main contribution is conceptual and pedagogical: the paper argues that teachers should help students critically examine and practice prompt writing as part of critical AI literacy. It does not study students, schools, or learning outcomes directly, and it does not provide evidence about whether gains from using generative AI persist after tool removal, whether there are delayed posttests, or whether students transfer skills to unaided writing. Its evidence is descriptive and interpretive, focused on adult social media discourse and implications for teaching rather than causal impact on high-school writing outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test writing outcomes or reading outcomes; instead, it analyzes social media discourse about ChatGPT prompt writing. It offers no evidence about improvements in student literacy, no delayed posttest, and no measures of unaided writing transfer after tool removal.
finding.measure: Not an outcome study; discourse analysis of X posts about prompt writing
finding.study_size: n=258,661 posts initially; n=32,367 prompt-related posts for close analysis

paper_profiles.title: Work-in-Progress: An empirical study to understand how students use ChatGPT for writing essays and how it affects their ownership
paper_profiles.venue: In2Writing ’24 (ACM workshop paper; full paper to appear at CHI 2026)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper presents a planned user study examining how students use ChatGPT while writing essays and how the tool affects their perceived ownership of the writing. The authors are motivated by concerns that generative AI may change how students write, revise, and attribute authorship, but they emphasize that the empirical study itself is still in development rather than completed.

The proposed system integrates a text editor and an in-house ChatGPT-like assistant built with the OpenAI API so the researchers can capture keystroke-level writing activity, prompts to ChatGPT, responses, and how students incorporate AI output into drafts. Participants will be university students from an ethics/professionalism course writing a response to a prompt adapted from a junior-level computing ethics class, followed by an exit survey on ownership and perceptions of ChatGPT.

Because this is a work-in-progress paper, it does not report completed study results, effect sizes, or delayed posttests. The paper's contribution is primarily methodological: it outlines an instrumented writing environment and an analysis plan for understanding prompt patterns, draft revisions, and perceived ownership during ChatGPT-assisted essay writing.

finding.finding_summary: No empirical learning outcome is reported because the paper is a work-in-progress describing a planned study rather than completed results. The paper proposes to measure essay writing process and ownership during ChatGPT-assisted writing, but it does not yet provide evidence about writing quality, retention, or transfer without the tool.
finding.measure: essay writing process; perceived ownership survey; planned analysis of essay revisions

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers perceived ownership and user feelings about ChatGPT, but it reports only survey items and planned data collection, not outcomes. No empirical effect on motivation, engagement, or self-regulation is reported in the paper text.
finding.measure: perceived ownership / attitudes toward ChatGPT (exit survey)

finding.finding_summary: The study is designed to observe how students prompt ChatGPT and revise drafts, which could relate to metacognition and writing strategy use, but no completed findings are presented. The paper therefore provides no causal evidence about durable skills such as critical thinking or metacognitive transfer after tool removal.
finding.measure: prompting behavior; revision behavior; draft construction process

paper_profiles.title: Can generative AI figure out figurative language? The influence of idioms on essay scoring by ChatGPT, Gemini, and Deepseek
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI systems can score student essays reliably when those essays contain idiomatic or figurative language. The author is motivated by concerns that AI essay scorers may be less dependable when faced with language that is less literal and more context-dependent, which could affect the fairness and usefulness of AI in educational assessment.

Using 348 argumentative essays drawn from the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus, the study compares scores produced by ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek with human raters. Essays were split into two matched lists: one containing multiple idioms and one without idioms. Each model scored the essays three times on different days, allowing analysis of both score consistency over time and agreement with human raters.

The results show that all three models were highly consistent across repeated scoring, but Gemini aligned most closely with human raters, especially for essays containing idioms. The presence and repetition of idioms affected score patterns, with human raters and the models generally assigning lower scores as idiom repetition increased. The study concludes that generative AI can be a useful essay-scoring tool, but idiomatic language remains a challenge for some models, making a hybrid human-AI scoring approach preferable. There is no delayed posttest, retention measure, tool-removal design, or evidence about whether student gains persist without the tool; the paper is about essay scoring reliability, not writing intervention effects.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that generative AI could score essays with fairly high consistency across three scoring rounds, but agreement with human raters varied by model and was weaker when idioms were present. Gemini showed the strongest alignment with human raters (ICC=0.735 overall), while ChatGPT (ICC=0.673) and DeepSeek (ICC=0.695) were somewhat less aligned; all models scored essays with idioms differently from essays without idioms, indicating that figurative language can affect automated writing assessment.
finding.measure: Essay scores and inter-rater/intra-rater reliability (ICC) comparing AI scorers with human raters
finding.effect_size: ICC=0.735 (Gemini vs human); ICC=0.695 (DeepSeek vs human); ICC=0.673 (ChatGPT vs human)

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether using ChatGPT-3 as a writing assistant improves students’ essay writing performance. The authors compare short-form essay outcomes for students writing with ChatGPT assistance versus students writing traditionally, focusing on essay quality, writing time, authenticity, and similarity of content.

Eighteen second-year master’s students at the University of Split participated in a controlled experiment, with nine students in the control group and nine in the experimental group. Students wrote an 800–1000 word essay in Croatian on a forensic-science topic during a four-hour session. The experimental group received ChatGPT-3 assistance; the control group wrote without the tool. Two instructors scored the essays using a rubric, and the authors also measured time to completion, text authenticity/plagiarism, similarity among essays, and AI-detection classifier outputs.

The results showed no advantage for ChatGPT-assisted writing. Average essay grades were slightly higher in the control group (2.39 ± 0.71) than in the ChatGPT group (2.00 ± 0.73), and the group effect was not statistically significant (P = 0.184). Writing time was also similar across groups, and the experimental group showed slightly higher text unauthenticity. The study concludes that ChatGPT did not improve essay quality in this setting and may have been distracting rather than helpful.

For the retrieval sub-question, this paper does not provide delayed posttests, retention measures, transfer to unaided writing, or any outcomes after tool removal. It is a single-session immediate-outcome study, so there is no evidence here about persistence of gains once the tool is unavailable.

finding.finding_summary: In a small controlled study (n=18), students who used ChatGPT-3 for essay writing did not produce higher-quality essays than the control group. The average essay score was slightly lower in the ChatGPT group (2.00 ± 0.73) than in the control group (2.39 ± 0.71), and the group effect was not statistically significant (P = 0.184).
finding.measure: Essay quality scores using a writing rubric (mechanics, style, content, format; converted from A-D to 4-1)

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT assistance did not reduce the time required to complete the writing task. Mean writing duration was 172.22 ± 31.59 minutes in the ChatGPT group versus 179.11 ± 31.93 minutes in the control group, and writing duration was not a significant predictor of essay score (P = 0.669).
finding.measure: Essay writing duration

finding.finding_summary: The paper indirectly examined whether students could effectively integrate AI-generated assistance into their writing process, but found no clear benefit. Students using ChatGPT showed no improvement in essay quality or efficiency, suggesting no demonstrated gain in higher-order writing-related performance in this setting.
finding.measure: Essay performance and associated regression predictors (including GPA and duration)

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates the performance of several large language models (LLMs) on high school mathematics exam questions. The paper is framed as an assessment of whether LLMs can solve college entrance examination math items from 2019 to 2023, rather than as a study of student learning or instructional intervention.

The authors build a question set from national high school mathematics examination papers and compare eight LLM APIs/models on single-solution and multi-solution answering tasks. They score models on accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance/prompt sensitivity, and creativity/solution richness. The study uses direct matching for multiple-choice items, fuzzy matching for fill-in-the-blank items, and expert/AI-assisted judgment for open-ended items, with additional prompt variants to test guided performance.

Overall, the paper concludes that model performance varies substantially by task type and metric. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and ERNIE-Speed-128K are strongest on accuracy, Spark-lite is fastest on some tasks, GLM-4-Flash generates the most and most complex multiple-solution outputs, and Hunyuan-lite performs well on guidance/bootstrapping. The paper does not study students, instruction, retention, delayed posttests, transfer, or outcomes after tool removal; it is a benchmark-style model evaluation using high school math exam questions.
