finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates eight LLMs on high school mathematics exam questions from 2019-2023 and finds uneven performance across models and item types. On single-solution tasks, the best accuracies reported were 0.64 for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on comprehensive questions and 0.63 for ERNIE-Speed-128K, while performance on many item sets remained modest (e.g., multiple-choice accuracy ranged from 0.10 to 0.20 across models).
finding.measure: Accuracy on high school mathematics exam questions (multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, comprehensive, and difficulty-level subsets)

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes a logical reasoning evaluation for LLMs using multi-round chain-of-thought prompting and counts of successful guidance attempts. Models differed in the number of attempts needed to guide incorrect answers to correctness, with Hunyuan-lite requiring about 3 attempts, several models about 4-5, and Yi-34B about 6; the paper also reports logic scores such as 0.42 for Hunyuan-lite and 0.406 for Spark-lite.
finding.measure: Logical reasoning / guidance performance measured by average guidance attempts, success rate, and a composite logic score

finding.finding_summary: The study directly measures model response time as an efficiency metric across question types and multi-solution settings. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and gemma-2-9b-it were fastest on several single-solution categories and difficulty levels (e.g., 0.32-0.57 s on some item types), while GLM-4-Flash was slowest on question-and-answer tasks (16.01 s average) and also had the longest multi-solution processing time (7400 s).
finding.measure: Response time / processing time on high school mathematics questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates creativity and multi-solution generation on mathematics problems, including the number of distinct solutions, richness, and complexity of responses. GLM-4-Flash produced the most solutions overall (472 total; 4.5 per question) and the highest complexity score (68), while other models generated fewer and less complex alternative solutions.
finding.measure: Creativity / multi-solution richness and complexity in mathematics problem solving

paper_profiles.title: One Small Step for Generative AI, One Giant Leap for AGI: A Complete Survey on ChatGPT in AIGC Era
paper_profiles.venue: ACM (survey article; manuscript submitted to ACM)
paper_profiles.population: Not population-specific; survey spans general ChatGPT applications including education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of ChatGPT and related generative AI developments in the early AIGC era. It reviews the technology behind ChatGPT (Transformer architecture, autoregressive language modeling, GPT-1 through GPT-4), its capabilities, and a wide range of applications across scientific writing, education, medicine, software development, management, and other domains.

In the education section, the authors summarize prior work on how ChatGPT may affect teaching and learning, including personalization, assessment, language translation, and support for assignments. They also briefly discuss subject-specific uses in STEM and non-STEM contexts, such as physics essays, economics exams, and law exams. The paper is a narrative survey rather than an empirical study, so it does not test an intervention, compare outcomes over time, or provide evidence about persistence of gains after tool removal. For the specific sub-question on delayed posttests, retention, transfer to unaided writing, or outcomes after removing a generative AI writing assistant, this paper does not report such evidence.

finding.finding_summary: This is a survey paper, not an evaluation study, so it does not report causal evidence that ChatGPT improves or worsens writing outcomes. The education section mentions writing-related uses such as essay generation, proofreading, and content generation, but it provides no delayed posttest, retention, or unaided-writing transfer results.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes broad educational applications of ChatGPT across subjects, including physics, economics, and law, but it does not present original data or an empirical comparison on these subject outcomes. No causal estimate, sample size, or post-intervention assessment is reported.
finding.measure: subject-specific educational performance mentioned in survey examples

paper_profiles.title: PB-LLM: Partially Binarized Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of compressing large language models to extremely low bit-widths while preserving reasoning performance. The authors argue that naïve binarization methods fail for LLMs and propose Partially-Binarized LLMs (PB-LLM), which keep a small subset of salient weights at higher precision while binarizing the rest.

The paper evaluates PB-LLM on OPT-1.3B and LLaMA-7B using post-training quantization (PB-GPTQ) and quantization-aware training (PB-LLM), with results reported on standard commonsense reasoning benchmarks such as BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and OpenBookQA, plus perplexity on C4, WikiText2, and PTB. The main finding is that partially binarized models substantially outperform naïve binarization baselines and can recover much of the lost performance, especially when a modest fraction of salient weights is preserved. The work is a model-compression/quantization study; it does not examine education interventions, writing assistants, student populations, delayed posttests, retention, transfer, or tool removal effects.

paper_profiles.title: Should You Fine-Tune BERT for Automated Essay Scoring?
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 15th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether modern Transformer-based models, specifically BERT, are worth using for automated essay scoring (AES) compared with more classical approaches such as bag-of-words, n-grams, and linear models. The authors frame the question as a tradeoff between marginal accuracy gains and much higher computational cost, with particular attention to whether deep neural methods actually outperform simpler baselines in the AES setting.

To investigate this, they compare several AES approaches on five ASAP essay-scoring datasets using 5-fold cross-validation. The models include traditional n-gram and word-embedding baselines, multiple BERT fine-tuning curricula, BERT feature extraction without fine-tuning, and DistilBERT. The data include one prompt with high school seniors, but the study is not a high-school-specific intervention study; it is a benchmark comparison across prompt datasets. The paper reports that fine-tuned BERT performs about as well as classical models and sometimes slightly worse, while requiring far more training time and hardware. DistilBERT reduces runtime somewhat, but still does not change the overall conclusion that neural methods offer limited scoring gains relative to their computational cost.

The paper does not study generative AI writing assistants, delayed posttests, retention, transfer to unaided writing, or outcomes after tool removal. Its relevance to the user’s sub-question is indirect: it concerns automated essay scoring rather than writing assistance, and it provides no evidence about persistence of gains after using a tool. The main takeaway is methodological, not pedagogical: for essay scoring, BERT does not clearly justify its additional complexity over simpler methods.

finding.finding_summary: Across five ASAP essay-scoring prompts, fine-tuned BERT and DistilBERT achieved performance similar to classical AES models rather than clear improvements. Mean quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) for BERT variants was roughly .64-.82 depending on prompt, while the best classical models and human IRR were in a similar range; the paper emphasizes that BERT improved over an n-gram baseline by no more than about 5% and often did not exceed prior published results.
finding.measure: Automated essay scoring reliability / quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) on essay-quality labels
finding.study_size: approximately n=9,000 essays total across five ASAP prompts; about n=1,800 per prompt

finding.finding_summary: Fine-tuning Transformer models imposed a substantial runtime cost with little accuracy gain. End-to-end training for BERT-based approaches was about 30-100 times slower than naive baselines, and BERT-CLR had total runtime 11,519 seconds versus 111 seconds for the n-gram baseline in their cumulative timing comparison.
finding.measure: Training time, feature extraction time, prediction time, total runtime

paper_profiles.title: Introduction to Large Language Models (LLMs) for dementia care and research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an introductory review of large language models (LLMs) for dementia care and research. It explains how LLMs work, their training and deployment, and key limitations and risks such as hallucinations, bias, privacy concerns, misuse, and overreliance.

The paper then surveys possible dementia-related uses of LLMs, including conversational companionship, reading/writing assistance, navigation support, and caregiver support. It also reports survey results from people with dementia and their supporters about the perceived usefulness of several LLM application scenarios and desired features of LLM-powered apps.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs may offer promising support for dementia care, especially for communication, cognitive enrichment, and caregiver assistance, but that empirical validation, user-centered design, transparency, and safety safeguards are essential before broad deployment. The study is primarily a conceptual review with a small survey component, not a causal evaluation of outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs could support dementia care systems through improved diagnosis, treatment support, communication, and caregiver assistance, but emphasizes that deployment requires privacy protections, transparency, auditing, and ethical regulation. These are conceptual claims rather than causal effects, supported by discussion of risks and a questionnaire of people with dementia and supporters about desired app features.
finding.measure: narrative review and stakeholder questionnaire on perceived usefulness/desired features

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating L2 writers’ metacognitive strategy use in argumentative writing using a process-genre approach
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This classroom-based study examined whether a process-genre writing intervention could improve L2 writers’ metacognitive strategy use in argumentative writing. The authors ask both whether students’ perceived use of planning, considering the audience, monitoring, and evaluation changes after instruction, and how those strategies appear in real-time writing processes captured through think-aloud protocols.

The intervention was delivered in two intact first-year college English classes at a university in Central China. The experimental group (n=40) received six 90-minute sessions of process-genre writing instruction over 17 weeks, while the comparison group (n=32) received conventional product-oriented writing instruction. Students completed a metacognitive strategy questionnaire at pre-test, post-test, and delayed post-test (4 weeks later), and two experimental-group students completed think-aloud writing tasks at pre- and post-test.

Quantitatively, the main retained effect was on the “considering the audience” subscale: the experimental group improved from pre-test to post-test and maintained the gain at delayed post-test, while the comparison group did not change. There were no statistically significant effects for planning, monitoring, or evaluation, and no between-group differences on those dimensions. Qualitative think-aloud data suggested more substantial changes in how two students planned, monitored, and evaluated their writing, with greater attention to rhetorical structure, discourse-level monitoring, and after-draft revision; however, this evidence came from only two case-study participants and cannot support broad causal claims on its own.

For the user’s sub-question about persistence without the tool or delayed posttests: this paper does include a delayed post-test, but it is about metacognitive strategy use after process-genre instruction, not generative AI writing assistants. It does not study tool removal, unaided writing after AI use, or generative-AI persistence effects.

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on argumentative writing instruction and examined changes in L2 writers’ metacognitive strategy use during writing, a literacy-relevant outcome. Quantitatively, only the 'considering the audience' subscale showed a significant and retained improvement for the experimental group from pre-test to post-test and delayed post-test; planning, monitoring, and evaluation were not significantly improved. Qualitative think-aloud data from two students suggested richer, more discourse-oriented planning and revision after instruction, but this was based on case-study evidence rather than a group-level writing-performance measure.
finding.measure: Metacognitive Strategy Questionnaire for L2 argumentative writing; think-aloud protocols during argumentative writing tasks
finding.study_size: n=72 for questionnaire; n=2 for think-aloud case studies
finding.std_deviation: reported subscale SDs in tables, but no single overall SD/effect size for literacy outcome

finding.finding_summary: This was the paper’s central substantive outcome area: metacognitive strategy use in writing, including planning, considering the audience, monitoring, and evaluation. The experimental group showed a significant improvement only in 'considering the audience' (retained at delayed post-test), while planning, monitoring, and evaluation did not show statistically significant group-level gains; the think-aloud data nonetheless indicated qualitative shifts toward more strategic, discourse-level regulation in two students.
finding.measure: Metacognitive Strategy Questionnaire (planning, considering the audience, monitoring, evaluation); concurrent think-aloud protocols
finding.effect_size: Reported partial eta squared for significant time effects on 'considering the audience' (ηp²=0.150 for time main effect; ηp²=0.044 for time×group interaction); other subscales not significant
finding.std_deviation: Subscale SDs reported in Table 2; e.g., considering the audience EG pre SD=1.390, post SD=1.018, delayed post SD=1.206

paper_profiles.title: Developing Critical Thinking in Second Language Learners: Exploring Generative AI like ChatGPT as a tool for Argumentative Essay Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a structured ChatGPT-use framework can improve second-language learners’ argumentative writing and critical thinking. The authors propose the ChatGPT Guideline for Critical Argumentative Writing (CGCAW), which combines the Paul-Elder Critical Thinking Model with an argumentative-writing framework and Hattie & Timperley’s feedback model.

The study used a small experiment with 10 university students from a state university, randomly assigned to an experimental group that used the CGCAW prompts and a control group that used ChatGPT without specific guidance. Participants wrote a 40-minute argumentative essay on social media, and the essays were scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and a course instructor. Results were mixed: ChatGPT’s scoring suggested the CGCAW group improved in clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence, but Grammarly and the instructor often favored the control group, indicating the framework may have helped some higher-order writing features while not consistently improving mechanics or overall essay quality.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT may support argumentative writing and critical thinking when used with structured prompts, but the framework needs refinement. The authors explicitly call for longer-term and longitudinal research, noting that their study did not include repeated measures, delayed posttests, retention testing, transfer tasks, or any post-tool-removal assessment.

finding.finding_summary: The study examined argumentative essay writing quality in 10 undergraduate second-language learners (n=10) using a ChatGPT-based guideline (CGCAW) versus unstructured ChatGPT use. Results were mixed across raters: Grammarly slightly favored the control group (mean 92.2 vs 90.6), ChatGPT favored the experimental group on clarity, logical coherence, and use of evidence (mean total 74.0 vs 72.2), and the course instructor favored the control group (mean 56 vs 35).
finding.measure: Argumentative essay quality scored by Grammarly, ChatGPT, and course instructor on clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness, thesis, reasoning, counterarguments, and summary
finding.std_deviation: ChatGPT total SD=7.6 (G1) vs 5.5 (G2); clarity SD=2.4 vs 1.8; evidence SD=1.7 vs 1.2; coherence SD=1.9 vs 1.5

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on critical thinking within argumentative writing, arguing that ChatGPT-guided prompts can help learners improve reasoning, evidence use, and logical coherence. In the experiment, the CGCAW group was rated higher by ChatGPT on indicators tied to critical thinking (clarity, logical coherence, and evidence use), but the instructor ratings were lower overall, so the evidence is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Critical-thinking-related features in argumentative essays (clarity, logical coherence, use of evidence, persuasiveness; paper frames these as critical thinking/argumentation skills)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses self-regulation, reflection, and self-monitoring as part of the feedback framework, but these are not directly measured with a separate instrument. The only empirical evidence is indirect: the CGCAW group produced essays that ChatGPT rated better on some process-related dimensions, while some participants could not complete the task in time, suggesting the intervention did not uniformly support persistence or task completion.
finding.measure: Task completion within the 40-minute essay writing session; indirect discussion of self-regulation/self-monitoring in the framework

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not directly study efficiency outcomes as a primary endpoint, but it does report that two participants could not complete the essay within the allotted 40 minutes and that the guideline may have complicated completion for some students. This suggests the structured AI prompting approach may have added process burden rather than improving task efficiency.
finding.measure: Essay completion within a 40-minute writing task

paper_profiles.title: Exploring EFL Secondary Students’ AI-generated Text Editing While Composition Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how Hong Kong EFL secondary students edit AI-generated text while composing an expository article, with particular attention to the kinds of edits they make and the broader patterns of how they write with generative AI. The authors note that prior work has examined perceptions and final writing products, but little is known about students’ actual drafting and revision behavior when using AI-generated text during composition.

The study used an exploratory mixed-methods approach centered on screen recordings from 29 Hong Kong secondary students who attended an AI-assisted writing workshop; 25 recordings showed AI-generated text edits and were analyzed. Students used POE chatbots (including ChatGPT access) and Google Docs/iOS writing tools while completing a 500-word expository writing task. The analysis identified 15 edit types across seven categories, including insertion, deletion, and several replacement types, plus unanticipated AI-initiated edits from Apple iOS predictive text and Google Docs grammar/spelling/next-word suggestions.

For the broader writing process, the authors identified four editing patterns combining planning vs. no planning with top-down vs. bottom-up drafting and revising. Most students used planning with bottom-up drafting and revising, suggesting that many maintained a more traditional writing process even when writing with AI. The paper concludes that students do not merely paste unedited AI text; instead, they actively evaluate, modify, and sometimes resist AI-generated output. However, the paper does not include delayed posttests, retention measures, transfer tasks, or any outcome after tool removal, so it provides no evidence about persistence of gains without the tool.

finding.finding_summary: In this qualitative/screen-recording study of 25 Hong Kong secondary students’ writing sessions (from 29 recruited), students frequently inserted, deleted, and replaced AI-generated text while composing an expository article. The paper reports 266 total edits across 15 edit types, including the most frequent insertion edits (n=68 across 22 students), deletion (n=58 across 13 students), and replacement of AI text with human text (n=44 across 12 students), showing active revision behavior rather than simple copying.
finding.measure: Screen-recorded expository writing edits during composition writing

paper_profiles.title: Better by You, better than Me? ChatGPT-3 as writing assistance in students’ essays.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether ChatGPT-3 can improve students’ essay-writing performance when used as a writing assistant. The authors compare essays written by 18 university students in Croatia, split into a control group that wrote traditionally and an experimental group that used ChatGPT-3 for assistance.

Students were given the same essay prompt, time limit, and rubric-based grading criteria. Outcomes included overall essay score, writing time, text authenticity/plagiarism, text similarity across essays, and AI-classifier judgments of whether the text appeared AI-generated. The experimental group did not outperform the control group on essay quality, writing speed, or authenticity; if anything, the control group had slightly higher average scores.

Because the study is a small, single-session comparison with no delayed posttest or follow-up, it provides no evidence about retention, transfer to unaided writing, or whether any gains persist after the tool is removed. The paper’s main conclusion is that ChatGPT assistance did not improve short-form essay performance in this sample, and it may have introduced some authenticity concerns without clear benefits.

finding.finding_summary: In a two-group comparison of essay writing (n=18; 9 control, 9 ChatGPT-assisted), using ChatGPT-3 did not improve essay quality. Mean overall essay grade was slightly higher in the control group (2.39 ± 0.71) than in the experimental group (2.00 ± 0.73), and the group effect was not statistically significant (P=0.184).
finding.measure: Rubric-scored essay quality / overall essay score

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT use did not reduce the time needed to complete the essay. Writing duration was similar in the experimental group (172.22 ± 31.59 minutes) and control group (179.11 ± 31.93 minutes), and the group effect was not significant (P=0.669).
finding.measure: Essay writing time

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group showed slightly higher text unauthenticity than the control group (11.87% ± 13.45 vs 9.96% ± 9.81), but the study also found low pairwise similarity across essays overall (Jaccard index median 0.002, range 0–0.054). The authors interpreted this as no strong evidence that ChatGPT produced more duplicated text, though AI-detection tools flagged more ChatGPT-assisted essays as potentially AI-generated.
finding.measure: Text authenticity / plagiarism / pairwise essay similarity / AI-classifier labels
finding.std_deviation: Unauthenticity SDs: 13.45 and 9.81; similarity median reported

paper_profiles.title: Cases of EFL Secondary Students’ Prompt Engineering Pathways to Complete a Writing Task with ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how four secondary school EFL students in Hong Kong used ChatGPT and other proprietary chatbots (via the POE app) for the first time while completing a timed blog-writing task. The authors focus on the content, quantity, and sequencing of students’ prompts, treating each prompt exchange as part of a “prompt engineering pathway” within a machine-in-the-loop writing process.

The study is a qualitative case study based on screen recordings of students’ iPad activity and the completed writing products. The four students, all relatively high-achieving in English within their form, were asked to write a blog entry using their own words and AI-generated words, with no explicit instruction on how to prompt chatbots. The authors coded 36 prompt turns and identified six distinct prompt types (e.g., auto-complete, natural language instruction, questions, search-like prompts, greetings), plus more sophisticated combinations of these types.

Findings show that students used different prompt engineering pathways and learned largely through trial-and-error. Some students began with simpler prompts and later shifted to more complex ones, while others repeatedly refined or extended prior prompts. The paper concludes that secondary EFL students are generally unsophisticated prompt engineers and would likely benefit from prompt-engineering education to better leverage chatbots for writing tasks.

For the retrieval question about persistence of gains without the tool: this paper does not measure delayed posttests, retention, transfer to unaided writing, or any post-tool-removal outcomes. It is a single-session qualitative process study, so it provides no evidence about whether benefits persist after ChatGPT is removed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies student writing processes while using ChatGPT and other chatbots, but it does not evaluate writing quality gains, delayed retention, or unaided writing performance. The evidence is limited to descriptive analysis of prompt engineering pathways across 36 coded turns from four secondary EFL students (n=4) during one timed writing task.
finding.measure: Prompt types and sequencing during an EFL blog-writing task; completed writing products were collected but not quantitatively evaluated

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Summarization: Designing AI Support for Real-World Expository Writing Tasks
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; no human study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position paper arguing that expository writing is an underexplored but high-value target for AI-assisted writing systems. The authors define expository writing as evidence-driven and knowledge-generating writing that synthesizes source documents into new information or insights, such as literature reviews, clinical notes, or other real-world expert writing tasks.

Rather than evaluating a specific intervention with users, the paper proposes a design framework for future AI support across three stages of expository writing: reading and collecting evidence, information synthesis, and text composition. The authors discuss how language models might assist with each stage while warning about risks such as hallucination, overreliance, and biasing authors' judgments.

The paper does not report an empirical study, intervention effects, or any learner outcomes. It is conceptual and forward-looking, intended to shape future research on AI support for real-world expository writing rather than provide evidence about student learning, retention, or transfer after tool removal.

paper_profiles.title: Approaching the Limits to EFL Writing Enhancement with AI-generated Text and Diverse Learners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how Hong Kong secondary school students interact with generative AI text when composing an English as a foreign language (EFL) feature article. The authors ask what textual features characterize human-AI compositions, what interaction patterns with AI-generated text can be identified, and whether those patterns are associated with stronger writing outcomes.

The study analyzed 59 student compositions collected after a two-hour school workshop on writing with ChatGPT-like tools. Students from seven secondary schools were instructed to compose with both their own words and at least one generative AI chatbot, and the researchers used content analysis, multiple linear regression, and cluster analysis to relate AI/human word use and chunk patterns to teacher-rated writing scores (content, language, organization, and total score). The design is cross-sectional and correlational; it does not include delayed posttests, retention measures, or post-removal writing assessments.

The main finding is that overall writing scores were driven primarily by the total number of words in the composition, regardless of whether they were AI-generated or human-written, rather than by the specific way AI text was integrated. However, the benefits of AI use differed by student academic banding. Higher-achieving students appeared better able to leverage AI strategically, while lower-achieving students did not gain reliably from more AI text and sometimes performed worse when revising AI output. The paper therefore argues that generative AI may help some secondary students write stronger compositions, but its benefits depend heavily on students’ existing writing competence and ability to draft and revise independently.

finding.finding_summary: Across 59 Hong Kong secondary school compositions, writing quality was mainly associated with the total number of words in the submission, not with how AI-generated text was incorporated. Partial correlations with total score were positive and statistically significant for both AI words (r≈0.417) and human words (r≈0.424), while chunk-type variables were mostly non-significant. However, subgroup analyses showed that high-banding students could use AI more strategically, whereas low-banding students did not reliably benefit from additional AI text and sometimes lost score when revising AI output.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated EFL feature article writing scores (content, language, organization, total score)

finding.finding_summary: The paper indirectly assesses process-writing competence, including students’ ability to draft independently, revise AI output, and integrate human and AI text. Higher-banding students showed signs of stronger independent writing and more effective strategy use, while lower-banding students appeared less able to manage drafting and revising with AI. These conclusions are based on correlational patterns rather than a direct intervention measure.
finding.measure: Observed interaction patterns with AI-generated text and inferred drafting/revising competence from cluster and regression analyses

paper_profiles.title: Chain-of-MetaWriting: Linguistic and Textual Analysis of How Small Language Models Write Young Students Texts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how small language models (SLMs) generate writing for young students, focusing on a French narrative writing task about violence at school and comparing model outputs with texts written by 10-12-year-old schoolchildren. The authors introduce a prompting framework called Chain-of-MetaWriting (COMW), designed to make the model explicitly describe a writing process that includes clarifying the task, listing steps, explaining choices, drafting, and self-evaluating. They also compare several multilingual 3B SLMs and ChatGPT-4o mini across baseline, adapted, writing-steps, and COMW prompts.

The study uses 123 student texts from the ANR Pro-TEXT corpus: 66 schoolchildren narratives (ages 10-12) and 57 undergraduate argumentative texts, though the paper’s core analysis for young learners is centered on the schoolchildren sample. The authors conduct qualitative linguistic analysis, vocabulary comparison against the Manulex French school lexicon, and an analysis of student writing-process pauses and bursts. They find that SLMs can produce superficially plausible narratives, but these outputs often contain coherence, cohesion, vocabulary-accessibility, and content issues, especially for sensitive topics. The models sometimes auto-censor, use words too complex for the target age, and fail to reproduce key aspects of children’s actual writing process, such as segmentation, revision, and content shaping.

For the young-student writing task, the paper’s conclusion is that current SLMs are not good models for supporting learning to write because they remain too far from the expectations of authentic schoolchildren narratives and do not adequately simulate the cognitive and metacognitive stages of child writing. The paper is exploratory and descriptive rather than causal: it analyzes generated texts and student writing behavior but does not test whether using an AI writing assistant improves student outcomes, and it provides no delayed posttest, retention, transfer, or post-removal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that SLM-generated text is often not well matched to young students’ literacy needs: outputs can be too complex, incoherent, or weakly coherent, and they diverge from the narrative structures used by 10-12-year-old schoolchildren. In a fine-grained comparison of generated and student narratives (two SLM texts of 89 and 133 words vs two child texts of 92 and 106 words), the authors report issues in topic progression, reference, deixis, cohesion, and language correctness, suggesting the models are poor writing aids for learning to write in this context.
finding.measure: Qualitative linguistic analysis of narrative cohesion/coherence; vocabulary analysis against Manulex; comparison of generated vs schoolchildren texts
finding.study_size: n=123 total texts in corpus; core young-student comparison uses n=4 texts (2 SLM, 2 schoolchildren)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that SLMs do not adequately simulate the higher-level writing processes associated with planning, revision, and metacognitive control. In the COMW analysis, the model produces a step-by-step rationale, but the authors conclude that the revision stage lacks the formal revisions central to natural language writing by 10-12-year-olds, and that important child-writing stages such as segmentation and content shaping are absent from the prompt model.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of Chain-of-MetaWriting outputs and comparison to writing-process features (pauses, bursts, revisions) in schoolchildren

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests SLMs can generate long, structurally complete texts quickly and can imitate some steps of writing, which could make them superficially useful as drafting tools. However, the authors emphasize that the outputs are often too long, sometimes censored, and frequently not suitable for young learners, so any efficiency benefit is undermined by quality and appropriateness problems.
finding.measure: Descriptive comparison of generated text length, prompt responsiveness, and apparent completeness

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing AI in Secondary Education to Enhance Writing Competence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a timely question in secondary education: how generative AI tools such as ChatGPT might support or undermine the development of students’ writing competence and personal writing voice. The authors frame the issue as a tension between productive augmentation of the writing process and risks such as dependency, plagiarism, and weakened independent thinking. The article is explicitly concerned with secondary-school writing instruction and the implications for tasks, assessment, and teacher practice.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study. Instead, it offers a conceptual and literature-based discussion of where AI may fit within the writing process, including pre-writing, drafting, revision, feedback, self-assessment, and peer assessment. It uses examples of prompts and classroom practices to argue that AI may be most defensible as a limited support tool for brainstorming and feedback, not as a replacement for students’ own drafting or for teacher judgment.

The main conclusion is cautious: the authors argue that schools should design writing tasks and assessment systems that preserve authentic student work and avoid shortcuts that could weaken learning. They also emphasize that current evidence is still thin, especially on whether AI improves writing competence in durable ways or whether students can transfer gains to unaided writing. For the specific sub-question of persistence after tool removal, the paper does not report delayed posttests, retention outcomes, or causal evidence; it mainly states that solid studies are lacking.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a conceptual review/commentary about writing competence in secondary education rather than a causal study of an AI writing intervention. It argues that there are currently no solid studies showing whether generative AI improves writing competence, and it does not report delayed posttests, retention data, or transfer to unaided writing.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses critical thinking, self-reflection, and ownership of writing as desirable outcomes, but it does not empirically test whether AI use improves these durable skills. Its main claim is normative: students should not rely on AI in ways that weaken independent judgment or the development of a personal voice.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that AI can lighten teacher workload by providing instant feedback, handling standard questions, and supporting formative assessment in writing instruction. However, this is presented as a practical possibility and literature-based claim, not as an evaluated outcome with measured gains.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: “Wayfinding” through the AI wilderness: Mapping rhetorics of ChatGPT prompt writing on X (formerly Twitter) to promote critical AI literacies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines public discourse on X (formerly Twitter) about ChatGPT prompt writing as a way to understand emerging critical AI literacies. Rather than evaluating an instructional intervention or measuring student outcomes, the authors collect and analyze a large corpus of social media posts to map how users talk about prompts, prompt engineering, and the rhetorical work involved in instructing generative AI.

Using an iterative, reflexive mixed computational-qualitative workflow, the authors first gather 258,661 posts containing “ChatGPT” and “writing,” then apply descriptive statistics and BERTopic topic modeling to identify broad themes. They then narrow to about 32,367 posts containing “prompt” and qualitatively code the discourse, identifying five themes: areas of communication impacted by prompt writing, micro-literacy resources, market rhetoric, rhetorical characteristics of prompts, and definitions of prompt writing.

The study is situated in writing studies and digital rhetoric, with the authors arguing that studying prompt-writing discourse can help teachers and researchers think critically about generative AI and design pedagogy for critical AI literacy. The paper does not test whether learning gains persist after tool removal, does not include high-school students, and does not report delayed posttests, retention, transfer, or unaided-writing outcomes. Its contribution is interpretive and conceptual rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure literacy outcomes directly; instead, it analyzes public rhetorics around ChatGPT prompt writing. The authors argue that prompt writing is presented in social media as a literacy practice and discuss implications for teaching critical AI literacies, but no student writing performance, retention, or transfer data are reported.
finding.measure: Social media discourse about ChatGPT prompt writing
finding.study_size: n=258661 posts (subset of ~32,367 prompt-related posts for qualitative analysis)

finding.finding_summary: The paper theorizes prompt writing as involving rhetorical judgment, audience awareness, and iterative tinkering, which are durable-skill-like concepts, but these are not measured as learner outcomes. No empirical assessment of critical thinking, metacognition, or transfer beyond the tool is reported.
finding.measure: Social media discourse and thematic analysis of prompt-writing rhetoric

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses broader institutional and pedagogical implications for writing instruction and critical AI literacy, but it does not evaluate policy, governance, or institutional change outcomes. Its claims are interpretive recommendations based on discourse analysis rather than measured institutional effects.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of X posts and implications for pedagogy

paper_profiles.title: GOD model: Privacy Preserved AI School for Personal Assistant
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint proposes the Guardian of Data (GOD) model, a privacy-preserving framework for evaluating and improving on-device personal AI assistants. The central problem is how to measure proactive personalization—such as anticipating user needs—while keeping user data on device and maintaining trust, autonomy, and privacy.

The paper describes a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)-based system that generates curriculum-style evaluation tasks of increasing difficulty, checks responses using minimal data disclosure, and uses scoring rules to estimate the value of personal data. It also sketches mechanisms for anti-gaming, data validation, token incentives, and future reinforcement-learning-based refinement of personal AI behavior.

The work is a conceptual systems paper rather than an empirical study. It does not report experiments with students, teachers, or school settings, and it does not evaluate educational outcomes. Its main contribution is a proposed architecture and evaluation methodology for privacy-preserving personal AI assistants, framed as an "AI school" for on-device agents.

paper_profiles.title: Towards AI-assisted Academic Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents an AI-assisted academic writing system with two main capabilities: contextual citation recommendation and introduction generation. The authors frame the problem as helping writers locate relevant prior work and draft structured introductions more efficiently, especially when citation search and synthesis interrupt the writing process.

For citation recommendation, the system uses a local scholarly corpus (OpenAlex) and a retrieval-augmented prompting pipeline to fabricate candidate citations from nearby text context, retrieve nearest-neighbor papers, and then rerank candidates with an LLM. For introduction generation, the system uses a prompt chain to identify novel claims in a manuscript, summarize those claims, and compose an introduction that situates the work relative to canonical and recent references.

The paper evaluates the citation recommender on 1,015 citation-containing sentences sampled from S2ORC papers, comparing retrieval performance across random distractors, nearest-neighbor distractors, and manuscript-reference distractors. It also evaluates introduction generation on 14 NBER papers using ROUGE and LLM-based entailment judgments, and reports qualitative interviews with six experienced academic authors about citation validation workflows. The main conclusion is that the system can produce useful citation suggestions and reasonably faithful generated introductions, and that authors want more precise in-situ support for scholarly writing.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the citation recommender can retrieve the ground-truth citation with moderate-to-strong ranking performance, suggesting it could reduce time spent searching for references. On 1,015 contextual citation retrieval cases, performance depended on distractor difficulty; for example, with 10 candidate citations, mean reciprocal rank was 0.320 for random distractors, 0.300 for nearest-neighbor distractors, and 0.308 for reference distractors, with precision@1 ranging from 0.109 to 0.124.
finding.measure: Citation retrieval quality (P@1, P@3, P@5, MRR) for contextual citation recommendation

paper_profiles.title: Approach Intelligent Writing Assistants Usability with Seven Stages of Action
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (design/position paper; no human study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper proposes Norman’s seven stages of action as a conceptual framework for designing and analyzing intelligent writing assistants built on large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that current LLM writing tools often struggle with usability issues such as coherence, trustworthiness, ownership, and predictability, and that these issues can be better understood by decomposing human-LLM interaction into goal formation, planning, specification, execution, perception, interpretation, and comparison.

Rather than evaluating a new system with participants, the paper is a design-oriented synthesis that illustrates how the framework could be applied to writing tasks, using software tutorial authoring as an example. The context is general human-LLM interaction and writing-assistant design, not K-12 education or student outcomes. The paper’s main conclusion is that the seven stages of action can help structure interface features, prompt design, output evaluation, and moderation strategies for LLM-based writing assistants, but it does not present empirical evidence about learning, writing gains, or retention.

For the retrieval question about persistence of gains from high-school generative AI writing assistants without the tool, this paper provides no causal or quasi-causal evidence and no delayed posttest, retention, transfer, or tool-removal outcome. It is a conceptual paper only; therefore, delayed evidence is absent.

paper_profiles.title: Understanding EFL Students’ Idea Generation Strategies for Creative Writing with NLG Tools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study examines how English as a foreign language (EFL) secondary school students use natural language generation (NLG) tools to support idea generation for creative writing. The authors focus on three questions: how students search for ideas with NLG tools, how they evaluate AI-generated ideas, and how they choose among different tools. The study is motivated by the claim that idea generation is a core challenge in creative writing and that prompt-based NLG systems may scaffold this process.

The intervention/context involved four Hong Kong secondary school students participating voluntarily in seven hour-long workshops. During the workshops, students learned about short-story writing, prompting NLG tools, and digital writing in Google Docs, then wrote short English stories using their own words plus AI-generated text from four custom Hugging Face tools (next sentence, next word, and two next paragraph generators). Students then completed written reflections after workshop sessions, which formed the main data source, supplemented by audio/video recordings. The design is qualitative and thematic rather than causal.

The paper finds that students often prompted tools with incomplete language fragments rather than clearly defined story elements, and that they tended to evaluate outputs by checking whether they fit an existing story idea or schema. Some students showed aversion to more novel or transformative AI suggestions, preferring outputs that stayed close to their intended story. When selecting tools, students generally preferred those that generated more ideas or longer outputs, because they could then pick usable pieces. The study concludes that EFL students may need explicit instructional scaffolds for prompting, evaluating, and selecting NLG outputs, but it does not test learning gains, delayed posttests, transfer, or outcomes after tool removal.

finding.finding_summary: This paper substantively studies students’ writing processes and idea generation for creative writing with NLG tools, but it does not report a causal effect on writing quality, writing achievement, or retention after tool removal. The evidence is based on thematic analysis of reflections from n=4 Hong Kong secondary students participating in workshops, with no effect size, confidence interval, or delayed posttest reported.
finding.measure: Written reflections about creative writing with NLG tools; qualitative analysis of story-writing/idea-generation strategies

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines strategy use, including how students prompt, evaluate, and select AI-generated ideas, which relates to metacognitive and strategic writing behavior. However, it does not measure whether these strategies persist over time, transfer to unaided writing, or improve durable skills causally; no delayed evidence is reported.
finding.measure: Written reflections and workshop discussions on prompting, evaluating, and selecting NLG outputs

paper_profiles.title: AIRCC-Clim: a user-friendly tool for generating regional probabilistic climate change scenarios and risk measures
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents AIRCC-Clim, a standalone software tool for generating probabilistic regional climate change scenarios and climate risk measures. The paper addresses a modeling and decision-support problem in climate science: how to produce spatially explicit temperature and precipitation projections, as well as threshold-based risk estimates, with low computational and technical requirements.

The tool combines a modified Schneider-Thompson simple climate model, precalculated output from reduced-complexity models (MAGICC6 and the Thermodynamic Climate Model), and pattern-scaling methods to create monthly and annual regional projections. It also computes user-defined probabilities of exceedance and dates of exceedance for climate thresholds. The authors illustrate the software with scenarios comparing a high-emissions pathway (RCP6.0), a deep-mitigation pathway (RCP2.6), and a version of RCP2.6 with mitigation delayed by 10 years.

The paper is not an education study and does not examine students, teachers, schools, or generative AI writing assistants. Its findings concern climate projections and risk under emissions scenarios, showing that delayed mitigation increases warming and precipitation-risk exposure relative to immediate deep mitigation. Because it is a software/methods paper with illustrative simulations rather than an empirical education study, it does not provide evidence relevant to high-school writing-assistant retention, delayed posttests, or tool-removal effects.

paper_profiles.title: AI in the Writing Process: How Purposeful AI Support Fosters Student Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how the design of generative AI writing support affects student writing processes, specifically whether a process-oriented interface can preserve writer agency and support deeper knowledge transformation better than a standard chat-based LLM assistant. The authors frame the work as a response to concerns that generic chatbots may encourage passive text acceptance, weaken ownership, and reduce the cognitive work involved in writing.

The study uses a randomized controlled trial with 90 undergraduate students assigned to one of three conditions: Script&Shift, a process-oriented AI writing tool; a custom chat-based LLM writing assistant; or a standard writing interface without AI support. Participants completed a source-based argumentative writing task based on an AP Language and Composition-style prompt, and essays were evaluated using AP rubric scores and a coding scheme for knowledge transformation (analysis, evaluation, synthesis, etc.), alongside post-task self-report measures of agency and ownership.

Results showed that Script&Shift generally led to stronger indicators of agency and higher knowledge-transformation markers than the chat-based interface, especially on analysis, evaluation, and self-reported control/ownership. However, essay quality scores were not clearly different across conditions, and the authors note that the short 1.5-hour treatment may have limited observable effects. This paper does not provide delayed posttests, retention measures, transfer to unaided writing, or outcomes after tool removal; its evidence is immediate, single-session, and based on undergraduate writers rather than high-school students.

finding.finding_summary: The process-oriented Script&Shift condition produced stronger writing-process outcomes than the chat-based LLM on several knowledge-transformation subscales. In particular, Script&Shift significantly outperformed chat and/or standard writing on Analysis, Evaluation, and Knowledge-coded markers in the final essays, but overall AP rubric essay quality did not differ clearly across conditions.
finding.measure: Source-based argumentative essay writing quality and knowledge-transformation coding (AP Language rubric; analysis/evaluation/knowledge markers)
finding.std_deviation: Script&Shift AP score σ=2.75; Standard σ=1.82; ChatLLM σ=2.59

finding.finding_summary: Script&Shift improved students’ self-reported writing agency relative to both the chat-based condition and the standard interface. On 7-point Likert items, Script&Shift showed higher perceived control during writing (M=6.59 vs. 3.34 chat; 5.83 standard), greater content satisfaction (M=6.34 vs. 2.83 chat; 5.50 standard), and more comfort publishing the essay in their own name (M=5.90 vs. 3.21 chat; 4.90 standard).
finding.measure: Post-test self-report agency items: perceived control, satisfaction with writing, comfort publishing under own name, original voice, AI not replacing writing

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates knowledge transformation, a metacognitive/durable-skill construct, and finds the process-oriented interface supported deeper cognitive processing than the chat-based assistant. Script&Shift showed significantly higher analytical and evaluative transformation markers, and interface use correlated moderately with knowledge transformation (r=0.61), suggesting more active engagement was associated with deeper processing.
finding.measure: Knowledge-transformation coding of essays; correlation between interface transactions and knowledge-transformation markers
finding.std_deviation: Interface transactions σ=5.95; knowledge-transformation markers σ=7.40

finding.finding_summary: The study did not directly measure productivity gains in a task-efficiency sense beyond within-session interaction counts and completion time context, but it does report usage patterns and task completion. Script&Shift participants made more interface transactions on average (M=14.43, σ=5.95), and the authors note a median task completion time of 1 hour 13 minutes, but they do not present a causal efficiency comparison showing that one condition was faster or more productive than another.
finding.measure: Interface transactions and task completion time

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT as an AI L2 Teaching Support: A Case Study of an EFL Teacher
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how one EFL teacher integrated ChatGPT into language teaching over seven months and how effective the tool was for supporting classroom practice. The authors are especially interested in the teacher’s prompt-crafting strategies, how she validated ChatGPT’s outputs, and what kinds of teaching tasks the tool could support.

The study is an exploratory single instrumental case study of a private language-school teacher in Spain who taught mixed-age EFL groups (children, teenagers, and adults) at levels A1-C1. Data came from the teacher’s ChatGPT history, lesson plans, and a semi-structured interview. ChatGPT was used for lesson planning, in-class implementation, and assessment, including vocabulary and writing activities, lesson sequencing, rubrics, feedback, and self-assessment tasks.

The main conclusions are that ChatGPT can support EFL teaching in practical ways, especially when teachers develop prompt-crafting skill, adapt prompts to age and level, and critically verify outputs. The teacher reported that more specific prompts produced better outputs over time, and that the tool helped save time, diversify materials, and increase student engagement. However, the paper is a single qualitative case and does not provide causal evidence of learning gains beyond the teacher’s reported experience and illustrative examples.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was used extensively for writing-related tasks, including composing prompts, correcting student compositions, generating writing tasks, and providing feedback/rubrics. The teacher reported that these uses helped refine student writing and supported assessment of written work; in one example, ChatGPT’s assessment of an FCE essay differed from the official Cambridge scoring by 3 points across categories, indicating usefulness but also limitations in accuracy.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported support for writing instruction and assessment; comparison of ChatGPT scoring with Cambridge FCE writing scales

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was used for speaking and interactional practice, including role-play, simulated conversations, real-time Q&A, and speaking prompts in class. The teacher reported increased student participation and enthusiasm when incorporating ChatGPT’s suggestions, but the evidence is qualitative and based on observation rather than measured fluency gains.
finding.measure: Teacher observation of classroom speaking practice and participation
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher; mixed groups of students

finding.finding_summary: The teacher reported that ChatGPT-supported activities increased student engagement, enthusiasm, and participation, especially when materials were tailored to age and proficiency level. The paper presents these as perceived classroom benefits rather than measured motivational outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student engagement and enthusiasm
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher; classroom observations across multiple groups

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that effective use of ChatGPT depended on prompt crafting, critical thinking, and students’ ability to cross-check and evaluate outputs. The teacher used increasingly specific prompts over seven months and explicitly taught students to review information critically, indicating that the tool supported metacognitive and critical-thinking practices.
finding.measure: Teacher prompt evolution; instructional use of cross-checking, fact-checking, and critical review
finding.study_size: n=1 teacher; multiple prompt instances and interview data

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT substantially reduced the teacher’s workload by helping with lesson planning, material creation, activity generation, grading, and feedback. The teacher described it as an invaluable time saver and noted that it allowed her to focus more on personalized feedback, although no quantitative workload measure was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported time saving and workload reduction in planning, materials, and assessment

paper_profiles.title: From Consumers to Critical Users: Prompty, an AI Literacy Tool for High School Students
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI-24 (Proceedings of the Thirty-Eighth AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging need for AI literacy tools that help high school students use large language models (LLMs) critically and effectively, especially for writing tasks. The authors introduce Prompty, a web-based classroom tool designed around three main learning supports: contrasting cases (three LLM outputs shown side by side), prompt guides (Role, Context, Task scaffolds), and a limited number of tries to encourage intentional use.

Prompty was co-designed with a high school English Language Arts teacher and pilot-tested in two high school ELA classes in California over a three-week writing project. Students used Prompty on laptops to generate and compare AI-written responses, iteratively revise prompts, and complete a creative writing assignment aligned with course goals and state ELA standards. The paper reports primarily qualitative, preliminary evidence from the teacher's post-implementation reflections rather than student test scores or controlled outcome data.

The main conclusion is that the tool appeared usable in classroom settings and may support both AI literacy and disciplinary writing goals. The teacher reported that multiple responses, prompt scaffolds, and usage limits helped students compare outputs, reflect on prompting, and use AI more intentionally. The authors argue that Prompty shows promise as a classroom-ready AI literacy resource, while noting that more guidance is needed for helping students revise prompts effectively and that broader implementation may require additional teacher support.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot implementation in two high school ELA classes (ages 14-16), the teacher reported that Prompty supported students in composing a creative writing piece using AI-generated responses and in revising writing for specific audiences and purposes. Evidence is preliminary and qualitative rather than based on a controlled comparison; the paper does not report effect sizes or standardized writing outcomes.
finding.measure: Creative writing performance and teacher-observed writing process

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on students' prompt engineering, comparison of multiple AI outputs, and evaluation of generated text, which the teacher described as requiring higher-order thinking, human judgment, and intentional revision. The implementation was reported to help students compare and evaluate outputs, though the evidence is qualitative and preliminary with no numerical effect estimate.
finding.measure: Prompt revision, comparison/evaluation of AI outputs, and teacher perceptions of critical thinking

finding.finding_summary: The limited-tries feature was intended to promote mindful, reflective use of the tool, and the teacher said it created a helpful structure that encouraged students to pause and think between attempts. The paper suggests increased intentionality and reflection during use, but reports no direct student self-report or behavioral outcome measure.
finding.measure: Teacher-observed intentionality, reflection, and mindful use

finding.finding_summary: The teacher described Prompty's interface as simple, clean, and effective for students to use, and suggested that its ease of use could make it easier for more teachers to adapt and implement in classrooms. This is an implementation-oriented claim rather than a measured productivity outcome, and no quantitative workload or time-savings data are reported.
finding.measure: Usability and teacher perceived adoptability

paper_profiles.title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines university students’ perceptions of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education, with attention to familiarity, willingness to use, perceived benefits, and concerns. The authors frame the study using Biggs’ 3P model and user-acceptance ideas, arguing that student perceptions of AI technologies may shape learning approaches and outcomes, and that understanding these perceptions can help institutions design more effective guidance and implementation strategies.

The study used an online survey of 399 undergraduate and postgraduate students from six universities in Hong Kong across a range of disciplines. The instrument included 26 Likert-scale items and three open-ended questions, and the analysis combined descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, t-tests, and thematic analysis of responses. Findings show generally positive attitudes toward GenAI: students viewed it as useful for personalized support, writing and brainstorming, and research tasks, while also expressing concerns about inaccuracy, privacy, plagiarism, over-reliance, and broader impacts on skills, careers, and values.

The paper does not test a generative-AI writing intervention or implementation feature experimentally, and it does not provide direct evidence about teacher mediation, task type, dosage, prompt design, or classroom norms as moderators of outcomes. Instead, it offers perception-level evidence suggesting that prior use and knowledge are associated with greater willingness to use GenAI, and it argues that policy guidance, AI literacy, and human oversight are important for responsible integration in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived GenAI as helpful for writing support, including grammar correction, paraphrasing, feedback, and idea generation. In the survey, willingness items related to assignment support and personalized feedback were moderately positive (e.g., means of 3.61 for personalized feedback and 3.74 for unique insights on a 5-point scale), and qualitative comments explicitly described ChatGPT as a writing assistant for improving written work.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived usefulness for writing, paraphrasing, grammar, brainstorming, and feedback on assignments

finding.finding_summary: Students expressed concern that GenAI could weaken higher-order skills such as critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving through over-reliance. This concern was reflected in the survey item about over-reliance (mean=2.85 to 2.89 on a 5-point scale, indicating some concern) and in open-ended responses that warned AI might reduce independent thinking and idea generation.
finding.measure: Self-reported concerns about critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, and over-reliance on GenAI

finding.finding_summary: Students saw GenAI as an efficiency tool that could save time, provide 24/7 support, and reduce workload for routine academic tasks. Quantitatively, the item that GenAI can help save time had a high mean of 4.20 (SD=0.82), and qualitative responses highlighted rapid answers, help with literature searching, summarising, formatting, and administrative work.
finding.measure: Self-reported perceived time-saving, round-the-clock support, and help with repetitive academic tasks

finding.finding_summary: Students viewed GenAI as something institutions should regulate and guide, but they also worried about uncertain policy and governance. The paper reports recurring concerns about academic integrity, privacy, and the lack of institutional guidance, and it argues that universities should develop policies, workshops, and safeguards for responsible implementation.
finding.measure: Self-reported concerns and recommendations regarding institutional policy, governance, ethics, and academic integrity

paper_profiles.title: What if the devil is my guardian angel: ChatGPT as a case study of using chatbots in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early discourse and user experiences around ChatGPT in education, with a focus on concerns and opportunities rather than measuring learning effects. The authors frame ChatGPT as a representative generative AI chatbot and ask what concerns arise when it is used in educational settings. To address this, they use a three-stage qualitative instrumental case study: (1) social network analysis and sentiment analysis of 2,330 English-language tweets about ChatGPT and education, (2) content analysis of 19 publicly posted interviews with early adopters (students, educators, developers, and AI freelancers), and (3) hands-on user experience testing by three educators over one week across 10 educational scenarios.

The paper does not study a K-12 intervention or compare student outcomes under different implementation conditions. Instead, it documents perceived issues such as cheating, response inaccuracies, privacy risks, manipulation, and inconsistent output quality, along with possible benefits such as instructional support, quiz generation, and workload reduction. Several scenarios suggest that prompt wording and user interaction style can change ChatGPT’s responses, and the authors argue that users need stronger prompt skills and that educators need new teaching philosophies and responsible-AI guidelines.

For the specific sub-question about implementation moderators, the paper offers only indirect evidence. It shows that the same prompt can yield different answers for different educators and that more specific wording can improve outputs, but it does not test teacher mediation, dosage, classroom norms, or task-type moderation in a high-school sample. The study is therefore best understood as exploratory and descriptive rather than as outcome evidence about generative AI writing assistants in high school.

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT can support writing-related tasks such as essay drafting, citation formatting, and generating learning content, but it can also facilitate cheating, produce inaccurate or generic text, and undermine authentic writing practice. Evidence comes from illustrative user-experience scenarios rather than outcome measures; no controlled comparison, effect size, or sample size for writing performance was reported.
finding.measure: Illustrative writing-task outputs, essay similarity/AI-detection examples, citation generation, and qualitative perceptions of writing support
finding.study_size: n=3 educators (user scenarios); additional qualitative interviewees n=19

finding.finding_summary: The study repeatedly highlights critical thinking, prompt skill, and question formulation as important for getting useful results from ChatGPT, while also warning that reliance on the tool may reduce students’ critical thinking and encourage laziness. The evidence is qualitative and scenario-based: different prompts produced different answers, and users reported needing more precise questions to elicit better responses, but no quantitative effect estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes and scenario-based prompt-response comparisons related to critical thinking and prompt skill

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that ChatGPT can lessen instructional workload, provide immediate feedback, and help educators prepare materials, quizzes, and outlines. At the same time, the paper notes that inconsistent or inaccurate outputs can make teachers’ duties more complicated, so the efficiency benefit appears conditional rather than uniform. No quantitative productivity outcome was measured.
finding.measure: Perceived teacher workload reduction and task-support utility in interviews and scenario testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may require new teaching philosophies, policy guidance, and institutional responses because of concerns about cheating, privacy, fairness, and responsible use. It does not evaluate policy outcomes empirically, but it does show that the same prompt can produce different outputs for different users, raising fairness and equity concerns relevant to institutional adoption.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of policy/ethics concerns, fairness observations from repeated prompts, and public sentiment around school adoption

paper_profiles.title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (no human participants; ChatGPT outputs applied to Year 7 science examples and science education generally)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory self-study examines how ChatGPT responds to prompts about science education and how it might be used by educators as a pedagogical and research tool. The paper asks three questions: how ChatGPT answers science-education questions, how educators might use it to design teaching materials, and how the author experienced using ChatGPT in the research process. Rather than evaluating student learning outcomes, the study focuses on the content, quality, and limitations of AI-generated responses.

The author prompts ChatGPT on topics such as effective science teaching, whether to use teacher-centred or student-centred approaches, how to respond when a student is failing science, and how to create a 5Es unit, rubric, and quiz for Year 7 renewable/non-renewable energy. The outputs are compared qualitatively with research literature and used to reflect on the usefulness of ChatGPT for lesson planning, scaffolding, and drafting. The paper argues that ChatGPT can be a helpful starting point for generating science teaching resources and may support teacher productivity, but educators must critically evaluate outputs because they can be generic, insufficiently grounded in evidence, and may reflect bias or unsupported claims.

The paper concludes that generative AI is promising but should not be treated as an epistemic authority or a replacement for teacher expertise. It emphasizes context, critical thinking, and responsible use, especially in assessment design and classroom implementation. The study offers implementation-oriented reflections rather than direct causal evidence about effects on student outcomes, teacher mediation, or writing-assistant impacts in high school.

finding.finding_summary: The paper qualitatively examines ChatGPT-generated science education content, including a Year 7 5Es unit, a quiz, and responses about effective science teaching. The outputs often aligned with themes in the research literature, but the author argues they were generic, insufficiently evidenced, and required substantial teacher judgment and contextual refinement.
finding.measure: Qualitative comparison of ChatGPT responses to science education literature and pedagogical frameworks

finding.finding_summary: The study directly analyzes ChatGPT-generated teaching resources for Year 7 science, including a 5Es unit plan, rubric, and multiple-choice quiz on renewable and non-renewable energy sources. The paper concludes that ChatGPT can generate usable draft materials, but the outputs need teacher editing and contextual adaptation to be instructionally sound.
finding.measure: Qualitative evaluation of AI-generated unit plan, rubric, and quiz materials

finding.finding_summary: The author reports that ChatGPT was useful for editing, rewriting sentences, and generating instructional drafts, suggesting potential productivity gains for educators and researchers. However, the paper does not quantify time saved; it presents this as a qualitative observation that the tool can help move beyond a blank page and clarify phrasing.
finding.measure: Qualitative reflections on editing, drafting, and resource generation utility

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT may support critical thinking by prompting educators and students to evaluate AI output, question evidence, and consider bias and context. At the same time, the author warns that the model can present unsupported claims as authoritative, so critical evaluation remains essential.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of AI output quality, evidence grounding, and bias implications

finding.finding_summary: In discussing prompts about a student failing in science, the paper highlights supportive classroom responses such as additional help, collaboration with guardians, and encouraging learning environments. This is not an intervention study, but the author presents these responses as potentially supportive of student motivation and persistence.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of supportive pedagogy and classroom climate in ChatGPT responses

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; discusses primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional education broadly)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper surveys the educational opportunities and risks of large language models, with a focus on ChatGPT-like systems. It asks how these models may support learning and teaching across schooling levels and what safeguards are needed for responsible use. The paper is not an empirical intervention study; rather, it synthesizes early applications and offers a conceptual framework for opportunities, challenges, and mitigation strategies.

The authors discuss likely uses for students and teachers, including personalized feedback, writing support, quiz generation, tutoring, lesson planning, assessment, and professional development. They also review risks such as bias, overreliance, plagiarism, privacy, difficulty distinguishing machine-generated text, and access inequities, arguing that human oversight, critical thinking, verification, and clear governance are essential.

For the specific sub-question on implementation features moderating generative AI writing assistants in high school, this paper provides only indirect guidance, not direct outcome evidence. It notes that teacher mediation, curriculum alignment, critical-thinking prompts, and hybrid human-AI approaches are important for responsible use, but these are presented as recommendations rather than empirically tested moderators.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models can reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, personalized feedback, grading, and generation of exercises and prompts. However, these claims are conceptual and illustrative rather than based on an empirical comparison, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher workload / productivity (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that large language models may support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking when used with human guidance and curriculum supports. At the same time, it warns that overreliance on model-generated answers could weaken students’ independent reasoning and investigation skills. These claims are not supported by empirical outcome data in this paper.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, fact-checking (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution of the paper is its discussion of governance, privacy, fairness, copyright, sustainability, and responsible integration of large language models into educational systems. The paper recommends institutional policies, human oversight, transparency, and training for educators, but these are normative recommendations rather than measured outcomes.
finding.measure: policy / governance / institutional implementation (conceptual discussion)

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th), Middle School, High School, Undergraduate, Adult
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
