For BERT, accuracy improves from 80.70% to 81.14% and macro-F1 from 60.01 to 62.38; RoBERTa declines slightly (80.70/61.98 to 79.39/58.88), while GPT-2 and LSTM are unchanged.
finding.measure: Automated essay scoring accuracy and macro-F1 on student essays

finding.finding_summary: The system is designed to make essay grading more efficient and usable for instructors by providing real-time, rubric-level feedback and allowing human-in-the-loop correction of concept scores with instant grade recalculation. The paper does not report workload reduction statistics, but it positions the tool as a practical workflow aid for classroom and grade-appeal settings.
finding.measure: Real-time grading workflow, concept-level feedback, and human-in-the-loop correction capability

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims the rubric-aligned feedback can help students understand weaknesses in concepts such as organization, evidence use, and critical thinking, which are durable writing and metacognitive skills. However, this is asserted through system design and illustrative examples rather than measured student outcomes.
finding.measure: Rubric-aligned concept scores for writing dimensions such as critical thinking, organization, and evidence use

paper_profiles.title: Hey AI Can You Grade My Essay?: Automatic Essay Grading
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatic essay grading (AEG), asking whether a collaborative deep learning architecture can score student essays more accurately than several standard machine learning and neural baselines. The authors propose a Collaborative Deep Learning Network (CDLN) that combines a recursive neural network for sentence structure, a convolutional neural network for idea/content, and an LSTM to fuse these representations into a final essay score.

The study uses the ASAP Automated Essay Scoring dataset, which contains nearly 13,000 essays written by students in grades 7 through 10 across 8 prompts. The paper compares CDLN against BERT, LSTM, RNN, ANN, and SVM using accuracy, Pearson correlation, and quadratic weighted kappa, and reports that CDLN performs best overall (average accuracy 0.8550, PCC 0.7545, QWK 0.7036). The authors also test robustness by paraphrasing 1,000 essays with Quillbot and find the model’s scores remain close before and after paraphrasing (reported MSE-like difference 0.34), suggesting the system is relatively stable to surface-level rewording.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed CDLN model improved automatic essay scoring performance on student writing compared with several baselines. On the ASAP dataset (roughly n=13,000 essays from grades 7-10), CDLN achieved the best overall results with average accuracy 0.8550, Pearson correlation 0.7545, and QWK 0.7036, outperforming BERT (0.8268/0.7390/0.6779) and all other compared models.
finding.measure: Automatic essay scoring performance on essay-writing prompts, evaluated with accuracy, Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC), and quadratic weighted kappa (QWK)

paper_profiles.title: Can Large Language Models Make the Grade? An Empirical Study Evaluating LLMs Ability to Mark Short Answer Questions in K-12 Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models, especially GPT-4, can accurately grade short-answer student responses in K-12 settings. The motivation is practical: formative assessment is valuable but expensive and time-consuming to score manually, so the authors investigate whether LLMs can support low-stakes assessment at scale.

The study uses a newly assembled dataset of 1,710 real student responses to 12 open-ended short-answer questions in Science and History drawn from the Carousel quizzing platform. Qualified teachers produced ground-truth labels, and the authors compared human rater agreement with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 under zero-shot and few-shot prompting. GPT-4 with few-shot prompting achieved the best model performance (Cohen’s kappa = 0.70), close to human agreement (kappa = 0.75), with relatively stable performance across subject, grade band, and question difficulty.

The paper concludes that LLMs may be useful for low-stakes formative assessment in K-12 education and could reduce teacher workload substantially. The authors estimate that marking the dataset manually would have taken at least 11 hours, versus about 2 hours using GPT-4 after script setup. The paper is about automated scoring rather than student writing support, so it provides evidence about operational efficiency and assessment feasibility, but not about direct learning gains, writing development, or subgroup effects for specific student populations.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 substantially reduced marking time for 1,710 short-answer responses while maintaining near-human agreement. The authors estimate manual grading would have taken at least 11 hours, whereas the GPT-4 workflow took about 2 hours after script setup, with model-human agreement at Cohen’s kappa = 0.70 versus human-human agreement of 0.75.
finding.measure: Time required to mark short-answer responses; model-human agreement on correctness labels

paper_profiles.title: Grade Guard: A Smart System for Short Answer Automated Grading
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of unreliable large-language-model (LLM) scoring for automated short-answer grading (ASAG). The authors argue that while LLMs can reduce grading workload, they can also produce inconsistent or inaccurate scores on subjective or partially correct responses, creating a need for confidence-aware grading methods before deployment.

To address this, the paper proposes Grade Guard, a framework with three components: a context-aware prompt, a creativity regulator that tunes temperature to reduce random variation, and an indecisiveness/self-reflection mechanism that estimates uncertainty via repeated scoring and standard deviation. If the model’s indecisiveness score exceeds a threshold, the response is sent to a human evaluator. The system is tested on the Mohler ASAG dataset, which contains 87 introductory computer science questions and 2,273 responses from 31 university students.

Across four LLMs (Upstage Solar Pro, Upstage Solar Mini, Gemini 1.5 Flash, and GPT-4o mini), the framework reduces RMSE relative to unguarded model outputs and reduces large grading errors in several cases. The paper concludes that temperature tuning plus confidence-based rechecking can improve ASAG reliability, but it is still limited by domain-specific data scarcity, model cost, and remaining variability in confidence thresholds.

finding.finding_summary: Grade Guard reduced grading error while enabling more automated checking of short answers, indicating improved efficiency for educators compared with fully manual grading or unguided LLM scoring. On the Mohler dataset (n=2,273 responses from 31 students), the best settings reduced RMSE by 19.16% for Upstage Solar Pro, 23.64% for Upstage Solar Mini, 4.00% for Gemini 1.5 Flash, and 10.20% for GPT-4o mini. The paper also reports that the system could automatically handle 2,085–2,416 confident instances depending on model/settings.
finding.measure: RMSE on short-answer grading; count of confident instances automatically graded vs sent for human review

paper_profiles.title: Complex Discontinuity Designs Using Covariates: Impact of School Grade Retention on Later Life Outcomes in Chile
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to estimate causal effects when treatment assignment is determined by complex discontinuity rules with multiple running variables and cutoffs. Methodologically, the authors propose a framework for complex discontinuity designs that uses observed covariates to establish local strong ignorability, allowing matching, weighting, regression-assisted estimation, and neighborhood selection around the cutoff region.

The empirical case study is grade retention in Chile, using administrative records for 1,377,089 students followed from 2002 to 2016. The treatment is being retained in elementary school under one of two rule-based assignment mechanisms that depend on school grades; outcomes include later school grades, future grade retention, school dropout, and juvenile crime. The authors select a neighborhood around the cutoffs using covariate-balance tests and then estimate neighborhood average treatment effects within that discontinuity neighborhood.

The main findings are that grade retention appears to improve subsequent school grades in the short run, with an estimated increase of 0.19 points one year later (95% CI [0.16, 0.21]) and 0.05 points four years later (95% CI [0.01, 0.08]). Retention also reduces the likelihood of future grade retention (estimated effect -0.104), but shows essentially no effect on dropping out of school or being prosecuted for a juvenile crime (crime effect estimate 0.006; dropout effect 0.002). The paper also reports that the crime and dropout null findings are somewhat robust to hidden-bias sensitivity checks, while the grade-gain effects diminish over time.

finding.finding_summary: Grade retention increased subsequent average school grades in the short run among students in the matched discontinuity neighborhood. Using regression-assisted weighting, the authors report an effect of 0.19 points one year after retention (95% CI [0.16, 0.21]) and 0.05 points four years later (95% CI [0.01, 0.08]).
finding.measure: Average school grades in 2008-2011 after 2007 retention/pass decision

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames grade retention as potentially affecting motivation and self-esteem, but it does not directly measure these constructs. The closest studied educational persistence outcome is future grade retention, for which the estimated effect is negative: retained students were less likely to repeat another grade later (bτ_NATE = -0.104, one-sided p < 0.001) in the matched sample.
finding.measure: Future grade retention (binary)

finding.finding_summary: The study finds no evidence that grade retention affects juvenile crime or school dropout in the selected neighborhood, suggesting limited downstream institutional impact on these endpoints. The estimated effect on juvenile crime was 0.006 (p=0.229) and on dropping out of school was 0.002 (p=0.379), both based on 1,141 matched pairs.
finding.measure: Juvenile crime prosecution and school dropout (binary outcomes)

paper_profiles.title: Sorting and Grading
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical model of how a planner should sort students into schools and choose grading rules when employers observe only school attended and grade received, not ability, effort, or productive value. The central question is whether it is socially optimal to track students by ability and, if so, how grading should differ across schools to maximize effort and social welfare.

In the model, students’ productive value depends on their ability and effort, employers infer productivity from school and grade, and grading rules can be made more or less informative. The authors show that optimal systems generally have either one pooled tier or two tiers: if students are sufficiently heterogeneous, high-ability students are separated from low-ability students, top-tier schools use a lenient grading rule, and bottom-tier schools use a tough grading rule. When all schools use the same grading rule, pooling students raises total effort; when students can self-select into schools, incentive compatibility without transfers collapses the system to a single tier, while transfers allow a constrained-optimal two-tier structure similar to the planner-controlled case.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main result is a theoretical characterization of optimal school-system design under tracking and grading. It shows that socially optimal systems are either single-tier (pooled) or two-tier, and when two-tiered, top-tier schools use lenient grading (G⋆) while bottom-tier schools use tough grading (G⋆). In the self-selection extension, incentive compatibility without transfers implies a single-tier structure, whereas with transfers constrained-optimal systems can still be two-tiered.
finding.measure: Optimal school system structure under alternative assignment and incentive-compatibility constraints

paper_profiles.title: Machine Learning Grade Prediction Using Students’ Grades and Demographics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of identifying secondary-school students at risk of failing or repeating grades in a resource-constrained educational context. The authors argue that early prediction can help schools allocate scarce support resources more effectively and reduce repetition-related costs.

The study proposes a unified machine learning framework that jointly handles two tasks: classification of pass/fail outcomes and regression prediction of continuous final grades. Using institutional records from 4,424 secondary school students collected over 2008–2019, the authors evaluate six classical models: Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest for classification, plus Linear Regression, Decision Tree Regressor, and Random Forest Regressor for grade prediction. Inputs include first-semester academic records and demographic variables such as gender, age, marital status, parental education, occupation, scholarship status, special needs, debtor status, and attendance type.

Results suggest that interpretable models performed strongly in this dataset. Logistic Regression achieved about 94.6% classification accuracy, while Linear Regression achieved an R² of about 0.705 for grade prediction, with tuned Decision Tree and Random Forest models also performing competitively. The paper concludes that a lightweight, interpretable early-warning system can help schools identify at-risk students and target interventions such as tutoring or remediation, though the evidence is correlational rather than causal and does not evaluate implemented interventions.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that machine learning models could predict secondary students’ pass/fail outcomes and continuous grades with strong accuracy from academic and demographic features. Logistic Regression reached 0.945824 accuracy, precision 0.951087, recall 0.983146, and F1 0.966851; Linear Regression achieved R²=0.704769 with MAE=0.080822 and RMSE=0.152431 on grade prediction using n=4,424 student records.
finding.measure: Pass/fail classification accuracy and continuous final-grade prediction (MAE, RMSE, MSE, R²)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the predictive framework can function as an early-warning system for schools and administrators to identify at-risk students and allocate support resources more efficiently. No causal deployment study was conducted, but the authors report that the model could support interventions such as tutoring, remediation, and annual monitoring within a school management information system.
finding.measure: Predicted failure probability and implementation-oriented risk scoring for institutional decision support

paper_profiles.title: Embracing AI in Education: Understanding the Surge in Large Language Model Use by Secondary Students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how middle and high school students in the United States are using large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT for schoolwork, and what students think about their usefulness, risks, and school policies. The authors aim to address a gap in the literature on secondary students’ real-world adoption of generative AI by surveying a large sample of students across grades 6–12.

The study uses a survey of 306 middle and high school students recruited through an online platform, Google Forms, tutoring programs, and social media. Respondents reported whether they had used LLMs, how often they used them, what subjects they used them for, how useful they found them, and their views on school restrictions and ethical concerns. The paper also compares usage across grades, school types, states with different technology indices, and paid versus free users.

Findings show that LLM use is widespread among secondary students: 71% had used an LLM at least once, and usage was similar across grades 7–12. Students used LLMs across subjects including writing, math, history, and foreign languages, but many noted concerns about hallucinations, inaccuracies, and possible overreliance. The survey also suggests access gaps: students in more technologically advanced states and those who can pay for premium models reported higher usage and more positive perceptions. The paper concludes with design suggestions for student-oriented LLMs, including better safeguards, personalization, and AI classroom concepts, while noting that the data are self-reported and may overrepresent students with internet access.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs for language arts and writing tasks, and 57% of LLM users said LLMs were useful for writing text. However, open-ended responses also raised concerns that increased reliance could weaken fundamental skills and that models sometimes provide inaccurate or hallucinated outputs. The evidence is survey-based and self-reported (n=306).
finding.measure: Self-reported LLM use for writing/language arts and perceived usefulness for writing text

finding.finding_summary: The survey found that 28% of students used LLMs for math, and 43% of LLM users found them useful for math and STEM questions. At the same time, students reported that LLMs can produce incorrect answers and have weaker mathematical abilities than open-ended language tasks, suggesting benefits are tempered by accuracy concerns.
finding.measure: Self-reported LLM use for math and perceived usefulness for math/STEM questions

finding.finding_summary: Students reported using LLMs in history and foreign language classes, and the paper notes that they use LLMs across all school subjects. Students’ feedback was mixed: some found the tools useful for simplifying complex topics, while others reported hallucinations in historical contexts and incorrect answers. The evidence comes from survey responses rather than direct performance measures (n=306).
finding.measure: Self-reported LLM use across non-literacy subjects, especially history and foreign languages

finding.finding_summary: The study measured students’ ethical concern about using LLMs and school-policy restrictiveness, finding average ratings of 2.83/5 for ethical concern and 3.48/5 for policy severity. Despite these concerns, usage remained high, and 2% of students who rated ethical concern as 5 still used LLMs at least weekly, suggesting that ethical concern does not necessarily prevent use.
finding.measure: Self-reported ethical concern and perceived school policy severity regarding LLM use

finding.finding_summary: Open-ended responses indicated concern that increased reliance on LLMs may lower students’ fundamental skills, and the authors discuss possible effects on critical thinking through model design suggestions. However, the paper does not directly measure critical thinking, metacognition, or writing independence, so the evidence here is indirect and based on student perceptions (n=306).
finding.measure: Self-reported perceptions of reliance and potential skill erosion

finding.finding_summary: The survey found that LLM usage persists despite generally restrictive school policies, with an average policy severity rating of 3.48/5. The paper also reports demographic gaps: 80.2% usage in the five most technologically advanced states versus 64.3% in the rest, and 76.7% usage among private school students versus 71.3% among public school students, suggesting institutional and access disparities.
finding.measure: Self-reported school policy severity and LLM usage by state technology ranking and school type

paper_profiles.title: Happy Are Those Who Grade without Seeing: A Multi-Task Learning Approach to Grade Essays Using Gaze Behaviour
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether reader gaze behaviour can be used as a useful auxiliary signal for automatic essay scoring, especially when gaze data are scarce or unavailable at test time. The authors argue that gaze features can be learned jointly with essay scoring in a multi-task learning framework, reducing the need to collect expensive eye-tracking data for every essay set.

The study uses the ASAP automated essay scoring dataset, focusing gaze collection on 48 source-dependent essays from four prompts and then testing transfer to four additional unseen prompts. Eight adult annotators read and scored essays while their eye movements were recorded with an EyeLink 1000 tracker; the model learned both essay score prediction and gaze-feature prediction (Dwell Time, First Fixation Duration, IsRegression, Run Count, Skip). The main conclusion is that adding gaze behaviour improves quadratic weighted kappa over strong neural baselines on both seen and unseen essay sets, with statistically significant gains in several prompts.

Although the paper is about essay scoring rather than generative AI writing assistants, it is relevant to writing assessment because it suggests that reading-behaviour signals can improve grading models and help detect essay quality features such as errors and off-topic content. The work does not study K-12 students directly, nor does it examine risks like misuse, dependence, academic integrity, self-regulation, or writing independence related to AI writing assistants.

finding.finding_summary: Adding learned gaze behaviour to source-dependent automatic essay scoring improved performance over strong neural baselines. On the four prompts with gaze data, Co-Attention+Gaze achieved mean QWK=0.788 versus 0.780 for co-attention alone, with prompt-level gains such as 0.698 vs 0.689 on Prompt 3 and 0.821 vs 0.813 on Prompt 6; improvements were reported as statistically significant at p<0.05.
finding.measure: Automatic essay scoring performance measured by Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK)
finding.study_size: n=48 gaze-rated essays for training gaze signals; approximately n=12,976 essays in the ASAP dataset overall

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that gaze behaviour can be predicted and then used without collecting gaze data for every target essay set, which reduces dependence on expensive eye-tracking collection at deployment. On unseen essay sets, augmenting training with the 48 gaze-labelled essays improved mean QWK from 0.738 (Only Prompt) and 0.747 (Extra Essays) to 0.754 (Extra Essays + Gaze), with significant gains on Prompts 7 and 8.
finding.measure: Essay scoring model performance on unseen prompts when augmenting training with gaze-labelled essays
finding.study_size: n=48 gaze-rated essays used as auxiliary data; 4 unseen prompts

paper_profiles.title: Integrating LLMs for Grading and Appeal Resolution in Computer Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the use of large language models (LLMs) in an AI-powered assessment tool (AI-PAT) for grading and appeal resolution in an undergraduate Object-Oriented Programming course. The authors ask whether LLMs such as ChatGPT and Gemini can grade programming-related exam responses consistently, how their scores compare with human graders, and whether LLMs can support a transparent appeal process for student objections to grades.

The system was deployed across nine quizzes plus midterm and final assessments for roughly 102 registered second-year computer science undergraduates, with analysis focused on about 73 final exam submissions for model comparison, 30 human-rated papers for reliability checks, and 185 grade appeals across approximately 850 evaluated papers. The workflow included scanning handwritten work, having students transcribe answers into digital forms, using LLMs to grade responses with rubrics and prompts, and allowing students to submit appeals that were then reviewed by LLMs.

Results show high correlation between ChatGPT and Gemini grading, but meaningful differences in absolute scores and sensitivity to prompts/configuration. Human graders were internally consistent but disagreed with one another, and the paper reports that 74% of appeals led to grade changes, suggesting that initial AI grading sometimes missed partial correctness or nuanced reasoning. Student feedback was mixed to negative: many valued the speed and detailed feedback, but trust and fairness concerns were strong, and most students did not want AI-PAT used for future assessments. The authors conclude that LLM-based grading can improve scalability and feedback, but requires rubrics, human oversight, and appeal mechanisms to support fairness and trust.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI-PAT scaled grading across over 850 exam submissions and handled 185 student appeals, indicating substantial automation of a labor-intensive assessment workflow. The authors argue that LLM-based grading reduced manual workload and sped up feedback delivery, while still requiring human review for contested cases.
finding.measure: Number of exam submissions and appeals processed; grading workflow scalability and feedback delivery

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that integrating LLMs into grading created institutional process changes, including rubric-based AI grading, student appeal handling, and human oversight checkpoints. However, the authors also report trust, fairness, and transparency concerns, and the need for clearer governance around grading decisions and appeals.
finding.measure: Appeal resolution outcomes, student survey responses on fairness/trust, and workflow implementation in a course setting
finding.study_size: n=102 registered students; n=185 appeals; n=49 end-of-semester survey respondents

finding.finding_summary: In the object-oriented programming exam context, ChatGPT and Gemini grading scores were strongly correlated overall (total score Pearson r=0.909, Spearman r=0.920; n=73 final exam submissions), suggesting similar ranking behavior. At the same time, absolute score differences remained, and 74% of the 185 appeals resulted in changed grades, indicating that the initial automated evaluations were not uniformly accurate for programming responses.
finding.measure: Programming exam grades and rubric-based scoring of code/theory responses
finding.study_size: n=73 final exam submissions for model comparison; n=185 appeals

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests some support for structured reasoning and reflection through the appeal process, since students used appeals to justify answers and challenge rubric-based decisions. However, the evidence is indirect and does not measure durable skills with a validated instrument; instead, it relies on appeal behavior and qualitative student responses.
finding.measure: Student appeals, appeal explanations, and challenge/justification of graded answers

paper_profiles.title: School Virus Infection Simulator for Customizing School Schedules During COVID-19
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to reduce within-school COVID-19 transmission while preserving face-to-face instruction. The authors develop the School-Virus-Infection-Simulator (SVIS), an agent-based simulation based on an extended susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed model and Wells-Riley air-transmission assumptions.

The simulator incorporates student lesson schedules, classroom volume, ventilation/air-change rate, and infectability parameters. It is used to compare multiple school scheduling structures, including self-contained versus departmentalized classrooms and several cohorting/hybrid attendance patterns inspired by UNESCO guidance.

The study is framed for teachers and education policymakers, with high-school-relevant discussion noting that some high schools adopt self-contained classrooms to reduce interaction. Across simulated scenarios, higher ventilation generally reduced the maximum number of simultaneously infected students, and schedule design meaningfully changed infection outcomes. The paper concludes that infection risk depends on the interaction between schedule type and classroom structure, not just the percentage of face-to-face lessons; however, it is a simulation study with no real-world student outcomes or AI writing context.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents SVIS as a planning tool that helps educators and policymakers simulate school schedules and compare infection-risk tradeoffs, reducing the need for ad hoc manual scheduling decisions. Although no direct workload or time-saving metric is reported, the authors argue the simulator can support schedule customization and decision-making for school operations.
finding.measure: Simulation-based scheduling decision support / planning utility

finding.finding_summary: The simulator is explicitly designed to inform school scheduling policy during COVID-19 and to help teachers and education policymakers plan safer reopening schedules. The main institutional outcome is reduced maximum simultaneous infections under different schedule and classroom-structure configurations, with no real-world implementation effect estimated.
finding.measure: Maximum number of students infected simultaneously under simulated school schedules
